PREFACE 


Tus book has been my chief occupation since returning from 
India over three years ago. It was conceived while the 
biography of Lanfranc was being written, and the kindly 
reception of that work encouraged me to undertake this larger 
study, especially as the Dean of Winchester, in his review in 
The Church of England Newspaper, suggested that some such 
attempt should be made. 

The Berengarian controversy, which the late Mr. W. H. 
Stevenson described as ‘a morass,’ has not hitherto been 
allowed the dimensions of a volume in English. The book is 
divided into two parts. The first part describes in detail the 
life and work of Berengar, and supplies in the footnotes a 
critical examination of the work of continental scholars. The 
history of modern Berengarian literature begins with Lessing’s 
important discovery of the De Sacra Cena in 1770, which was 
not printed until 1834, when the Vischers issued their edition 
under the general editorship of Neander. ‘The next stage was 
marked by the publication of Berengar’s letters by Sudendorf in 
1850. In 1880 five more letters bearing on the controversy, 
discovered by Edmund Bishop in the British Museum, were 
printed in the Gérresgesellschaft Historisches fahrbuch. Schwabe 
published his penetrating inaugural lecture in 1887, and cleared 
up many points in the Angevine aspect of the controversy. He 
was criticised on some details by Loofs in the Géttingische 
gelehrte Anzeigen of 1888. For example, he over-emphasised 
the relations of Berengar with the court of Anjou as Gfrérer 
had over-stressed the connection with Henry I of France 
in his elaborate Allgemeine Kirchengeschichte IV, Part I 
(1846). Yet Schwabe’s study will remain a permanent 
contribution to the literature of the subject. The first and 


Vill PREFACE 


only complete account of the life and teaching of Berengar 
was published by Schnitzer in 1891. Between 1891 and 
1895 appeared a number of valuable articles by Brécking in 
various German periodicals, which are, however, open to 
criticism on some points. In French no noteworthy biography 
of Berengar has appeared, but a sympathetic examination of his 
teaching was made by Ebersolt in the Revue d'histoire des 
religions (1903). Since Schnitzer’s book was written, the 
publication of the French cartularies has been greatly increased, 
and the cartularies have been used for the first time in the 
following work for details of Berengar’s earlier career. I hope 
that I have removed the doubt created by Schwabe concerning 
Berengar’s original connection with Tours. 

The second part of the book is mainly doctrinal. It begins 
with a sketch of eucharistic theories from Caroling times to the 
eleventh century, leading on to an account of the teaching on 
both sides in the Berengarian dispute. The various contribu- 
tions made by Berengar are treated in their chronological order, 
and are not merged together as in the works of previous writers. 
Then follows the history of eucharistic doctrine in the twelfth 
century, when medieval theory was developed by the orthodox 
writers in the era before the Fourth Lateran Council (1215). It 
is necessary to emphasise this point because in this country the 
opinion appears to exist in some quarters that Transubstantia- 
tion was not the recognised doctrine of the Church until the 
age of the systematists of the thirteenth century. But ‘Thomas 
Aquinas was no more than the last exponent of a theory which 
had been clearly enunciated by Guitmund two centuries earlier. 
The book closes with a sketch of the influence of Berengarian 
teaching upon the English Church. For the doctrine involved 
in the controversy an indispensable work is Geiselmann’s 
Die Eucharistielehre der Vorscholastik (Paderborn, 1926). 

I have attempted to show that a strong Augustinian or 
Evangelical tradition existed all through the early Middle Ages 
until its defeat at Rome in 1079, when Berengar was finally 
condemned. In the present work the account begins approxi- 
mately with the Caroling era, but I have traced the earlier 
influence of Augustine on eucharistic doctrine in a volume 
written by several contributors on the Evangelical doctrine of 


PREFACE 1X 


Holy Communion from New Testament days to the present 
time, which will appear shortly. If the thesis is approved 
it follows that the Evangelical interpretation of eucharistic 
doctrine, put forth by the Reformed Churches, does not merely 
issue from Reformation times, it is no mere teaching of yester- 
day, but has a long and honourable history from the Apostles 
to Berengar. It is necessary to go behind the Reformation in 
order to trace adequately the venerable history of the Evan- 
gelical tradition, and when we do that we find it flourishing in 
the very centuries when Catholicism was in the making. 

Although dealing with a controversial subject, effort has 
been made to avoid a polemical tone, and to avoid giving offence 
to the deep susceptibilities of those who hold other views. My 
obligation to Catholic writers, both ancient and modern, is 
made clear in the footnotes, and I hope that even when tren- 
chant phraseology in defence of Berengar has seemed necessary, 
I may not have treated unfairly honoured names in the history 
of doctrine, and honourable figures in the history of medieval 
Christendom, particularly as my biography of Lanfranc was so 
kindly received by Catholic reviewers. 

The bibliography will indicate the sources from which the 
new book is derived. It has been made as complete as possible 
in view of the abbreviated references in the footnotes. One 
statement in the bibliographies of Vernet (Dictionnaire de 
Théologie Catholique, 11, 1905, col. 742) and of Leclercq 
(Hefele—Leclercq, Histoire des Conciles IV, Part II, 1911, 
p. 1042) needs correction. They both quote a work on 
Berengar by de Crozals, which does not seem to have been 
written. Certainly it cannot be traced by the librarians at 
the Bibliothéque Nationale at Paris. De Crozals deals with 
Berengar in his Lanfranc Archevéque de Cantorbéry (1877), 
and this appears to be the work to which Vernet and Leclercq 
refer. 

I cannot let this book go to press without acknowledging the 
kindness and encouragement received from Professor Whitney 
ever since I became his pupil in Cambridge over twenty years 
ago. Without this incentive it is doubtful whether my historical 
studies would have been maintained. I owe a similar debt 
to Dr. G. T. Lapsley of Trinity College. I have to thank 


x PREFACE 


Archdeacon Lilley for the loan of Berengar’s De Sacra Cena, 
which is not very accessible and ought to be reprinted. He 
allowed me to retain his copy for several years, and the 
work has greatly benefited by constant reference to it. This 
book does not claim to be a complete history of the doctrine of 
the Eucharist or of the Liturgies in the period which it covers. 
Consequently, some matters have received only cursory treat- 
ment. Certain valuable suggestions made by two scholars 
were embodied after the type was set up, and Professor 
A. H. Hamilton’s chapter in the Cambridge Medieval History 
(vol. vi. 1929) did not come into my hands until the work had 
gone to press. Professor Hamilton has written a clear and 
succinct account of medieval doctrine, although some minor 
historical details are not quite in order. I should like to 
thank Messrs. Longmans, Green and Co. not only for promptly 
accepting the work, but for their expedition in passing it 
through the press; and also the compositors and_proof- 
readers of Messrs. Spottiswoode, Ballantyne and Co. 


A. J. MacDOoNaLp. 
May, 1930.

PART I 


CHAPTER I 
EARLY LIFE 


In the first decade of the eleventh century two men were 
born on opposite sides of the Alps who were destined to 
become at first friends and then bitter enemies. ‘They died 
within a year of each other. During his lifetime one of them 
exerted a remarkable influence on the Church in England, 
and if we cannot trace any such direct connection between 
the other and our own Church, yet he belonged to a school of 
interpretation of the doctrine of the Eucharist which, through 
one of its leaders, made a decisive impression upon the 
dogmatic system of the Church in England five centuries 
later. Lanfranc was born at Pavia, and sprang from a dis- 
tinguished family associated with the law.1. Berengar? was 
born probably at Tours,®? and came from a family which had 
won distinction in the Church. 

Berengar was a name famous among the Lombard kings 
of the tenth century.4 It figures among the nobility of

recognised by the world (‘te scilicet a mundo ignorari’), a remark which he 
would hardly have made after 1040, when Berengar was the principal 
archdeacon at Angers (cf. infra, p. 39 f.) and was constantly witnessing 
charters. Drogo says that Berengar was no longer young (‘ nec aetas, que 
iam juventutum excessit’). He must therefore have been on the verge of 
forty when Drogo wrote shortly before 1o4o. 

(6) Another clue is the Evreux MS., the Mivacula de Sancto Nicolao 
(Porée, i. 69), which says that Lanfranc was Berengar’s pupil for a time 
at Tours. Lanfranc left Italy after the end of 1036 (cf. Macdonald, 
Lanfranc, pp. 10, 43 n. 1) and probably went to Tours about 1037, before 
going on to Avranches. This source says that Lanfranc was attracted 
by Berengar’s fame as a teacher, a reputation which a man less than 
thirty-five years of age is not likely to have gained. Porée does not credit 
this report of Lanfranc, but the document comes from the early twelfth 
century. 

(c) The charter quoted by Mabillon, Acta, vi. pt. ii., Praef. 9, refers 
to Berengar as Canon of Tours. It must be dated not later than 1031. 
But it is improbable that Berengar would have been made a member of 
the foundation by this date if he was not born till roro. 

(@) Guitmund, writing c. 1075, referred to him as old (Hurter, xxxviii. 
112: ‘nec tua senectute parceres’). The statement suggests 1005 as the 
latest date for his birth. 

(e) In aletter written to Berengar in 1054, Frollant salutes Berengar 
as the‘ beloved Master’ (Migne, 143, 1369f.; cf. infra, p. 117). Frollant 
was then Bishop of Senlis, and could hardly refer to anyone as ‘ Master’ 
who was born much later than 1000. 

These clues point to a year soon after rooo as the date of Berengar’s 
birth. Cf. Clerval, p. 77.

middle age, the life of the cloister did not preclude a vigorous old age.

It is probable that Berengar received the rudiments of his 
education at the cathedral school of S. Martin’s at Tours,? 
but we hear nothing of the young Berengar until he appears 
at the famous school at Chartres, where Fulbert was Scolasticus 
or Rector, when he was made Bishop of Chartres in 1006.3 
In the first half of the eleventh century the cathedral schools 
at the leading diocesan centres, together with the monasteries, 
were the chief places not only of academic education but of 
the elementary instruction of boys. ‘They fulfilled the functions 
of both grammar school and university of later times. The 
cathedral schools dated from the days of the Merovings and 
were refounded in some cases by Charles the Great, who re- 
vived, even if he did not institute, the Royal School of the 
Palace, and placed it under the supervision of Alcuin of York 
in the year 782.4 The location of the School of the Palace is 
not known, and it has been suggested that it followed the Em- 
peror, together with the rest of theimperial suite.®> If this were 
so, its scholars were given an admirable opportunity of study-

and problems of statecraft. In 789 Charles issued general 
instructions to the bishops and abbots, urging them to found 
schools in which the sons of rich and poor alike were to 
receive instruction in the same class-rooms. ‘These general 
capitularia were followed by letters issued to particular 
bishops or abbots,? with the result that famous schools were 
founded at ‘Tours—where Alcuin taught—at Lyons and 
Orleans, at the abbeys of Fulda, Fontenelle, Corbey, and 
elsewhere.2, Nor was primary education in the parishes over- 
looked. ‘The Emperor commanded the clergy to open village 
schools.? Theodulf, Bishop of Orleans (808-821), attempted 
to organise schools in the parishes of his diocese,* and similar 
instructions were issued by Pope Eugenius II (824-827).5 
During the disturbances caused by the break-up of the 
Carolingian empire and the onset of the Northmen, the 
imperial scheme of education fell to pieces ; but the monastic 
schools suffered more than the cathedral schools. In the time 
of Berengar the latter still flourished at Reims, Laon, Orleans, 
Poitiers, Angers, Tours, and Chartres, and beyond the borders 
of France at Tréves, Metz, Toul, Verdun, and Liége.6 The 
mantle of the great teacher Gerbert of Reims’ had fallen upon 
his pupil Fulbert, at Chartres. Under Fulbert’s liberal regime 
the schools of Chartres heralded the proportions and influence 
of the later universities, institutions which, while presenting 
definite contrasts with the older educational establishments, 
yet derived their teaching system from the educational

At Chartres, in the days of Fulbert, all the arts and 
sciences known at that time were taught and studied. The 
foundation of medieval learning was the study of Latin 
grammar, and with rhetoric and dialectics this constituted 
the ‘ trivium,’ leading on to geometry, arithmetic, astronomy, 
and music, the four subjects of the ‘ quadrivium.’ ‘The 
trivium and quadrivium formed the graduation course in arts 
and science of those days, and represent a classification of the 
famous seven liberal arts, drawn up by Martianus Capella, 
in the fifth century, which was handed on by Cassiodorus 
(480-575) and Alcuin (755-804).? 

The study of grammar included composition in Latin 
prose and verse. Chartres was a great school of Latin poetry. 
In its library more poets than writers of prose were to be 
found. Of the secular poets, the works of Virgil, Ovid, 
Horace, Terence, Stacius, and Servius were in the catalogue, 
while the Christian poets were represented by Fortunatus, 
Sedulius, Arator, Prudentius,and Boethius. Thesecular prose 
writers included Livy, Valerius Maximus, Orosius, and 
Gregory of Tours.2 In the making of verses the scholars of 
Chartres surpassed those of Fleury and Liége, and we possess 
many specimens of Fulbert’s poems. The ancient or classical 
metres were used as well as the rhymed and accented poetry 
of the Middle Ages. ‘The Christian poets of medieval days 
created a new glory for the old Latin tongue in the chiming 
rhythms composed for the singing churchmen of the cathedral 
and abbey choirs, and for the gleemen of the baron’s hall. 
When these lyrics were set to the plain-song tones of the 
Gregorian school, they formed a body of music for male 
voices which has never been surpassed by the triumphs of 
later masters and doctors of music. Among the poets of

Chartres no higher place was taken than that reached by 
Berengar.t One contemporary has described him as the 
leading poet of the age. A splendid specimen of his Latin 
verse has survived in a noble appeal to the deity, written 
at the Council of Rome in 1078. The Juste Fudex, Fesu 
Christe composed when contemplating the ordeal by fire, 
touches the highest flights of medieval poetry, and breathes 
_the spirit of mysticism three centuries before the medieval 
mystics cast the gracious mantle of their gentle theology 
around the otherwise rigid corpus of medieval theological 
thought. 

As a writer of Latin prose, Berengar does not take a high 
place. The broken, tortuous style of the De Sacra Cena, 
and of most of his letters, indicates a mind so distraught by 
polemical animus or by urgency of business that the formal 
rules of composition were carelessly abandoned. Yet the 
beautiful letter to the hermits* shows that he was capable of 
writing prose which equalled the charm of his Latin verse. 

The study of rhetoric, as a training for public speaking, 
was mainly occupied with the reading of Latin authors. 
Among the works read at Chartres were some of the writings 
of Cicero and Livy and Victorinus. Chartres produced good 
speakers, among them Everard, Herfast, Renaud of Angers, 
Arrald, and Fulbert himself, whose sermons survive.® But 
high distinction in this art was again reached by Berengar. 
Guitmund of Aversa, who was no friendly critic, was com- 
pelled to pay tribute to the effects of Berengar’s eloquence 
upon his students in later years.®

more attention because of the part played by dialectics in 
Berengar’s treatment of the eucharistic question. An examina-

hardly have been richer in the works of preceding centuries

For the application of logic to systems and ideas, it is 
not certain whether they had Chalcidius’ translation of the 
‘'Timaeus ’ of Plato, but Fulbert said that Plato was superior 
to all the writers of antiquity,? and Berengar referred to him 
as the gem of philosophy. Neo-Platonists like Dionysius 
the Areopagite, John Scotus Erigena—the translator of Dio- 
nysius—and Boethius (‘ Consolations ’) were sympathetically 
read. Commentaries on the old works on logic were written, 
and glosses were inserted in the texts. ‘The synoptic tables 
of Cicero and Themistius were in use. Clerval complains 
that the study. of the rules of reasoning and of the forms of 
thought at Chartres did not result in the production of great 
theories and systems.5 But he goes on to claim, in somewhat 
contradictory fashion, that Nominalism originated at Chartres 
during this era, and that its founder was John the Sophist, the 
physician of Henry I of France, who was at Chartres 1037-45.° 
The conclusion depends on the interpretation of the term.

If Nominalism means the application of Aristotelean logic to 
the classification of ideas, then the date of its origin might be 
put back to the time of John the Scot. If, on the other hand, 
it means the criticism of universals, then even Clerval dates 
its origin too early, for that discussion did not arise until the 
twelfth century.1 Clerval states that Chartres was Aristotelean 
in method and Platonist in spirit and ideas. But even this 
description appears to be too sharply outlined. The day had 
not yet come when medieval teachers could be classified into 
schools or even methods of thought, although divergence of 
thought was beginning to appear, and we may agree with 
Clerval that at Chartres this was indeed already apparent, 
some were inclined to follow the spiritual and idealist 
tendencies of Plato, while others followed the critical and 
scientific method of Aristotle.2, But both tendencies were at 
work in the same individuals, and any distinction which 
existed was rather one of stress, or emphasis, than an un- 
deviating pursuit of either method of thought. Scholars of 
Chartres, and critics of Berengar like Adelmann,? Hugh of 
Langres,* and even Fulbert ® himself, who can be claimed 
more decisively as disciples of Plato rather than Aristotle, 
were not without resort to the dialectical method, when, in 
defence of their position, they distinguished between the 
senses, reason, and faith, and we shall see that Berengar, who 
deliberately set up reason against the authority of mere 
tradition as the final standard of criticism in matters of dogma, 
none the less remained under the influence of Platonism.

a revival of interest had indeed taken place in the study of 
dialectics or logic, and here Berengar received his earliest 
training in the use of rational methods of thought, so far as 
they were then understood. Such studies, undertaken by a 
mind naturally inclined to a critical view of life and ideas, 
were bound to be followed by tangible results later on. With 
justification Clerval says that the schools of Chartres did not 
produce new ideas during this epoch, but that statement 
must be supplemented by the provision that after he had left 
Chartres, Berengar brought a new method of interpretation 
to bear upon the doctrine of the Eucharist, based on ideas 
which were assisted in their formulation by the training 
received in the dialectical studies at Chartres. 

There is no evidence that Greek was taught at Chartres, 
although it was being taught at Reims by Gerbert, when 
Fulbert was a scholar there, and Fulbert’s writings indicate 
some knowledge of that language.1 Sigon of Saumur, a con- 
temporary of Berengar at Chartres, collated Biblical texts 
with the Greek original, and Hildegaire, another alumnus of 
Chartres, used Greek words in his medical writings.2 But 
Greek was not included in the regular curriculum of the 
trivium in the Middle Ages. 

In the quadrivium the studies of arithmetic, geometry, 
astronomy, and music supplied the merest smattering of 
scientific knowledge, and, with the exception of geometry, the 
instruction given in these subjects was completely lacking in 
scientific method. Arithmetic included the use of the abacus. 
Geometry was largely occupied with discussions on the 
properties of angles. Astronomy comprised the computation 
of the Ides, Nones, and Kalends, and the details of the 
Christian Calendar, together with a study of the movements 
of the stars. Strange notions were prevalent concerning the 
movement of the heavenly bodies. Adelmann, the Chartrain, 
complained in later years to Berengar of those astronomers 
who taught that the sky and stars stood still while the earth 
passed through them with a rapid, whirling motion, and also

Chartres had a fine school of music. Sigon, who excelled 
in painting and the illumination of manuscripts,? was a 
proficient organist. Liturgical chants were composed by 
Fulbert, Sigon the painter, Arnulf, Angelran, Ralph Mala 
Corona, Adelmann, Hildegaire the physician, Sigon of 
Saumur, the Greek student, Olbert of Gembloux, and others. 
Fulbert’s themes have been woven into the three Responds 
of the Nativity, the Antiphonary of Paris, the Office of the 
Benedictines of Solesme, the Office for S. Giles, and other 
music still to be found in the Missals. Arnulf drew up the 
Office of S. Evroul.3> 

The higher studies included law, medicine, and theology, 
or patristics, with special reference toliturgiology.4 The study 
of law covered both civil and canon law,® although the latter 
was still in its infancy. ‘The most famous medical school of 
the day existed at Salerno,§ but on this side of the Alps an 
efficient medical school was to be found in the first half of 
the eleventh century at Chartres, where the principles of 
Hippocrates, Galen, Sorin, and Oribase were taught. Here 
Hildegaire, the musician and writer of medical books, was 
trained, also Guizo, Goisbert, and Ralph Mala Corona, another 
musician. Once more we find Fulbert’s name among those 
mentioned, and medicine was one of the many subjects 
professed by that accomplished teacher.? So also, among 
his varied achievements, Berengar counted proficiency in 
medicine,® and so well known was his medical skill, that it 
has been suggested that, after leaving Chartres, Berengar 
adopted, for a time, the practice of medicine at Tours.2 Of

Evidence of the range of theological teaching at Chartres 
is to be found in the names of the Fathers quoted in Fulbert’s 
writings. The Greek Fathers do not appear, but of the Latin 
Fathers we find Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, 
Jerome, Gregory, Fulgentius, Bede, Rabanus Maurus, and 
Bacharius, a commentator on the lives of the saints. Fulbert 
discarded the allegorical interpretation for the literal and 
historical. He trained his students to trace a statement back 
to the scriptural text and to read that many times. After 
ascertaining the literal sense, he emphasised its moral applica- 
tion and psychological import. Reasoning was used rather 
for exegetical purposes than for demonstration.2 Here is 
revealed a combination of old and new methods characteristic 
of the study of dialectics at Chartres, a mode of treating 
Scripture which Berengar used in later days. Again and 
again he attempted to tie Lanfranc down to a literal interpre- 
tation of a disputed passage, and this method was learned at 
Chartres under Fulbert. 

In this glowing academic cathedral centre, occupied by 
studies so varied, and surrounded by friends so accomplished, 
Berengar passed the golden years of youth, winning success 
in poetry and medicine and in the school of logic.4 Among 
his fellow-students at Chartres, in addition to Adelmann, later 
Bishop of Brescia, Hildegaire, and Sigon, already mentioned, 
there were Lambert of Paris, Ralph and Englebert of Orleans, 
Rainald® of ‘Tours, Gerbert or Walter the Burgundian,

Alesta, all of whom are named in a satirical poem ® which

Thus did Fulbert endeavour to train the minds and souls 
of his pupils by kindly admonitions, springing from 
personal interest in them and friendly converse with them, 
reminding us of the methods used by Anselm at Bec.! In the 
light of this letter we may disregard the story of William of 
Malmesbury,? who records that when Fulbert lay dying and 
his pupils were standing around him, Fulbert noticed Berengar, 
who had probably come over from Tours, or may have been 
on his way back from Paris.2 He ordered Berengar to go 
away, crying out that he could see a demon standing on him, 
beckoning the others with a blandishing gesture and persuasive 
tones to follow him. The tale was almost certainly invented 
after Berengar had been declared a heretic. It does no more 
than reflect the critical treatment offered by Berengar to some 
of Fulbert’s teaching. That his attitude to Fulbert was 
consistently critical is disproved by his own statement, for 
in the De Sacra Cena he made use of one of Fulbert’s 
illustrations. His enemy, Guitmund, reported that he had 
heard from contemporaries of Berengar at Chartres that, 
puffed up by conceit of mind, he cared not for the teaching 
of his master, regarded his fellow-students as of no con- 
sequence, and made light of the books used for grammatical 
studies.5 Guitmund also charges him with neglecting the 
study of Scripture when he was a youth.® That these state- 
ments were spitefully made is clear, but they indicate that 
while a student at Chartres Berengar possessed sufficient 
independence of character and clearness of mind to be able 
to discuss the teaching of Fulbert, to maintain his own con- 
victions against other scholars, and to criticise the text-books 
in use.’ But such an attitude is characteristic of a bright 
and alert-minded youth who received his education in the

stimulating atmosphere of a centre like Chartres, especially 
when a varied curriculum was supervised and partly taught 
by a kindly and sympathetic preceptor like Fulbert, who 
invited the friendship of his pupils. In such a setting and. 
under such an influence the special traits of individuals have 
an opportunity of developing into useful talents, and this 
cannot be achieved by any system of education which crushes 
the critical faculty of the young. 

A curious incident is reported by Berengar,1 which may 
refer to the period spent at Chartres. One day a student, who 
had only recently begun the study of grammar, and who had 
been reading about interjections in the text-book of the gram- 
marian Donatus, heard the other boys asking to what part of 
speech ‘only’? belonged. Various answers were given. He said 
that it was neither a noun nor an adverb, as some maintained. 
They contradicted him, and he undertook to prove his con- 
tention on condition that they gave him a reward if he was 
successful. ‘They agreed, and he said that ‘only’ was an 
interjection, and, opening his book, he said ‘ Read that verse.’ 
The verse was in a passage which he had heard from the 
master on the same day on the force of an interjection, and 
it had been shown that an interjection was a demonstrative 
only. ‘So,’ said the fool,? ‘ “‘ only ” is an interjection,’ and 
claimed his reward.

Note on the Date of Fulbert’s Death. 


The date of Fulbert’s death (April 10, 1028) was settled by Pfister, 
De Fulberit Vita (1885), p. 47, and by Merlet and Clerval, Un Manuscrit 
chartrain du XI siécle (1893), pp. 47 0. 2, 49 N. 3, 52n.2,159. Yet some 
modern authorities still use the old date 1029, viz. Brucker, ii. 134; 
Schnitzer, p. 5; Ebersolt, p. 19; Chevalier, p. 1624; Vernet, Dict. de 
Théologie Cath., V. 1217. 

The conclusion in favour of 1028 is based on three early documents : 
(z) A codex in the Bibliothéque Municipale of S. Etienne, Reims, written 
1026-28, and containing the necrology of S. Mary at Chartres, Fulbert’s 
church. This manuscript is described at length by Merlet and Clerval 
(p. 1 ff.; cf. Introduction, p.i). The entry of Fulbert’s death on April 4, 
1028, occurs on p. 159. 

(2) Codex 14167 (Latin) in the Bibliothéque Nationale, a copy of the 
S. Etienne document dating from the middle of the eleventh century (Merlet 
and Clerval, pp. 50-53, with footnotes). It originally belonged to S. Pére, 
at Chartres. Pfister attributed this document to Sigon, a pupil of Fulbert 


EARLY LIFE 19 


(De Fulberti Vita, p. 2); this is disputed by Merlet and Clerval, p. 53 n. 2, 
but Sigon made the entry of Fulbert’s death in the S. Etienne MS. (Merlet 
and Clerval, p. 159). There is some obscurity at the end of Pfister’s 
first paragraph on p. 47. He also misquotes the MS. in the Bibliothéque 
Nat. as No. 14161. The number is 14167. No. 14161 is an extract from 
the Latin poets of Italy of the seventeenth century (cf. Delisle, Inventaive 
des manuscrits Latins conserves a la Bibliotheque Nationale, 1863-71, p. 130). 

(3) Codex 1037 in the Bibliothéque Communale de Chartres, a twelfth- 
century (?) document, containing the obituary of S. Pére de Chartres, 
gives the day of the month, but not the year of Fulbert’s death (Merlet 
and Clerval, p. 49 n. 3). 

The date, April 10, 1028, is confirmed by the Chronicon Dol (Bouquet, 
X. 323e), which fixes it by reporting an eclipse of the moon (cf. Pfister, 
p. 47). The dates for Fulbert in the Cartulaive de Notre Dame de Chartres 
(Lepinois and Merlet), i. 14 f., are quite wrong. 

Later writers, on the assumption that the year began with Easter 
Day, could find no room for April 10 in 1028 (which year began on April 14 
and ended on the following April 5 of our 1029), and so placed it in 1029 
(Mabillon, Annales, iv. 351; Bouquet, x. 443, n. a; Samarthan, Gallia 
Christiana, viii. 1116; Hust. Litt., vii. 265). The Hirst. Litt. and Mabillon 
reckon the twenty-one years and a half of Fulbert’s episcopate, given in 
his epitaph by Sigon, from 1007. Pfister (p. 48) shows that Fulbert’s 
episcopate dates from 1006. But is he accurate in counting twenty years 
and eighteen months? Should it not be twenty years and twenty-three 
months? The solution of the difficulty, supplied by Pfister, lies in the 
fact that the civil year was reckoned from March 1 (Etudes sur le régne 
de Robert le Pieux, p. XxXxviil). 

The correct date is given by Schwabe, p. 7; Hauck-Herzog, vi. 310 ; 
and the Camb. Med. Hist. v.3. Among earlier writers, Oudin, ii. 624 f., 
has 1028. 


CHAPTER II 
SCOLASTICUS OF TOURS AND ARCHDEACON OF ANGERS 


WE have seen from the cartularies that the name Berengar 
was widely used among the families of ‘Touraine and Anjou 
in the eleventh century. It is also frequent among the clergy 
and monks who signed the numerous charters of the period. 
In most cases there are indications which point more or less 
decisively to the identification of our Berengar, but in many 
instances we cannot be sure that the Berengar, or ‘ B.,’ who 
signs a charter or writes a letter was the Scolasticus of Tours 
and Archdeacon of Angers, although in some cases we can 
say definitely that he was not that personage. 

It will be well to begin by noting those ecclesiastics who 
bore the name, but who can be definitely distinguished from 
our Berengar. ‘The document signed by Berengar, the Arch- 
priest, at Paris in 10051 is much too early to cause any 
confusion with our Berengar.2 At Chartres we can dis-

could not agree upon a member of their own foundation, the 
right lapsed to the Emperor. But during the latter part of the 
ninth century not merely the right of appointment but the 
occupancy of the abbacy fell first to a member of the royal 
house and then to the King of France himself. During the 
next century Tours maintained its reputation, and counted

objected, but were informed that they had no voice in the matter until 
after the death of the heir, Archembald Vindunellus. ‘The case is com- 
plicated because Ulger’s son was also named Archembald, and he in- 
herited the church on the death of Ulger. When that took place the 
monks of Cormery again challenged the arrangement, but failed to obtain 
satisfaction until after the death of the original heir, Archembald 
Vindunellus, son of Letard. When that occurred, they allowed Ulger’s 
son to retain the church for life, on condition that he built another church, 
and promised to hand everything to the monastery at his death, and to 
keep the property cultivated. The last item was not fulfilled.

Both grants were confirmed by Charles the Bald in 845.1

often unable to avoid dipping itself in vitriol.

If he was a man of austere life, his self-discipline did not 
hinder him from inspiring affectionate friendships. Drogo 
of Paris 1 was not a pupil of Berengar, but a letter written 
when the latter had been for a few years in charge of the 
schools at Tours may well be quoted in illustration of the 
influence exerted by the Scolasticus upon other people at this 
time. The letter was written shortly after Drogo had visited 
him at Tours. 


If I told you to your face how great was my admiration for your 
most strenuous care in apprehending the Scriptures, and your perfect 
and most happy eloquence in expounding them, I should seem to 
be a flatterer. But now that I am absent, lest by my silence I should 
appear to have an ordinary opinion of your excellence, I am glad 
to let you know by letter what I feel about you, since you hold in 
my estimation a unique and chief place. I can find no one to whom 
I can liken you. Neither the vast number of things you have to 
do in connection with your own affairs and in advising those who 
consult you, nor your age, which is no longer that of youth, nor your: 
body which you afflict with much abstinence, withdraw or hinder 
you from a close scrutiny of the Scriptures so that you are prevented 
from understanding them, or grasping them clearly. Moreover, 
who does not admire your excellence in the medical art, in 
which you surpass those who are professed physicians ? What more 
shall I say? One thing I mourn and deplore, that apparently 
you are unknown by the world, but I am partly consoled, because, 
since I left you, I have sung your praises, so far as possible, and to 
no obscure men.?

During this period Berengar was consulted by another 
friend, Joscelin of Partenay, the Treasurer of the Cathedral 
of S. Hilary at Poitiers, on a dispute which seems to have 
arisen between Isembert,! Bishop of Poitiers, and some of his 
clergy. The details are made known by Berengar’s reply.” 
After greeting his ‘ beloved brother Joscelin,’ he points out 
that it would be rash not to examine the causes of the 
trouble. 


The clergy have either a good case against the Bishop, or a 
bad one, or one which is partly good and partly bad. If their case 
is good the Bishop ought not to disguise the fact,* for it is the part 
of a bishop first to cast the beam or straw out of his own eye, which 
means, according to Scripture, hate and anger, for does not a doctor, 
since he is a doctor, cure his own sickness? If their case is bad, 
he ought to remember what the Apostle said to bishops, ‘ Not 
lording it over the clergy, but being examples to the flock,’ so that 
for their satisfaction he may not appear inhumane because they 
are in the wrong, but humane, because he ought to be himself 
an example to them of charity and patience. Thus, having the 
desire he will not pretend the correction of them, but remain 
satisfied as God says that He is satisfied: ‘ Be ye converted and 
live.’* If they are partly justified, as appears to me to be the case, 
since they allege that he ought not to introduce anything into the 
church against their just desire (no prelate indeed, especially a 
bishop, may do anything in a church which he ought not to do) ; 
but also partly unjustified, for it seems that they were rash in going 
away from him in the chapter-house—he should be restrained so far 
as they were right, just as he is annoyed because they were wrong. 
He should remember that saying which, although it be poetical is 
not without point, ‘ Evil levels those whom it pollutes.’ The gospel 
precept seems to apply to the case, ‘ They do not gather grapes from 
thorns.’ So also let him first depart from all indignation, and then, 
so far as he can, by kindness urge that they also may recover their 
senses. It is the duty of all Christian prelates, much more of 
bishops, to do nothing with the desire of injuring, but all from a 
love of helping. If this is done the blessed Augustine prescribes 
that nothing be done unkindly, nothing inhumanly. For the rest, his

Students from all parts of France came to Tours during 
the first ten years of Berengar’s work as Scolasticus.? Several 
of them reached high office and dignity in later life. Among 
them were Eusebius Bruno,®? who became Bishop of Angers 
and gave Berengar his support during the first period of the 
eucharistic controversy ; Hildebert, who became Bishop of. 
Le Mans and then Archbishop of Tours, the writer of 
Berengar’s epitaph ;+ Bruno the founder of the Carthusian 
order; possibly Robert of Landrecies and Hubert of 
Marmoutier ;° possibly also Baudry of Bourgueil,® who wrote 
obituary verses on Berengar ; and, for a short time, Lanfranc,’ 
soon after his arrival from Italy, and before he began to 
lecture in the cathedral school of Avranches.

CHAPTER III 
OUTBREAK OF THE SECOND EUCHARISTIC CONTROVERSY 


A CERTAIN similarity is characteristic of the breaking-out 1 of 
great periods of advance or recovery in the history of doctrine. 
A restlessness is felt in the minds of thinkers, a dissatisfaction 
with accepted dogmas takes a hold on thought, which comes 
to expression in formal or informal conferences and through 
the medium of published treatises. ‘Then appears a master- 
mind which grasps the scattered strands of thought, unites 
them, and produces a doctrine which appears to a wondering 
world to be entirely new. ‘The power of intellect and force 
of personality of this interpreter cause him to be regarded 
as the creator of the new system of ideas which thenceforth 
strongly influences thought and conduct. This was the 
process witnessed in every controversy from Monarchianism 
to Monophysitism and Pelagianism. It characterised the 
period of enlightenment of the Reformation time. It has 
been seen in our own day manipulating the great contribution 
made to human thought and philosophy by the men of science. 
Ideas are generated and get about in the intellectual atmo- 
sphere, but they do not come to an outbreak, which in turn 
issues in an advance of doctrine, until one acute mind begins 
to act as an interpreter. 

In the Middle Ages the process, while remaining true to 
this type, possessed some special features. ‘The interpreter 
appeared, but the ideas upon which he took hold were not 
simmering in men’s minds; they were rather floating in the 
stream of tradition, and were therefore only accessible to the 
few who had sufficient learning to detect and make use of 
them. They were not always detected by those who had 


i “ Aufklarung ’ expresses the idea more clearly. 


SECOND EUCHARISTIC CONTROVERSY = 45 


the necessary qualification. Consequently, when a Paschasius 
Radbert or a Berengar of Tours adopted and popularised a 
strand of teaching already existing in the intellectual traditions 
behind them, they were regarded as innovators by an 
astonished world. ‘This occurred more especially in the case 
of Berengar than of Radbert. It partly explains why, in his 
own day, he failed to reach the dimensions of a reformer, and 
why, for centuries, he was regarded as a mere innovator. 
Yet, if the conditions of medieval thought prevented him 
from influencing the development of doctrine in his own day, 
they came round full circle and preserved his teaching—or at 
least the ideas to which he gave adherence—in the stream of 
tradition, floating and unattached indeed, but waiting in 
silent potency until they got loose at the Reformation, when 
they influenced men’s minds so strongly that they became, 
through the instrumentality of the Reformers, part of the 
new body of doctrine.? 

These conditions of doctrinal development in the Middle 
Ages should be recollected when we seek for the sources of 
Berengar’s teaching. ‘The personal factor was certainly at 
work. His inquiring mind and rational habits of thought 
obviously disposed him to criticise accepted standards and 
doctrines. But he did not become the spokesman of ideas 
which were ranging around in men’s minds. He received 
his inspiration from a tradition not generally accepted by the 
orthodox, but actually existing in the body of teaching or 
interpretation handed down from the past. That tradition 
was embedded in the ancient Augustinian doctrine? His 
nearest channels of communication with Augustinianism lay 
in the writings of John the Scot and in those of Ratramn, 
which Berengar by a strange mischance attributed to John 
the Scot. The nature of Berengar’s obligation to these 
writers we shall investigate in the doctrinal section of this 
work. All that is required here is to observe that the teaching

The high estimation in which Berengar held the teaching 
of John the Scot was made clear in the early days of the 
controversy. In his letter to Lanfranc in the spring of 
1049,2 Berengar rebukes the Prior of Bec because he counted 
‘as heresy the opinions of John the Scot on the sacrament of 
the altar, in which he disagrees with your accepted Paschasius,’ 
and concludes with his often repeated dictum :? ‘ If you hold 
John a heretic, whose opinions on the Eucharist we approve, 
you ought to hold as heretics Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine, 
not to mention others.’ 

Writing to another friend, Ascelin,* towards the end of 
1050,° Berengar complained that a certain William had boasted 
that Berengar could not deny that John the Scot was a heretic. 
Ascelin could testify, if he remembered Berengar’s words, 
that this was false, although Ascelin himself held that John 
the Scot was a heretic, which was an opinion quite unworthy 
of his priesthood. If he held the doctrine of Paschasius he 
acted against reason and evangelical and apostolical opinions. 
With regard to his own utterances, Berengar did not maintain 
that everything that John the Scot said was true, but he could 
prove from the writings of the Fathers, mentioned in his letter 
to Lanfranc, that they also must be regarded as heretics if 
John the Scot were condemned. He ends by warning Ascelin 
against saying that he (Berengar) had condemned John the 
Scot. 
About a year later, in the autumn of 1051, he wrote to 
another friend named Richard.* In this letter Berengar 
maintained that John the Scot had been unjustly condemned, 
and Paschasius Radbert had been equally unjustly approved

Throughout the controversy of the next thirty years 
Berengar, in spite of formal recantations, did not relax from 
his adherence to John the Scot and his teaching,” and coupled 
with this positive attitude was his equally consistent criticism 
of Paschasius Radbert. That appears in each of the letters 
already quoted, and is a constant theme in his great polemical 
work, the De Sacra Cena’ Whether he began by dis- 
agreeing with the teaching of Paschasius, and then found a 
basis for his own constructive thought in John the Scot’s 
writings, or whether, when already under the influence of the 
latter, he found himself unable to agree with Radbert’s 
doctrine, is not clear; but so far as John the Scot supplied 
a positive foundation for Berengar’s interpretation of the 
doctrine of the Eucharist, we may safely attribute the rise 
of the controversy to the influence of Augustine exerted 
through that channel, and also through Ratramn, if, as is 
probable, Berengar also studied Ratramn, although wrongly 
with his contemporaries attributing Ratramn’s work on the 
Eucharist to John the Scot. 

The influence of John the Scot upon Berengar as a source 
of the controversy was particularly noticed by the writers of 
the next generation. Some of his contemporaries attributed 
to him quite unworthy motives, which indeed are often, 
without justification, assigned to the exponents of new or 
unfamiliar ideas. Guitmund accused him of seeking to 
obtain the admiration of men through the medium of his 
teaching,® even to the extent of gaining the favour of evil- 
living communicants.6 Lanfranc accused him of desiring to 
acquire a cheap popularity.? That he was perhaps susceptible

Why was Lanfranc criticising John the Scot’s views on the 
Eucharist ? Obviously the subject was a matter of public 
discussion at the time in ecclesiastical circles. 'The incident 
supplies final proof that Berengar’s teaching was well known 
for a year or two before 1049.2, We know of only one source 
from which such a discussion was likely to arise at that date— 
the school of S. Martin at Tours. The letter of Berengar 
does not suggest that Lanfranc had so far attacked him, and 
although formerly they had disagreed on the subject,’ on this 
occasion Lanfranc seems to have been content to challenge 
rather the teaching of John the Scot than to embroil an old 
friend in the dispute. 

It is probable that up to this point of time, and until after 
the Council of Vercelli, Berengar was content with teaching and 
expounding the views of John the Scot or Ratramn or both, 
without developing any independent conclusions, although, as 
the letters of Adelmann and Hugh of Langres show, his own 
name was being associated widely with heretical teaching.

The only serious objection to this sequence of events lies 
in Berengar’s statement in his extensive apologetic work, 
the De Sacra Cena,1 written many years later. He there 
contends that at the time of the Council of Vercelli (September 
1050) his views on the Eucharist were not formed.? But this 
statement must be read in the light of his letter to Ansfroi, 
Abbot of Préaux, written shortly before the Council of Vercelli, 
in which he says that his theory on the Eucharist is clear and 
altogether manifest to those who have eyes to see Con- 
sequently, the statement in the De Sacra Cena, which was 
written after a long interval, when accurate recollection was 
difficult, can only refer to the absence of a full and reasoned 
explanation of his doctrine, which in 1050 had not yet been 
published by him. It may also be added, as Schnitzer has 
pointed out, that unless Berengar’s views were formed at the 
- time when his letter to Lanfranc was written, he would hardly 
have challenged the latter to a discussion, and so have run 
the risk of public blame, and of damage to his reputation as 
ascholar.* It is also difficult to see that Lanfranc’s reputation 
could have been compromised by the letter unless public 
opinion was already sensitive on account of Berengar.

fact that he himself was not summoned to Rome for this 
occasion, and by the fact that he was condemned unheard. 
Of this procedure he naturally complained with sarcasm. 
Lanfranc’s report of the Council, said he, shed the aspersion 
of sacrilege upon the holy Leo. Human as well as divine 
law prohibited the condemnation of anyone unheard. The 
blessed Gregory had said that he deprived himself of the 
power of binding and loosing, who exercised it, not against 
the behaviour of his subordinates, but to indulge his own 
wilful caprice. Until Leo, by citing him, had tested whether 
he would appear or not, sentence should have been suspended, 
and the falseness of Lanfranc’s charge, that his belief was 
contrary to the common faith, would have been recognised. 

Throughout the long dispute, and especially at this stage, 
Berengar did not realise the extent to which he was being 
made the tool of ecclesiastical policy and political intrigue, 
both by the Papacy and by his own patrons. It was quite 
contrary to the procedure of the Curia at that day to condemn 
a man unheard, but the incident fits in with the political 
expediency of Leo’s opportunist policy, which was so clearly 
revealed at Reims. At the Council of Rome the Pope had 
weightier matters in mind than the heresy of Berengar. The 
postponement of a final settlement to the Council of Vercelli 
was also partly related to the affairs of Count Geoffrey. If 
Geoffrey had appeared and given satisfaction to Leo at Rome, 
the verdict against Berengar might not have been issued. 

On the other hand, if the outbreak of the Berengarian 
controversy was thus made use of in the hostile attitude of 
Anjou to the Papacy, there is little justification for the con- 
tention that Berengar obtained the vital power for his steady 
heresy from the political opposition of his countrymen,? that 
the anti-papal tendency of the second eucharistic controversy 
was the principal result of the interdict placed on Anjou 
and ‘Touraine,® and that Berengar was the arch-plotter who

quietly schemed behind the walls of S. Martin’s! a great 
anti-papal, anti-imperialist combination, which was to include 
not only the Count of Anjou, but the King of France and 
the Duke of Normandy. In his long polemical treatise and 
throughout his correspondence Berengar shows a singular 
lack of political knowledge, or insight, or even interest. In 
the former he never refers to the great political personages 
with whom he came in contact. The dispute was for him 
a theological controversy simply. ‘This made him an easy 
opponent for astute politicians like Lanfranc and Humbert, 
and his lack of a political sense made it easy for patrons like 
Henry I and Eusebius Bruno to drop him when he was no 
longer useful for their aims. 

Some of the confusion surrounding the affairs of Berengar 
at this period arises from the divided loyalties which the 
feudal organisation of Church and State imposed upon many 
individuals in those days. If Berengar was a factor in the 
contest between the Papacy and Anjou, he occupied a similar 
role, though with even less happy consequences for himself, 
in the parallel battle of wits and policies being carried on 
between the Papacy and the Emperor Henry III on the one 
side, and Henry I of France on the other. Gfrérer has re- 
vealed the steps by which the Emperor attempted to establish 
imperial influence over the great magnates of France. If the 
Emperor gave his support to the schemes of Leo [X, German 
interests had everything to gain, although the independence 
of Leo was greater than Gfrérer allows. Moreover, Gfrérer 
stresses too strongly the part played by Berengar in the effort 
of Henry I of France to counter the encroachment of imperial- 
papal politics in France, by attempting to supply, in obedience 
to the royal wishes, a dogmatic basis for a French national 
Protestant church, or at least to create a kind of Gallicanism.”

The authorities in Anjou continued, after the Council of 
Rome, to give their support to Berengar. In a letter written 
some months later to Guy, Archbishop of Reims, Eusebius 
complained of the ill-treatment of Berengar by the Pope. 
Although entirely free from error and fault, ‘ this clerk of our 
Church ’ had been most unjustly and unworthily defamed by 
the apostolic chair. Eusebius would have written at greater 
length about Berengar if the bearer of the letter could have 
tarried longer.1 But the failure of his powerful friends, 
Count Geoffrey and Bishop Eusebius, to ward off the papal 
attack of Rome in the spring of 1050 caused him to look 
around for increased support and ampler protection, although 
we cannot see in this obvious step the attempt to take a leading 
part in the great combinations outlined by Schwabe? and 
Gfrérer. If Berengar had been capable of so masterly a 
stroke he would not have been so easily overcome at later 
stages of the controversy. ‘That a political movement was 
soon inaugurated at Angers in order to obtain allies outside 
Anjou against the Papacy, after the failure of Bishop Eusebius 
to get the interdict rescinded, is proved by the letter of 
Eusebius to Guy, Archbishop of Reims,® in which the Bishop 
attempted, though unsuccessfully, to secure the chief Primate 
of France* for the combination, and the impression that 
Eusebius, rather than Berengar, was regarded at this time as 
the chief agent of political schemes in Anjou is confirmed 
by the fact that the French clergy looked to Eusebius rather 
than to Berengar as the chief representative of the heretical 
eucharistic teaching.®

century. Hincmar (843-882) set up the claim for Reims. The institution 
had no constitutional right behind it, but was a practical fact. On the 
question in England, cf. Macdonald, pp. 70-94, 270-291.

A humbler and much more probable réle must be attributed 
to Berengar. He began his tour with the object of securing 
fresh support for his teaching, especially in view of the con- 
demnation issued against him at Rome. The reports which 
have survived show that Berengar’s theological views were the 
subject of discussions during this journey, and they contain no 
reference to contemporary politics. 

He first visited Préaux in Normandy, where his friend 
Ansfroi was Abbot.2, The esteem in which Berengar held 
Ansfroi is revealed in the letter which he afterwards wrote to 
him from Chartres. ‘ ‘There is nothing either splendid or divine 
which I can say, as I have no authority or dignity or merit, if it 
be not sanctioned by your authority, which seems to dwell in 
heaven.’? Ansfroi had already heard of Berengar’s condemna- 
tion at Rome through Richer, Abbot of S. Julian at Tours, 
who had returned from the Council,* and possibly for this 
reason Berengar failed to convince Ansfroi of the merits of his 
teaching. He had a long conversation with the Abbot in his 
cell ‘ concerning the question, yea it is not a question, for the 
thing is altogether clear, if anyone has the eyes not of a beast, 
but of a man, eyes capable of bearing light, not accustomed to 
be bound by darkness.’*> He continues: ‘I listened to you 
on the question, and I had your advice that I should turn to the 
statements of the gospel and apostles. I was greatly amazed, 
and did not presume to claim for my stupidity a more vigilant 
knowledge of the gospel and apostolic sayings, as if my per- 
spicacity ought to have pronounced more mildly concerning 
elther..?

to a monastery of S. Albert, which did not exist. Sudendorf (pp. 105,

Of this church the King was Abbot by an ancient tradition. La Vérité

falls into the same trap and confuses S. Martin’s and Marmoutier. Loofs, 
P- 575 ff., draws attention to Schwabe’s slip and shows that Berengar was 
not a Canon of S. Martin’s ‘ Cathedral,’ but a member of the collegiate 
church of S. Martin, which was built at the tomb of 5S. Martin, 550 paces 
from the town, in the time of Gregory the Great, quoting Gregory of Tours, 
Hist. Francorum, ii. 14 (Migne, 71, 212a f.), and Gallia Christiana, xiv.152 ; 
cf. Besse, p. 2. This church, which was erected originally by S. Brice 
over the tomb of S. Martin, was rebuilt by S. Perpet (470) and again by 
Herveus(roor). Loofs points out that the ‘ ecclesia beati Martini’ mentioned 
by Eusebius (Sudendorf, p. 222) was the cathedral. We may add that this 
is indicated by the fact that Eusebius also calls it ‘ecclesia Turonensis ’ 
(ibid.), the current designation of the leading church of a cathedral city, a 
designation which he clinches by also referring to it as ‘matri nostrae 
ecclesiae Turonensis’ (ibid. p. 223), t.e. the metropolitan church of Tours. 
Bartholomew refers simply to ‘the church’ (‘ ecclesiz,’ zbid. p. 221), and 
his reference to the canons’ houses means the dwellings of the canons of 
the cathedral, not of S. Martin’s collegiate church. The cathedral was 
named after S. Maurice (cf. infya, p. 110 n. 4). For the history of the 
fabric of S. Martin’s, cf. Vaucelle, pp. 383-396. Most of the authorities 
clearly report Berengar as a Canon of Tours, and this can only refer to 
the collegiate foundation. In his writings Berengar refers to his fellow- 
clergy as canons, not monks: ‘ Epis. to Joscelin’ (Sudendorf, p. 230), 
‘canonicus noster’; D.S.C., p. 46, ‘concanonicus.’ In the ‘ Epis. to 
Philip of France ’ (Sudendorf, p. 226) he distinguishes between ‘ monastici’ 
and ‘ canonici.’ 

Much of this confusion would have been avoided if Mabillon’s state- 
ment in the Annales had been noticed. He quotes (ii. 658, 746) 
documents dated January 1 of the sixth year of Charles the Bald, showing 
that a Count Vivian (d. 851, Gallia Christiana, xiv. 199a) ruled both the 
Abbey of S. Martin’s and the Major Monasterium. One of these charters 
(ibid. ii. 658; cf. Gall. Christ., xiv. 199b) proves that both congregations 
agreed upon the restoration of an oratory to S. Martin’s. It was signed 
by Amalric, then Dean of S. Martin’s. The secular and therefore distinct 
character of S. Martin’s is indicated by the reference to it as a ‘ basilica.’ 
But the exact significance of ‘ basilica’ is not clear. Vaucelle (p. 39 ff.) 
distinguishes it from ‘ monasterium’ or abbey, and ‘ecclesia,’ a term 
applied to cathedrals and parish churches (following Mabillon and 
Ducange). A ‘ basilica,’ he says, was a collegiate church, partly monastic 
and partly secular in constitution. But Eusebius Bruno (Sudendorf, 
Pp. 222 f.) uses ‘ ecclesia’ of S. Martin. Vaucelle’s conclusion is questioned 
by Levillain (Moyen Age, May-June 1909, p. 197 ff.). Boissonnot, p. 5, 
seems to be on safer ground with the suggestion that a ‘ basilica’ was 
originally a burial chapel attached to a cathedral for the reception of the 
‘ saints,’ and that it became a centre of pilgrimage. This would suit the 
original condition of the chapel of S. Martin’s built by S. Brice over the 
tomb of Martin. But Boissonnot distinguishes a ‘ basilica’ constructed 
by S. Lidore for the cathedral church of S. Maurice from that built 
by S. Brice. In the Martyrol. Usuardi . .. Eccles. Turon, (Bourassé)

The King’s position was difficult. When Leo IX was in 
France in the autumn of 1049, Henry had contested his right 
to exercise jurisdiction upon French soil, and he had succeeded 
in preventing many of the bishops and abbots of France from 
attending the Synod of Reims, on the ground that he wanted 
the presence of the bishops in the army which was about to 
begin a campaign.?, Now came the application from a dis- 
tinguished scholar, who was also a Church dignitary, for per- 
mission to answer a summons which in a similar way offended 
French national prestige, and was contrary to an ancient 
custom whereby an ecclesiastic must be tried in his own 
province. Henry therefore determined to retain Berengar for 
judgment before a French synod. Moreover, he was at war 
with Count Geoffrey of Anjou, the protector of Berengar.* 
Throughout his reign the King had been occupied with the 
endeavour to continue the policy of Robert the Pious (g96—1031) 
which had for its object the repression of the great magnates 


S. Martin’s is called ‘ basilica’ on pp. 37, 42, 65, ‘ ecclesia beata Martini ’ 
(p. 30), and ‘ Sancti martini’ (pp. 37, 41). 

Mabillon sketches (p. 451) the process by which the King of France 
became Abbot of S. Martin’s. When the right of appointment lapsed to 
the Crown, through the inability of the canons to select one of their own 
number, the Emperor appears on occasions to have appointed a local 
magnate, viz. Count Vivian (p. 658). On the break-up of the Carolingian 
empire, the right fell to Robert the Strong, Duke of the French, and to 
Odo his son, King of the West Franks (888-899). Under the Capetians 
the right became hereditary, and so the dignity of Abbot of S. Martin’s 
was finally annexed to the royal house of France.

In his reply Ascelin corrects one of Berengar’s statements 
concerning the conference at Chartres, and says that he had 
misunderstood the remarks of Provost William. He expresses 
surprise that a man of such prudence as Berengar should 
praise the book of John the Scot after confessing that he had 
not read it through, for if he had read it he would not have 
praised it. Ascelin objects to the suggestion that he had 
‘inconsiderately, impiously and in a manner unworthy of his 
priesthood ’ condemned the Scot’s teaching ; on the other hand 
he would retain to the end inviolable the sacred conviction 
of his heart that the bread and wine of the altar, by the power 
of the Holy Spirit and through the ministry of the priest, are 
made? the true body and true blood of Christ. He then 
refers to the discussion which took place at Chartres on 
Gregory’s prayer, and continues: ‘ Your prudence knows 
whether the words of heretics or the cup of poison should be 
avoided, because the latter at first soothes sweetly and then 
silently kills.’ For the rest, with Paschasius and other 
Catholics,” he holds, nay venerates and embraces, the true 
body and true blood of Christ which are to be received by 
the faithful on the altar beneath the form of bread and wine. 
Nor is this contrary to reason. He warns Berengar that his 
own. warning concerning those who retain the keys of know- 
ledge, and neither enter themselves nor permit others to do 
so, may come back on his own head. He urges him to give 
up his perverse ideas, not to be cruel to his friends in an 
unheard-of and vain manner, not to commit himself so freely, 
nor to refuse to submit himself to the wings of the evangelical 
hen,® lest he caused the splendour of mind which God had 
given him to become silly, so that he found himself cast out

need of their support, for new troubles were brewing in

CHAPTER. V 
THE COUNCIL OF VERCELLI 


At Préaux, at Brionne, and at Paris Berengar’s efforts to secure 
support against his enemies had ended in complete failure. 
During this early period of the controversy Berengar does not 
appear to have thought out his own theological position with 
sufficient clearness to convince even his friends of the effec- 
tiveness of his case. So much he admits himself,! and all 
through the dispute the lack of a driving personality prevented 
him from presenting an impressive appeal against the con- 
sistent antagonism of his enemies. It was one thing to 
convince the students of Tours, who were already under the 
influence of his beneficent supervision of the schools, it was 
quite another matter to make headway against strong-willed 
opponents like Lanfranc and Humbert, whose influence in all 
respects was thrown with the heartiest emphasis into the re- 
forming policy of the Papacy. Yet when his powerful friends 
in Anjou had failed to succour him, and when the leading 
magnates of Normandy and France had deliberately checked 
him, he still had friends in Tours and in Italy who dared to 
say a word in his defence at the Council of Vercelli. 

It has been suggested, with probability, that Lanfranc was 
retained in the Pope’s entourage after the Council of Rome 
on account of his familiarity with the Normans.? At Vercelli 
the number of distinguished clergy who assembled for the 
Council on September 1, 1050,3 was not small, but they

In his letter to Henry I, Theoduin of Liége charged 
Eusebius as well as Berengar with reviving old heresies, 
a charge repeated by Durand. ‘They taught that the 
eucharistic body was not a body, but a shadow and figure of

adopt an attitude not entirely consonant with that of the 
Church. Pope Alexander II later on referred to the same 
matter in a letter to Eusebius.t However, these reports 
indicate that the assistance given by the Bishop of Angers to 
Berengar was inspired by more than the desire to support 
the politics of Geoffrey Martel. He sympathised with the 
dogmatic teaching of Berengar. 

About this time the inclination of Eusebius materialised

The clerks of Chartres, like everyone else at that stage of the 
controversy, possessed no written statement of Berengar’s 
views to which they might appeal, so they resorted to the 
curious but unfair device of quoting an inscription upon a silver 
cup which had once been the property of Fulbert, ‘ Woe to the 
prophets, who prophesy from their hearts, saying, “ Thus 
saith the Lord,’ when the Lord hath not spoken!’ They 
persuaded the King that these words were Fulbert’s own, and 
that he had uttered them against Berengar, whereas they were 
a quotation from Augustine,! who took them from Ezekiel.? 
This is a sample of the curious theological mentality of the day, 
which did not scruple to wrench any verse of Scripture from 
its context in order to give point to an accusation or an argu- 
ment. Berengar alleges that Ascelin had attempted to secure 
authority from Augustine in the same way, so also had a com- 
patriot of Ascelin’s in a discussion at Poitiers.2 Henry I 
yielded to these persuasions and gave notice of a council to 
be summoned on French soil in order to deal with Berengar’s 
case.4 Whether or not this correspondence took place before 
the second visit of Leo IX to France in the late autumn of 1050 
is not clear. If it preceded the Pope’s visit, it suggests 
that the King was still jealous of papal interference in the 
ecclesiastical affairs of France, for there is no record of any 
communication between Henry and the Pope. Moreover, 
as Berengar was now a guest of Eusebius at Angers, and 
thus a refugee under the protection of Geoffrey of Anjou,

Augustine, Basil, Eusebius,! and Hilary, showing that Eusebius 
Bruno and Berengar were already anathema. Further action 
against them should be postponed until the French and 
German bishops, ‘ Your friend the Emperor,’ and the Pope 
had deliberated upon the matter.” 

In this last sentence Theoduin reveals his motive in writing. 
It was a clever attempt to win over Henry I to the imperial 
and ecclesiastical policy of Emperor and Pope.? The prior 
place is given to the Emperor because Theoduin knew that 
Henry had resented Leo IX’s action at Reims. Eusebius 
Bruno, the political and ecclesiastical agent of Geoffrey of 
Anjou, Henry’s enemy, is kept.in the foreground all through 
the letter. No reference is made to Berengar’s condemnation 
at Rome and Vercelli, partly because Henry and some of the 
French bishops objected to this action as being contrary to 
the ancient privileges of the French Church, partly because 
Theoduin, a zealous upholder of canonical action, probably 
regarded the condemnation of Berengar, in the absence of the 
latter, as irregular. It is even possible that Theoduin’s letter 
was inspired from Rome, and that a door was being opened 
which would allow a rapprochement between Henry I and the 
Papacy. The Pope had held no Council on French soil during 
his second journey at the end of 1050. If Henry would now 
ask his permission to hold a Council for the examination of 
Eusebius and Berengar, it would be granted, and the royal 
dignity, ruffled by the Synod of Reims, would be placated. 
At the same time, by applying to the Curia, Henry would give 
public, if tacit recognition of Leo’s claim to supervise ecclesi- 
astical affairs in his kingdom. If Eusebius of Angers were 
reprimanded in a French council, Geoffrey of Anjou would 
become further isolated. Thus the case of Berengar was being 
used as a pawn in the ecclesiastico-political policy of the Papacy.

On the other hand, if Henry declined the proposal, offence

the less was this clever despatch an attempt to counter Angevine

Bishop of Angers, was casting around for a combination against 
the Papacy, as the letter of Eusebius to Guy, Archbishop of 
Reims, shows. ‘Theoduin knew that both Eusebius and 
Berengar desired an examination of their case before a French 
council. Berengar informed his friend Richard that, if the 
King wished, he would satisfy him that the condemnation of 
John the Scot and the approval of Paschasius at Vercelli were 
unjust.1_ So Theoduin advised the King not to play into their 
hands. But if Theoduin was an instrument of the Papacy, 
the scheme miscarried, and Henry proceeded with his arrange- 
ments for the Council, although the fact that it did not meet 
until October 1051 may reflect a delay brought about by the 
receipt of Theoduin’s letter. |

Drogo was certainly a writer of beautiful letters, and this 
one contains some significant points. ‘The hostility to Berengar 
at Chartres had now passed beyond the ranks of the illiterate 
clergy whom the nameless good-for-nothing had led against 
him in that city. If Ivo the Grammaticus and later Scolasticus 
of Chartres! was now among his critics, Berengar had cause 
enough to be susceptible to the slightest and least grounded 
report of the disloyalty of his friends, and his complaint against 
Drogo appears to have been justified. In later years a rumour 
of Drogo’s hostility to the Archdeacon reached Liege and 
perhaps Mainz.? It is probable that at this time Drogo’s 
disloyalty had not assumed serious proportions, and that his 
repudiation of the charge was therefore partly justified, yet 
Berengar’s instinct proved to be correct.

On the other hand, Sudendorf shows (p. ror) that the name ‘ Gaufredus ’

The rest of the letter is occupied with a long extract from 
Augustine’s Commentary on S. Matthew x1., on the difference 
between good and bad Catholics, and heretics and schis- 
matics. An extract of this passage was probably sent to 
Berengar by Paulinus of Metz. Heretics are they who 
believe wrongly, bad Catholics are they who believe rightly 
but do not live up to their convictions. Schismatics are they 
who do not hold a different faith but break the fellowship 
of the Church. Yet it is doubtful whether both are to be © 
counted among the tares, rather they should be compared 
with damaged ears of corn... . Nor does it follow that 
every heretic and schismatic should be cut off from com- 
munion with the Church. Indeed, if his doctrine is 
fundamentally wrong, a heretic is in spirit outside the Church, 
although within it in the body. The Church contains many 
of this kind, and they are not driven out unless their numbers 
become great. Schismatics through their conventicles or 
disturbances may be cut off from the unity of the Church in 
spirit, although because they are not discovered they share 
in the sacramental fellowship of the Church. Bad Catholics 
are they who, although believing the true doctrine, yet think 
they have a right to discuss things of which they are ignorant, 
and without hurt to their piety discuss the matter without 
any prejudgment of the truth; or they are those who while 
loving and honouring as much as possible those who are 
good, or whom they think good, yet scandalously and evilly 
live contrary to what they believe. Although such may be 
reprimanded and suspended from Communion, they do not 
themselves think it necessary to withdraw from Catholic 
communion, always seeking an opportunity to return, and 
if death intervenes they remain straw to the end. Their 
desire to return is not moved by a sincere love but rather 
from fear of punishment. . . . For the sake of the unity of 
the Church they are not to be counted among the tares, for 

H 


98 BERENGAR 


they are separate roots; nor among the stalks with ears of 
corn, but among the straw which will be separated at the 
winnowing. ‘The characteristics of good Catholics are then 
described, and the letter ends with the statement that the 
time of the coming of the Son of Man is hidden, in order 
that despair may not make men more cold, but that desire 
may render them more capable of salvation. There are three 
kinds of soil which produce thirty-fold, sixty-fold, and a 
hundred-fold respectively. So the tares and heretics are to 
be tolerated down to the harvest. 

This broad principle of toleration was seldom left on 
record in the eleventh century, yet the action of many leading 
churchmen in that day revealed it. ‘The spirit of persecution, 
which grew increasingly as the Middle Ages advanced, and at 
length became their most cruel vice, was not yet abroad. It 
was tragic that one of its first victims was the man who made 
so noble an appeal for toleration. Several passages in the 
letter are characteristic of Berengar’s thought and method of 
Scriptural exegesis.1 Scripture, if taken at its face value, can 
lead into error. Reason, or common sense, must be applied 
if the truth underlying the words is to be reached. In the 
De Sacra Cena we shall see that this application of the 
dialectical method, in order to supplement the authority of 
tradition, whether Scriptural or patristic, which here only 
outcrops while he discusses a disputed interpretation of a 
particular text, becomes the foundation of the whole system 
of Berengar’s exegesis. The long quotation from Augustine 
on heretics and schismatics may reflect the charge of heresy 
which had been brought against Berengar himself, and may 
indicate that he realised that the day had arrived when he 
and his supporters would be proscribed as heretics.

SYNOD OF TOURS (1054) 


Three years after the assembly of Touraingelle and Angevine 
clergy at Tours in the spring or summer of 1051, another 
and more famous synod was gathered together in that city, 
at which Berengar received more favourable treatment than 
he had ever experienced before, or was to meet for ever 
afterwards. ‘The genesis of this phase of the controversy is 
to be seen in the cessation of hostilities and in the develop- 
ment of a rapprochement between Geoffrey and Henry I, 
which took place not later than August 1052. ‘The result 
of the earlier Synod of Tours, a year or so before that event, 
was not lost upon the Curia. ‘There was a danger lest, with 
the declaration of peace between King and Count, and the 
withdrawal of Henry from the persecution of Berengar, the 
teaching of the Archdeacon might gain a hold in France and 
Anjou, beyond the power of the Papacy to check.t Up to 
this point the attitude of the Curia, if not wavering, had at 
least been one of opportunist manipulation of the eucharistic 
question, and especially of the fortunes of Berengar, in the 
interest of the political policy of the Papacy in France and 
Anjou. Even so early in the Middle Ages, politics, not religion, 
engaged the attention of the astute ecclesiastics at Rome, and 
the case of Berengar was the first instance where the natural 
development of religious doctrine, and the personal rights of 
an individual, were sacrificed to the growing political pro- 
gramme and necessities of the Papacy. In the spring of 
1054. opportunism and expediency gave the cue for the 
change of front among the papal diplomatists which was 
about to be inaugurated. Yet the influence of new person- 
alities on the controversy was making itself felt. Henceforth 
at Rome there were two parties on the Berengarian question.

The rigorous dogmatists were led by Humbert,! supported 
by Lanfranc.? In their hostility to Berengar and his teaching 
they never wavered, and in the end secured his utter defeat. 
But not for a quarter of a century. In the meantime 
Hildebrand and Peter Damiani came to the front. The 
former was a new and rising hope among the practical re- 
formers of the Church, and was therefore in complete 
sympathy with the rigid aims of Humbert and his following, 
yet Hildebrand always considered rather the practical ends of 
politics than of dogma as being the true concern of the 
Church. This did not mean that Hildebrand was any less 
zealous for the reform of clerical life or the revival of spiritual 
religion, but it did imply that he was prepared to allow con- 
siderable latitude to the form in which doctrine was expressed, 
provided that the fundamental teaching of the Church was 
at least tacitly admitted. Moreover, the simplicity and per- 
fection of Berengar’s personal life, and his obvious sympathy 
with the practical aims of the reforming movement, could 
not fail to deflect the attention of a practical mind like 
Hildebrand’s from the real implications of his eucharistic 
teaching. 

Besides Hildebrand there was at the arm of the Curia 
another moderating spirit, of equal zeal on behalf of practical 
reform, in the person of Peter Damiani. Damiani? possessed 
the spiritual vision which Hildebrand lacked, and with 
encouragement might have passed from a halting refusal to 
condemn Berengar into a generous appreciation of the Arch- 
deacon’s somewhat self-assertive mode of handling the 
sensitive fibres of Catholic teaching. He might have accepted

might have moulded it into a winsome expression of spiritual

Europe, with far better results for religion and culture than 
the Radbertian miracles and cultus were able to achieve. 
There is a catholicism of man’s spirit which moves along 
the heights of advancing human endeavour, just as there is 
a catholicism of his behaviour which keeps his feet dragging 
heavily along the trenches of mere ecclesiasticism. It is the 
difference between a Francis and an Ignatius Loyola. 

But Damiani, like Hildebrand, took no active part in the 
reform of dogma or development of doctrine. His interest lay 
even more narrowly within the confines of practical reform. 
Hildebrand shaped his policy with the object of bringing ever, 
more and more, the relations between Church and State 
under the dominance of the Curia. Reform for him meant 
something much wider than the Cluniac ideal of the revival 
of the Benedictine life and the enfranchisement of the secular 
clergy from the sway of territorial magnates. It meant the 
definite entry of the Church into the civil politics of the 
European state-system, in order there to occupy a dominating 
position.1 Damiani, on the contrary, was content to limit his 
activities to the revival of monastic life ;2 to the removal of 
illiteracy from the clergy by the aid of the study of the liberal 
arts as an introduction to theology ;* to the reform of their 
morals by the suppression of simony and clerical marriage,* 
without manifesting the harsh zeal of Humbert ; ° tothe reform 
of ecclesiastical administration by opposing lay-election.® His 
attitude to the Emperor Henry III, whose influence on the 
reform of the Church Damiani supported with unflinching 
consistency throughout the Emperor’s life,’ was something 
more than the idea that without the Emperor’s support the 
practical reform of the Church was impossible. In Damiani’s 
view the Emperor remained predominant over the Pope in civil
