The selection of Tours for the assembly of the Synod is 
significant. It suggests more than the hesitancy of the Curia 
to risk another rebuff from Henry I by ordering it to meet on 
royal territory. The peace between Henry and Geoffrey was 
the result of events in Anjou and Normandy. On the death 
of Hugh, Count of Maine, the citizens surrendered Le Mans to 
Geoffrey, and Henry I was now amenable to Geoffrey’s hostile 
plans against the Norman Duke.* Geoffrey was more than 
ever the dominant political figure in Gaul. Throughout this 
stage of the eucharistic controversy Angevine rather than 
French politics took precedence in the papal policy in the 
West. Moreover, from the point of view of ecclesiastical 
affairs, ‘Tours was a vital centre. It was the one place in 
France or Anjou where the papal policy had been ignored. 
The interdict laid upon the territories of Geoffrey had been 
disregarded, and Berengar was openly supported by the clergy 
of S. Martin’s. It was necessary to deprive the clergy of 
Tours and Angers of their influence upon the course of the 
controversy and to neutralise the assistance given by Geoffrey 
to the Archdeacon. The eucharistic question had now 
assumed for the Papacy a proportion equal to that of other 
questions outstanding between it and the Count, such as the

imprisonment of Gervase of Le Mans. Not only was the 
orthodox faith of the West threatened by the rapprochement 
between Henry and Geoffrey, but the latter was now free to 
make unhindered use of Berengar for his political aims. The 
eucharistic question possessed larger political significance than 
ever.! The matter required careful handling. Any hasty 
condemnation of Berengar, such as had been issued, perhaps 
with sound political insight at Rome and Vercelli, was not 
possible at Tours, where Geoffrey could not be struck at 
through his protégé. Humbert therefore was not selected for 
the business, but the more amenable and versatile Hildebrand, 
whose sympathy with Berengar was probably observed at 
Rome. Two years before, in the midst of his difficulties, 
Geoftrey had written to Leo IX, asking for the despatch of 
a papal legate to examine his case against Gervase,? and 
although Geoffrey’s affairs were now in a prosperous condi- 
tion, he was unlikely to raise objection to an embassy which 
fulfilled his own request, especially as his success in France 
rather imposed an appellant attitude on the Curia.

When the Synod opened its proceedings, Hildebrand pro-

examination of the case themselves, when he would place before

and the Archbishop of ‘Tours together with their clergy.” 

To this procedure Hildebrand agreed. The committee

CHAPTER VII 
NICHOLAS II AND THE COUNCIL OF ROME (1059) 


Durinc the spring of 1054, and probably after the Synod 
of Tours, Berengar regained the favour of Henry I, through 
the intervention of Frollant, Bishop of Senlis.t He had 
apparently written to Frollant asking for his intervention with 
the King, who acceded to the request possibly partly because 
he wished to improve the good relations with Geoffrey, by 
a concession made to Geoffrey’s protégé, partly as a boon 
granted to a dying man.2. On announcing the result of his 
negotiation Frollant sought the intervention of Berengar before 
a higher tribunal. 


1 Frollant speaks of ‘ this Lent,’ so that the letter was written in the 
spring of the year. It can hardly fall in the spring of 1050 (as Schnitzer, 
p-. 13 n. 1, suggests), for Berengar had not then lost the royal favour ; he 
went to Paris in the summer of that year, with full conviction that he 
could secure the King’s moral support for the coming Council of Vercelli. 
It cannot have been written in 1051 (as Bulaeus, p. 421 f., and Oudin, 
p- 629 f., record), or in 1052 (Gfrorer, Kivchengesch., p. 509 n. 1), for Henry 
was not likely to consider Berengar favourably until after the peace 
between the King and Geoffrey of Anjou (not later than August 1052). 
Frollant’s letter might have been written in the spring of 1053, but he was 
probably too ill to be able to write a letter then, for in the letter he refers 
to his approaching dissolution. Sudendorf, p. 25, suggests that he died 
in 1055. The Lent of 1054 is left open as the time when the letter was 
written. But we cannot be certain, for we do not read of Frollant’s 
successor Guy until 1058 (Sudendorf, p. 24), although, of course, his 
election before this date is not excluded. Schnitzer meticulously criticises 
Sudendorf’s statement that Frollant had regained the royal favour for 
Berengar, whereas Frollant says that he had gained it (‘ adquisivi tibi 
gratiam Domini mei Regis’). The absence of allusion to Berengar’s 
teaching or to the persecution of the Archdeacon is natural in a letter 
written by an intimate friend, who was possibly a dying man, especially 
as Frollant had private requests to make of Berengar. Schwabe, p. 72, 
says that the letter was not addressed to Berengar. 

2 Sudendorf, p. 25, suggests that Henry was impressed by the Synod 
of Tours in favour of Berengar, but Frollant had secured the reconciliation 
in Lent, and the Synod did not meet till the end of April or beginning of 
May, well after Easter, which fell on April 3 in 1054. 


THE COUNCIL OF ROME (1059) 117 


Detained by two infirmities, I have not been able, as arranged, 
to come to you, but I beg you to pray for me more than ever that 
I may be released from this sickness which destroys my life. 
I know not whether I shall be able to see you again in this life, 
beloved Master, but take care that I shall see thee in another world 
in peace. But if God preserves my life long enough to give me 
an opportunity of seeing you, I should not lose it, but should fulfil 
my old desire for you by coming to you, for I dare not ask that you 
should come to me this Lent.1 If I am beset by the double mis- 
fortune of not being able to come to you, and of your not being 
able to come to me, and if death seizes on me first, I commit my 
soul to you. Send on behalf of my soul pleading messages to the 
court of heaven. Ask the chief of the archangels and apostles, and 
other leaders of that court, who sit with the great King as friends, 
that they may deign to suggest in so far that He should command 
the liberation of my sinful soul from the prison of death. Yea, do 
you yourself, in prayer, sometimes, yea often, as you do for others, 
approach for me the most reverend and benign King—pray faith- 
fully that He may deign to spare me. The Lord Abbot R.?... 
and his monks and brethren, whom thy love secured for me, salute 
in my name, and ask that they may remember me in their prayers. 
Whatever is pleasing to you let me know. I desire your fraternity 
to know that I have gained completely® the favour of my Lord the 
King for you. Farewell, and although you need no reminder, see 
that you pray for me.‘

before answering, and perhaps he wrote during the period

Council of Rome (1059).®

I would have replied with as much care to your worship’s letter as 
my numerous and most troublesome occupations permit, hoping with 
no small desire if God willed to discuss much with you, and that 
you should hear all that is necessary, but that I had conceived the 
certain hope of seeing and hearing from you, with opportunity for 
delay and revision, on what you wrote at the end of your letter on 
my ideas, if it were in any way possible. It did not seem to me to 
be by any means uncertain that it could be brought about in many 
ways, so that I might see you and hear from you at leisure, among 
which the easiest obviously is that you should make use of the Bishop 
of Chartres in the business. Concerning this I marvel, and mean- 
while I must not be silent, that you seem to think in your letter that 
the blessed Augustine felt differently from others. Clearly I hold, 
and can easily satisfy every lover of truth, and I pray much that 
you may not escape from believing me, that in the matter of the 
Lord’s Table, the blessed Hilary, Jerome, Ambrose and Gregory, 
not to mention others, undoubtedly think the same as Augustine. 
May He who desired to be lifted up that He might draw all 
things unto Himself, carry on the good beginnings in you to better 
endings. 


Evidently the relations between Berengar and Drogo were 
becoming estranged, as SBerengar’s previous complaint 
showed,! but they had not yet reached the acute stage re- 
vealed in Gozechin’s letter of about 1070, when the latter 
could refer to Drogo as the open enemy of Berengar.? 

During these years the enemies of Berengar were not idle. 
In 1055 Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen, held a synod of 
the clergy of Normandy at Rouen, and drew up a definition 
on the doctrine of the Eucharist, to which he required all 
the bishops present to swear,? a proceeding which shows how 
little impression Berengar had made on the Norman clergy 
at Brionne, and how little they regarded the Synod of Tours 
(1054) as a victory for him. The formula was drawn up

We believe with the heart and confess with the mouth that

Victor II was consecrated Pope on April 13, 1055, and 
in June of the same year he held a Council at Florence, in 
the presence of the Emperor Henry III, when the sentence 
passed on Berengar by Leo IX in 1050 was confirmed ;? but 
during Victor’s short pontificate—he died July 27, 1057— 
Berengar was not personally cited by the Curia, nor was any 
action. taken against him during the time of Stephen IX, 
August 3, 1057, to March 29, 1058.

any period of his career, of definite propaganda organised by 
him.? His teaching was becoming more widely known all 
through his life. Naturally it was better known in the towns 
and villages of France? and Anjou than elsewhere. It spread 
to Normandy,* Belgium,® and Germany,§ and by 1059, at the 
latest, it was known in Italy.? But the dissemination of the 
Berengarian teaching was the actual consequence of the 
activity of his pupils when they took up work in the parishes 
and monasteries of France and other parts of Europe, after 
leaving ‘Tours. Lanfranc alleges that Berengar’s writings 
were circulated in this way by his disciples.® If they taught 
the Berengarian doctrine, that was because it represented the 
only theology which they had absorbed during their student 
days. ‘Their peculiar ideas were not confined to the 
Eucharist. ‘They had been trained in a new method of 
scriptural exegesis, which was applied especially to the 
Psalms, the Pauline epistles, and the Apocalypse.!® All this 
gave a new tone and character to their teaching, which by its 
novelty created the impression of a large propaganda being 
at work. Again, there is no evidence that his scholars were 
able to effect any change in the cultus of the Mass. We

was concerned with doctrine, and seems to have been used

was not accompanied by popular outbursts, which would 
have occurred if his doctrine had caused changes in the Mass. 
It took the form of literary activity, proving that their teaching 
was confined mainly to the discussions of the learned. 

At Liége the refutation of Berengar’s doctrine was carried 
on for many years. Adelmann wrote him from Liége.} 
Theoduin addressed Henry I from that city,? both letters 
being written by 1051. Gozechin of Mainz sent his letter 
to Walcher at Liége before 1070.2 ‘The first formal treatise 
against Berengar was written by Hugh, Bishop of Langres, 
by 1049.4. In 1054-58 Durand, Abbot of Troarnin Normandy, 
wrote the first extensive work against the Scolasticus, although, 
as it is not mentioned in the works of Lanfranc or Berengar, 
probably it did not appear till many years later. ‘This book, 
the De Corpore et Sanguine Christi, was written to check the 
spread of Berengar’s opinions in France and Normandy.® 
It briefly traces the history of the controversy from the visit 
of Berengar to Ansfroi at Préaux to the Council of Paris, 
and closes with a passing allusion to another Council which 
can only be that of ‘Tours. He lays chief emphasis on the 
proceedings at Brionne, Chartres, and Paris. ‘To the history 
of this dispute Durand’s book makes a useful contribution, 
and its value for the history of the development of the doctrine 
of the Eucharist from the orthodox standpoint is second only 
to that of Guitmund of Aversa’ in the eleventh century.

Whether a report of this literary activity reached Berengar 
is not known. He makes no reference to it in his writings, 
where the absence of any comment on Durand is curious. 
However, during the period before the Council of Rome 
(1059) he sent a long overdue reply to Adelmann. ‘The 
letter 1 contains the earliest extensive treatment of his theory 
of the Eucharist which has come down to us. Freedom from 
persecution by the civil or ecclesiastical authorities after the 
Synod of ‘Tours may well have encouraged him to begin the 
literary formulation of his views, and to send the first instal- 
ment of them in the form of a reply to Adelmann. Although 
not written in the violent terms of the De Sacra Cena, the 
note of controversy is already struck. His antagonism 
fastens upon Paschasius and Lanfranc, and their supporters 
are described as a ‘ mob’ with whom Paschasius and Lanfranc 
‘rage,’? epithets which occur in the De Sacra Cena? ‘The 
epistle closes with a pun on Adelmann’s name, a literary 
licence which was not regarded with much offence in those 
days; he calls him ‘ Aulusmannus ’—the ‘ Fluteman’ or 
Flutist.4

case had been already tried in his absence by two papal 
councils, no final decision could be reached without the 
appearance of the defendant in Rome. Moreover, the 
eleventh century witnessed a growing tendency on the part

To Hildebrand, venerable son of the Roman Church, Count 
Geoffrey would shew himself not unworthy ? of so great a Mother. 
According to your pleasure, and as you urged in your letter, Berengar 
comes to Rome. You must now act with Christian magnanimity, 
lest he feel you are the same as he found you when you came 
to us empowered with the apostolic authority. He then looked 
for your coming as that of an angel of light. Then indeed you 
came to give life to those who did not live, and to mortify those 
who lived.? Although you observed the falseness of the charge 
of heresy, which extremely evil men, reeking with the fumes of 
envy and pride, invented against him, you did not exert the censure 
of the apostolical dignity by fighting on the side of truth to the 
confusion of its adversaries; rather you appeared to fill the part 
of him who ‘ was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the 
Jews.’ From regard for you I do not refer to him who when he 
had said ‘I find no cause of death in Him,’ did not obtain His 
acquittal from death by the imperial authority, although, indeed, 
you seem to have done even less, for Pilate did not fear to bring 
the Lord Jesus before him, and to bear witness to His innocence. 
You feared to plead for Berengar, and after his enemies had come 
together, you feared to meet him without a crowd, and you did 
not proceed to the excommunication of that fool who hurled an 
anathema against all who denied that the bread did not remain 
on the Lord’s Table, although you knew that he did this with 
impious boldness, contrary to the truth of sound doctrine. You 
were quite silent, contrary to the Gospel saying ‘ He who is ashamed 
of me and my words, of him will I be ashamed in the presence of 
my Father,’ and ‘ Woe to you who hold the key of knowledge, 
who enter not yourselves, and do not permit those who were

Schwabe refers to this letter as a proof that at Angers, in 
spite of Hildebrand’s attitude in 1054, they had not lost con- 
fidence in Berengar.? But it is obvious that the letter reveals 
considerable hesitation in the mind of Berengar concerning 
the support he might expect from Hildebrand at Rome. If 
he was hopeful of a successful issue of the case, he relied for 
the time being rather upon the effect of Geoffrey’s advocacy 
upon Hildebrand ? than upon any conviction existing in the 
mind of the latter which was favourable to his interests. At 
the same time the letter does not preclude the possibility 
that Berengar had received the impression that privately 
Hildebrand was convinced by his views. It is also possible 
that, following the custom of the times, Berengar had sent 
gifts to people at Rome who had promised him support.* 
But his confidence must have been chiefly grounded upon a 
conviction of the righteousness of his cause, and sustained by 
this he travelled willingly to Rome.®

If Berengar counted upon the open support of Hildebrand 
he was grievously disappointed. But in his embittered

against the Cardinal-Archdeacon. Possibly he perceived that

was determined to bring the Scolasticus to absolute sub-

When he attempted to explain his views, the assembly stopped

and untamed spirits, and urged Nicholas to hear him with 
Christian sympathy and fatherly care, or, if that were not

With the intervention of Humbert, the Bishop of Silva 
Candida, an ecclesiastic whose influence at the Curia 
threatened to overshadow that of the great Archdeacon, the 
affair of Berengar was quickly brought to a close. Humbert 
drew up a confession of belief, expressing the doctrine of the 
Eucharist, but couched in terms which never appeared in 
any later official definition of the doctrine. This was placed 
in Berengar’s hands.1 The assembly stood hostile and 
threatening, and he realised that death would be the penalty 
of a refusal to submit. He did not dare to speak again, but 
in silence fell on the ground ? and read the document aloud : 4

for the time being the Curia and its supporters rejoiced in 
their victory over the humiliated Scolasticus. It was regarded 
not only as a triumphant vindication of papal authority,! but 
as the conversion of a famous heretic. ‘ Rejoicing in thy 
conversion,’ writes Lanfranc, ‘ Pope Nicholas sent thy written 
oath to all the cities of Italy, France, and Germany, and 
wherever the report of thy depravity had reached.2 As the 
scandalized churches had before sorrowed over thy falling 
away from truth, so now they rejoiced and gave thanks to God 
for your return and conversion.’? ‘That the Curia sent far 
and wide the news of Berengar’s submission need not be 
questioned, but how far it was from being justified in its 
conviction that the controversy had ended, and that Berengar 
had been won over, the sequel will show.

CHAPTER VIII 
CHANGES IN ANJOU AND ROME 


UNDER great dejection of mind Berengar returned from Rome 
to Anjou. The oath which had been extracted from him by 
threats did not trouble him,! but his conscience could not rest 
under the recollection of having thrown into the fire the 
writings of those whom he admired. This was an entirely 
consistent attitude. Only he who felt that he had missed the 
crown of martyrdom could regret the oath, and Berengar 
never craved for distinction of that kind. He quite properly 
complained of the valuelessness of an oath obtained under 
fear of death. But the surrender of writings of those who had 
enlightened his own mind, and inspired him to stand out 
against the massed opinions of the orthodox churchmen of 
the day, even though also done under compulsion, was an act 
which a less sensitive mind might well look back upon with 
regret and shame. ‘I confess my wickedness to the Lord, 
that heimay forgive the impiety of my sin.’ . ... “Iam an 
unhappy man, most wretched in mind . . . not because I was 
a heretic, but because under the fear of death I did not assert 
the truth, but at the orders of the mob, cast prophetic, evangelic, 
and apostolic writings into the fire.’ ? 

However, no public demonstration was made for the time 
being by Berengar. In the following year (1060) a papal legate, 
Cardinal Stephen, held a synod at Angers.? ‘The acts of the 
Synod were directed against simony, lay investiture, the tenure 
of clerical offices in more than one town,' clerical marriage,

The pamphlet appears to have contained an attack on Lanfranc, 
but was mainly directed against Cardinal Humbert, whom he 
calls the Burgundian.1 ‘The oath which they made him swear 
at Rome was contrary to the Catholic faith, and expressed the 
error of ‘ the foolish Burgundian ’ who drew it up.” But may 
he, like Goliath, perish by his own sword.® Lanfranc is only 
mentioned once in the fragments preserved by the latter, in the 
passage in which Berengar compared the opinion of Humbert, 
that the bread and wine do not remain on the altar after conse- 
cration, with the folly of the mob and of Paschasius and 
Lanfranc. Humbert claimed that his view was that of the 
holy Roman Church, but that Church did not understand 
truth, it was a Church of malignants, a Council of vanity, not 
apostolic, but a chair of Satan.° This pamphlet Berengar 
circulated through his disciples. -

although a material interpretation was expressly condemned. 
The ancient appeal to the almighty creative power of God was 
sustained, and an analogy was drawn from the spiritual process 
of the Incarnation and Resurrection, which were stated to be 
supernatural. At the same time the mystical effectiveness of 
the words of institution—related to the Divine Word—when 
used by the priest, was upheld. 

However, this local settlement of the dispute was soon 
upset by Geoffrey, a canon of S. Martin’s,t who had been 
present at the Council. The facts are made known in the 
letter of Berengar to Eusebius Bruno : 


To Eusebius,” the reverend Lord Bishop of Angers, Berengar 
sends all humble and devout greetings as toa father. It has reached 
me through those who declare they have heard it that Geoffrey of 
S. Martin’s has made a great stir in support of the mad and foolish 
Lanfranc, contrary to evangelical and apostolical truth, which 
is so clear and firm to him who loves truth rather than darkness, 
to him who does not choose himself to be darkness rather than 
light so that the darkness does not understand the light, to him 
who trembles everywhere to say to his God ‘ Depart from me, 
we will not know thy ways ’—truth which is as certain as that two 
and two make four. He has spoken contrary to that public pro- 
nouncement of your Lordship’s dignity and authority, which faith- 
fully written down and committed to memory I can quote, and 
which he himself heard in the chapel of the Countess Hildegarde, 
when Hugh, the Lord Archbishop of Besan¢gon, was present with 
his clerks, together with you and the Bishop of Le Mans and the 
clergy of Angers and Le Mans, whose names I did not delay to

This view of the conduct of Eusebius is entirely disputed by Brécking.

of Eusebius to Geoffrey Barbatus (infra, p. 150) shows that he was not so 
completely bound up with politics as Semisch and Schwabe maintained.

Sudendorf showed that this letter, as well as that of Berengar which 
called it forth, could not have been written before the Synod of Angers in 
1062, nor after the death of Bougrin (1065 ; cf. Bishop), one of the bishops 
mentioned by Berengar in hisletter(p.14o0f.). This conclusion was followed

The conclusions of the latter were challenged by Schnitzer in Der 
Katholik (Mainz), ii. (1892) 544 ff. 

Broécking (Deut. Zeit. f. G.-W., v. 361 ff.) maintains that the last pro- 
vincial synod mentioned by Eusebius is that of Angers, 1062, and the 
last Roman synod referred to by him as settling the dispute could not 
have been one which came before this date. It was thus the Synod of 
1079, not 1059. Consequently the letter of Eusebius, and also that of 
Berengar, were written after the Synod of Rome, February 11, 1079. 

Replying to Broécking, Schnitzer contended that Eusebius did not refer 
to the four Councils in chronological order ; that the expression “ extincta ’ 
applies as little to the Roman Council of 1079 as to that of 1059, for 
Berengar was not silenced by either Council, and that at neither date 
would the statement of Eusebius have suited the orthodox doctrine of the 
day. Brécking has overlooked the strained relations between Berengar 
and Eusebius before 1079. Wemay add that the four councils referred 
to by Eusebius appear to have been Tours (1051 and 1054), Rome (1059) 
and Angers (1062). 

Brécking’s answer (Deut. Zeit. f. G.-W., xii. 344 ff.) produced little 
more than his previous argument. The word ‘extincta’ cannot 
apply to the Roman Council of 1059, because the matter was again 
discussed in 1062, according to Eusebius’ report. The term ‘ extincta’ 
strengthens the word ‘terminata’ applied to the three provincial 
synods, and so refers to a synod held after them, otherwise Eusebius 
expresses himself badly. He cannot follow Schnitzer’s logic when he 
alleges that ‘ extincta’ applies as little to 1079 as to 1059, for in 
that case Eusebius’ head was as confused as Schnitzer’s. He declines 
to discuss the relation of Eusebius’ orthodoxy to the question. Eusebius

This letter contains no proof that Eusebius now abandoned 
Berengar, withheld from him all further support, and became 
fully orthodox on the eucharistic question himself.1_ Relations 


does not write as a historian, taking note of chronological order. If 
Eusebius, according to Brécking, does not refer to the Council of 1059, 
that was because he does not deal completely with the synodal decisions, 
as is proved by the fact that he does not mention Rome and Vercelli 
(1050). Theletter of Alexander II to Bartholomew and Eusebius (Bishop,

and Berengar, but Brécking admits that in his previous article he ought 
to have noticed the strained relations between them in the period before 
1079 (Deutsche Zeitschrift fir Geschichtswissenschaft, Xli. 349 D. 4). 

The only fair comment in the whole of Brécking’s elaborate defence 
is his contention (zb7d. p. 348 f.) that Schnitzer’s argument ex stlentio, from 
the absence of any reference to the Roman Council of 1079 by Berengar, 
is not material, for its proceedings did not greatiy help his case, although 
Brécking agrees with Schnitzer that they did, and so weakens his criticism. 
He slurs over some significant points, viz. Schnitzer’s contention that 
‘ extincta ’ applies as little to 1079 as to 1059; the question of Eusebius’ 
orthodoxy ; and in one or two instances he unwittingly concedes the force 
of Schnitzer’s remarks, viz. by alleging that Eusebius does not deal as a 
historian chronologically with his details. 

Brécking’s argument is built up on the interpretation of a single 
passage (the concluding sentence in Eusebius’ letter reporting the three 
provincial synods and one Roman Council). It omits to notice that 
Eusebius’ answer is concerned with a revival of the controversy which 
had recently taken place at Angers, that he refers to Hildebrand as ‘ Hilde- 
brand’ and not ‘ Gregory VII,’ a curious slip if his letter was written 
after 1079. He does not perceive that in 1079, with seventeen years of 
the controversy in retrospect, Eusebius could not have referred to the 
controversy as having been stamped out in 1062. Moreover, Eusebius 
makes no reference to Berengar in his letter to Alexander II (Sudendorf, 
p. 222 ff.), so that the relations between the two were very strained in 1067 
when that letter was written (ifra, p. 151). 

Broécking states that the date of Berengar’s letter to Eusebius depends 
on the date of Eusebius’ answer (Zeztschrift fiir Kirchengeschichte, Xii1. 173). 
The reverse is true. If Berengar wrote in 1079 he would not have appealed 
to the proceedings of an obscure provincial synod which had taken place 
seventeen years before, nor was a man of about eighty years of age, who 
had endured the severe humiliation imposed upon him at Rome in 1079, 
likely to trouble much about the action of an obscure ecclesiastic at Angers 
seventeen years before. The setting of Berengar’s letter is clearly that of 
the Synod of Angers (1062), and the action ascribed to the Canon Geoffrey 
is closely related to that Synod, at a time when it would have been 
peculiarly irritating to Berengar, who had interpreted Eusebius’ action 
at the Synod as peculiarly favourable to himself. So that Sudendorf’s 
date, as corrected by Bishop, for Berengar’s letter to Eusebius may stand. 

All parties are agreed that the reply of Eusebius followed within a 
year after Berengar’s letter, so that Sudendorf’s date, also corrected by 
Bishop for that letter, may also stand. Francke, p. 616, dates it c. 1063. 
The critical word ‘ quarto’ was a loose expression referring to the Roman 
Council of 1059. We have seen that even Brécking is compelled to admit 
that Eusebius did not write chronologically. The question of Eusebius’ 
relation to Geoffrey Barbatus is discussed above in the text.

In the opinion of contemporaries, Eusebius was a supporter of 
Berengar’s teaching, if not the leader of the whole Berengarian 
movement,” and we do not read that this estimate was ever 
modified. By his recantation at Rome in 1059 Berengar escaped 
the repetition of the condemnation of 1050, and officially was 
regarded as a true member of the Church, so that there was no 
reason for his friends to fear that they might become involved 
in any judicial proceedings with the Curia. The Papacy at 
this date was willing to leave its servants to their private 
opinions on dogma, provided they did not by public action 
create disturbance or inspire doubts of orthodox teaching in 
the public mind. Thus, continued sympathy with Berengar’s 
doctrinal views was quite consistent with the action taken 
against him by Eusebius in his letter.

In my anxiety I can only think of your activity at Rome, which 
has experience for every contingency and to which I would make 
known what has been done concerning me. Your kindness, well- 
disposed towards me in everything, will know that the hatred of 
the Court has disturbed all which the divine bounty gave me at 
Angers—access to the city, and attendance, which as a clerk and 
archdeacon I owed to the Church at Angers, has been for several 
years altogether denied to me. It were superfluous to urge you 
to pity my vicissitude, or to suggest in an official way, how the 
eminence of the Roman dignity ought to meet my great persecu- 
tion. It is commonly said ‘A friend and physician are proved 
by necessity.’ For what reason I say this you can understand— 
for this certainly, that you will not disdain to discharge for me now 
a kindness, as much as you were never able to do before—that it 
may not be burdensome for you to secure the papal condescension 
to my devoted salutation. I was worthy of receiving his salutation 
and apostolic blessing through Rahard of Orleans, and the Bishop 
of Nantes, although not through a letter.1_ Therefore the merciful 
God will not deny to me a great benefit through you, if you are 
able to secure papal letters concerning me to the Archbishop and 
the Bishop of Le Mans and Angers, to check the madness of the 
envious, the insane and the dastardly. For this purpose no one 
occurs to me so suitable, so efficacious and so necessary, if you will 
not deny the labour of your love for this object. All that you 
desire from me by way of compensation shall be paid.2 Let no 
expense deter you from this, I will repay your charges fourfold if 
you wish it. For the rest, brother Rahard has notified me that 
the Lord Pope is disposed to send here one of his relations, to be 
educated.* If he does decide this, let him not delay or pro- 
crastinate from seeing that he does come to us, and for the rest 
let him not be solicitous concerning his sojourn with us or return 
to him if he orders it so.*

This letter was accompanied or followed by another directed 
to Bartholomew, Archbishop of Tours,! and to Eusebius, 
Bishop of Angers. The Pope says that Count Geoffrey 
Barbatus had been stirred up by certain people who were 
enemies of Berengar to hatred of the Scolasticus, as if he (the 
Count) were burning for the defence of the Christian faith. 
Berengar, frightened by the threats of Geoffrey, dared not 
exercise his function as Archdeacon in the church at Angers. 
The bishops are charged to warn the Count, on the authority 
of the Curia, not to disturb Berengar any further. It was not 
the Count’s business to interfere in a dispute on the Eucharist.? 
Berengar’s request that the Bishop of Le Mans might be 
admonished by the Pope was not fulfilled, possibly on account 
of the death of Bougrin (May 10, 1065), or because of political 
incidents at Le Mans.® 

About the same time the Pope wrote to Geoffrey, expressing 
surprise that he had despised the authority of the blessed Peter, 
and had not obeyed, but persistently disobeyed, the directions 
senttohim. Hecommands Geoffrey to desist from persecuting 
Berengar, whose life and conversation are, by the report of good 
men, worthy of God, so that there could be no doubt that true 
charity rules in him. Clearly his assiduity in alms-giving can 
hardly be equalled by that of any bishop. So Geoffrey is 
ordered not to disturb him, but, preserving the honour of the 
holy Roman Church, he is to give him opportunity to remain 
in his office so that he may happily reach the door of 
salvation.*

to conduct his business, to carry on his office, and to feel that 
in the Count he had a protector and helper. If Geoffrey con- 
tinued to disobey, no further admonition would be issued, but 
excommunication would follow. 

Still the Count paid no heed to the papal warnings, and 
by this time was involved in a violent dispute with the Abbey 
of Marmoutier at Tours, and with Bartholomew, the Arch- 
bishop, so that if Berengar suffered increased persecution, 
this was because, as a Canon of S. Martin’s, he became 
involved in Geoffrey’s dispute with Archbishop Bartholomew. 
The quarrel arose over the question of lay-election, or in- 
vestiture, which was assuming burning proportions all 
over western Europe. On May 20, 1064, Albert, the Abbot 
of Marmoutier, a supporter of Berengar, had died. On 
January 26, 1065,? the monks elected Bartholomew, who is 
to be distinguished from the Archbishop of Tours. Geoffrey 
Barbatus ordered the new abbot to receive investiture with 
the symbols of his office from himself.? Although the right 
had been conceded to the Courts of Anjou in the case of 
many other abbeys, the right of free election at Marmoutier 
had been expressly preserved at the cession of Touraine to 
Geoffrey Martel in 1044. Geoffrey Barbatus threatened to 
destroy the monastery if Bartholomew did not submit, and 
violently rejected the intercession of no less a personage than 
Hugh, Abbot of Cluny. The Count shouted that he knew 
how to subdue these monks like asses, and when the Abbot 
of Cluny, with an imploring gesture, grasped the flap of his 
mantle, Geoffrey tore off the buckle and left him without 
further reply. The monks remained obdurate and he

The accession of Fulk to the territories of his brother 
alleviated, for a time, the persecution which Berengar had 
suffered from the Count of Anjou. He seems to have 
supported the policy of both Fulk and Eusebius, and of the 
clergy and people of Tours, which opposed the appointment 
of Radulf by Philip of France, in succession to Bartholomew, 
as Archbishop of Tours.2 For a time the Papacy approved 
the opposition to Philip, doubtless in accordance with its 
campaign against lay-election; but in later years Radulf 
received recognition from the Curia, and proved a strong 
supporter of its action against simony.4 In the meantime 
Fulk appears to have left the eucharistic controversy to take 
its course, and if he did not persecute Berengar, still less did 
he give him the active assistance which the Scolasticus had 
enjoyed in the days of Geoffrey Martel. From the beginning 
of the eucharistic controversy he had been involved in 
Angevine politics, and had experienced the extremes of 
favourable and hostile treatment from the Counts of Anjou, 
but now he found himself ignored by the Angevine Court.®

Drogo’s view that he could not claim support from Augustine. 
The strained relationship between the two friends was now 
relieved. Possibly reports of Count Geoffrey’s ill-treatment of 
Berengar had revived Drogo’s former loyalty towards him. 
If so, the rapprochement was reciprocal. About this time 
Drogo became ill, and Berengar seized the opportunity to 
write to him a letter which was quite free from the querulous 
complaint of his last epistle. 


To Drogo, the well-beloved brother in the Lord Jesus, Berengar 
sends greeting, worthy of a lord, worthy of his learning. I know 
I ought to have written to you far otherwise, but after I had heard 
that God had restored to me the solace of your kindness, I thought 
better to write to you than to ignore any longer the moderation of 
God’s dealing with you. Moreover, it was in my mind to offer to 
your dignity, by the speedy pen of a letter, whatever the office of 
my love could do for you as a blessing. God is my witness that 
I have not more gladly written to you, than I should be to see you 
and hear you, to enjoy your personal observation and conversation, 
if He had made it safe for me to go anywhere to see my friends. 
Farewell! May the equality and inseparability of the godhead and 
of eternity graciously preserve your love for me uninjured.*

A passage in the long epistle of Gozechin, the Scolasticus 
of Mainz, to Walcher, his successor as Scolasticus at Liége, 
includes Drogo among the enemies of Berengar. Gozechin 
says that Hermann of Reims, Huormann of Speier, and 
Mainhard of Bamberg, who had formerly been attracted by 
Berengar’s teaching, had now surrendered it. This letter 
was written about 1069,1 and need not indicate that the 
renewal of friendship between Berengar and Drogo was not 
lasting. Gozechin was writing at Mainz,? where the contents 
of a private correspondence, about 1068, between Berengar 
and Drogo could scarcely have been known to him, and 
obviously could not have percolated through by devious 
routes so soon as 1069. Even if it had done so it was 
improbable that Gozechin would give much attention to 
it. His object in writing to Walcher was to condemn the 
Berengarian teaching, and especially its author. He there- 
fore made use of public reports of Drogo’s hostility, which 
had been in circulation for some years.? 

The chief significance of Gozechin’s letter, which has the 
proportions of a treatise, lies in its testimony to the spread 
of Berengar’s teaching, through the medium of his scholars, 
when they had left Tours. ‘See what a sound doctrine,

THE enemies of Berengar did not rest, and at this time his 
most watchful and persistent opponent took a step which 
might have upset Alexander II’s kindly toleration of Berengar 
if the Pope had lived much longer. Whether Berengar’s 
pamphlet, written between the autumn of 1059 and the year 
1062,1 reached Lanfranc immediately, or was delayed by the 
persecution of the Scolasticus by Geoffrey Barbatus, which 
broke out in the latter year, is not known. But between the 
years 1066 and 1068 or 1069 Lanfranc replied in a treatise, 
the De Corpore et Sanguine Domini, which he directed to 
Berengar in the form of a letter.2. It is divided into twenty-

Lanfranc,’ as Berengar alleged, but formed the view of the 
Catholic Church, although they certainly were not held by 
Berengar or his following, who preferred proudly to separate 
themselves and to make a schism, rather than to be humble 
members of the Church, and to maintain common faith with it 
in a healthy manner.t Lanfranc preferred to be rather a simple 
man with the mob and a stupid Catholic than a courtier and 
an elegant heretic with Berengar.? 

He was not concerned with Berengar’s alternatives that if 
the bread and wine of the altar only are sacraments, or if the 
bread and wine of the altar only are the true body and blood of 
Christ, in either case the elements of bread and wine remained. 
He was not asked to believe this by the Roman Council, nor 
was it delivered to him by Humbert. The first proposition 
was his own, the second was held by no one. Lanfranc was 
concerned only with the formula drawn up at Rome, by the 
denial of which Berengar now committed perjury, in the little 
work which Lanfranc had received to be destroyed. Pope 
Nicholas, understanding that Berengar denied that there was 
a material change in the elements, granted him leave to defend 
his position, but Berengar had not dared to do this. Then it 
was that from compassion the Pope granted his request that 
the formula, already quoted, should be handed to him. So, 
if Berengar went back on the words of the oath which had been 
handed to him, he was guilty of perjury. ‘O! unhappy man. 
O! wretched soul. Why did you swear that you believed 
that which you yourself understood quite otherwise ? Would 
it not have been better, if you thought you had the truth, 
to have ended your life by an honest death, than to swear 
perfidiously and to abjure your faith?’* Lanfranc defends 
Humbert against Berengar’s charge that the former could not 
escape from the belief that the bread and wine remained on 
the altar by taking refuge in the statement that it survived in 
a supermaterial ° form. To speak of the Roman Church as 
a Church of malignants, a Council of vanity and chair of Satan 
was to say what no heretic, schismatic, or false Christian had 
ever said before.®

The remainder of Lanfranc’s first seventeen chapters are 
occupied chiefly with a refutation of Berengar’s quotations from 
Augustine and Ambrose,! and with quotations from those 
Fathers which Lanfranc himself discusses in support of his 
own arguments.2, He quotes Gregory? and Cyprian‘? and 
makes frequent reference to the Scriptures. 

The second part of the treatise,® in which Lanfranc develops 
his own theory of the Eucharist, consists mainly of an exegesis 
of passages of the Fathers, taken from the writings of Augustine ® 
and Ambrose,’ although statements of Jerome,® Gregory,’ and 
Leo the Great 1° receive attention. Lanfranc’s chief contribu- 
tion to the development of the doctrine was his theory of a 
change of essence which did not involve a change of accidence. 
It only remained for Guitmund to substitute the theory of 
a change of substance, and the terminology as well as the theory 
of T'ransubstantiation had been worked out.1! The De Corpore 
et Sanguine Domini does not rise to the level of Guitmund’s 
great work on the Eucharist. Still less does it contain the 
philosophic insight and originality of illustration of Berengar’s 
own work, the De Sacra Cena, nor does it present a more 
orderly and methodical treatment than Berengar’s book. 
Indeed, so far as Berengar follows Lanfranc’s points almost 
seriatim, the disorganisation of his own work is partly a 
reflection of Lanfranc’s method, although the De Corpore et 
Sanguine Domini is not marred by the constant and wearisome 
repetition of the De Sacra Cena. Perhaps the qualities of 
a sustained and closely reasoned treatise, which had marked 
the work of Paschasius Radbert and of Ratramn in the ninth 
century, and were revived again in the treatises of Durand and 
Guitmund in the eleventh, could not be expected in a work 
which was undertaken as a polemical letter, and was chiefly

Soon after completing his treatise, Lanfranc left Caen for 
England (August 1070). The first eighteen months of his 
archiepiscopate were occupied by the dispute with Thomas, 
Archbishop of York, on the primacy question. In the midst of 
this, in 1071, he visited Alexander II at Rome, when the Pope 
referred the question back to an English council.1 During 
this visit Lanfranc was the honoured guest of the Pope,? and 
the Berengarian controversy must have been discussed. If 
Alexander had not heard of Berengar’s pamphlet, he would 
then learn about it from Lanfranc, and then, or later by letter, 
the Pope requested the Archbishop to send him a copy of his 
reply to Berengar. ‘This was despatched in 1072,3 together 
with a long letter reporting the issue of the primacy question 
in England. Bernold of Constance says that Alexander II 
wrote a friendly letter to Berengar, urging him to desist from his 
opinions, and to cease scandalising the Church.* ‘This report 
has been discredited.® But Bernold had received the testimony 
of eye-witnesses and was a contemporary of Berengar, and was

Berengar had stated in his earlier work that although Humbert

To the charge of perjury Berengar replies: ‘ If I swore 
what I ought not to have sworn, and then, overcome by 
penitence, did not keep my oath, it was neither wise nor 
prudent to regard that as an execrable perjury. ‘To swear 
what ought not to be sworn is to depart from God, to surrender 
a bad oath is to return to God. S. Peter, after he had sworn 
that he did not know Christ, could not have remained a 
disciple of Christ if he had persisted in his bad oath.’ He 


continues, later on : 


Certainly, driven by fear of death, not being dealt with by 
Christian charity, I was able to swear something not in the name 
of the living God which was contrary to law and right, and fully 
repenting of this oath, I could break it, as it has not escaped your 
watchfulness. But that was not a base, but a virtuous and credit- 
able action. It ought not to have been shameful, as you say, to read 
out what was handed to me, but rather, it was shameful not having 
refused what was to be handed to me, then to refuse it. I confess 
—apart from what is concerned with the oath, for there is nothing 
against me there—my sin to the Lord, that He may forgive my 
wickedness, so far as, being disturbed by fear of imminent death, 
I was silent on the truth, that I did not abhor casting the prophetical, 
gospel and apostolical writings into the fire. But who art thou, 
priest and monk, that doest business with me with no consideration 
for mercy? You, a priest, having seen me torn by robbers, and 
left half-dead, passed by on the other side, but God hath provided, 
since He did not leave me to the invective of thy righteousness. 
No less than against me is thy invective directed towards Aaron, 
the priest of the ancient people; towards Peter, the rock of the 
Church; towards Plato, the pearl of philosophy. . . . I beg that 
the bowels of mercy of all who chance to read this book may be 
extended towards me, not as a heretic, which you, by the mercy of 
God, lyingly ascribe to me, but because from fear of imminent 
death I kept silence from defending the truth, because at the order 


of the mob I threw prophetical, gospel and apostolic writings into 
the fire.’

returns to Pope Nicholas and the Roman Council of 1059,? 
and passes on to a long and involved discussion of the doctrinal 
aspects of the dispute. 

This trenchant refutation of Lanfranc’s statements is 
accompanied by language which treats the Popes with scant 
respect. He alludes to ‘that Leo’* and ‘thy Leo,’ ® ‘ that 
Nicholas ’® with the same scorn as ‘thy Humbert’’ and 
‘that Humbert.’§ He would not call Leo holy, certainly not 
a lion of the tribe of Judah. The words ‘ Ye are of your 
father, the devil,’ applied to him. He had not found him 
to be an honest man.? He speaks with opprobrium of the 
Church as ‘a crowd of simpletons,’ 1° the Roman Council is 
‘a Council of vanity,’ 44 ‘a blind leader of the blind,’ * ‘a flock 
of illiterates,’ 4% and the bishops and abbots come under the 
lash of his invective. The uncanonical election of the bishops 
and abbots is an indication of their worthlessness,!4 and he 
bewailed the days of the Church’s infancy, when elections to 
bishoprics and abbeys were canonically made, and good men 
were appointed.!® ‘This is the only reference in all his writings 
to the burning question of lay-investitures, which was soon 
to involve Church and State, from Pope and Emperor down- 
wards, in an internecine strife.

the Church,® and his defence of papal revenues shows that

writings. It was the function of authority to supply a proper

About 1075 1 appeared an equally extensive work on the 
Eucharist from the pen of Guitmund.? This writer was an 
old pupil of Lanfranc at Bec, who became a monk at Lefroy 
in Normandy. He travelled to England, where he refused 
an English bishopric from the hands of William, because he 
could not condone the slaughter entailed by the Conquest? 
In 1079 he declined the archbishopric of Rouen on the same 
grounds, and passed on to Italy, where Gregory VII 
nominated him to the college of Roman cardinals, and 
Urban II made him Archbishop of Aversa. His work, the 
De Corporis et Sanguinis Christt Veritate in Eucharistica,* 
was written in Normandy before his departure for Rome.® 
The first two books are in the form of a dialogue between 
Guitmund and another monk named Roger on the main 
points of the Berengarian teaching. In the third book he 
deals with some additional matter, notably the theory of 
impanation.6 At the beginning of the dialogue he draws 
attention to four types of Berengarianism.’ His wide travels 
gave him ample opportunity of estimating and comparing the 
results of Berengar’s teaching, although he writes with a 
strong bias against Berengar, yet without the acrimonious tone 
of Lanfranc. ‘The work is of less value than that of Durand 
and Lanfranc for the history of the controversy,’ although

CHAPTER X 
GREGORY VII AND THE ROMAN COUNCILS (1078~79) 


On April 21, 1073, Alexander II died, and on the next day, 
before the funeral services were over, the crowd from the 
city invaded the Lateran, shouting for Hildebrand to be Pope. 
Hildebrand tried to calm the multitude, but he was put aside 
by Cardinal Hugh, who addressed the people and proposed 
the election of Hildebrand. ‘The unanimous shout of cardinals, 
clergy, and people overcame the protests of Hildebrand at 
the nature of the proceedings, and he was hurried to the 
Church of S. Pietro in Vincoli, where the election was 
formally confirmed.1 No such enthusiasm and unanimity 
had ever before marked the elevation of a Roman bishop, and 
a parallel is to be sought in the election of Ambrose at Milan, 
when the popular will obtained the consecration of the 
Consular of Liguria and Aemilia, but no better choice could 
have been made than of him who for twenty years and more 
had been the safest brain and surest hand behind the politics 
of the Curia. 

When Alexander II died, the clouds were again threatening 
to gather over Berengar. We have seen that the Pope was 
beginning to become uneasy. The generous but wise friend- 
ship shown by him towards Berengar had not been met by 
restraint and submission on the side of the Scolasticus. 
If the waning support of his friends in Anjou had fore- 
shortened the opportunity for an active propaganda from his 
archidiaconal stall at Angers, and from his lecture-room at 
Tours, Berengar had taken up the formal defence and propa- 
gation of his eucharistic teaching by entering into a literary 
contest with the orthodox leaders of the day. At first he 

1 W.R.W. Stephens, Hildebrand and his Times (1903), p. 8o f. 


176 BERENGAR 


concentrated his criticism upon Leo IX and Humbert, but 
when Lanfranc defended the Pope and Cardinal, Berengar 
widened his attack and included the Abbot of Caen and 
Nicholas II within his strictures. 

Quite early in his pontificate Gregory VII found it 
necessary to warn Berengar to remain quietly at Angers, to 
be silent under attack, and not to discuss the question until 
an opportunity was provided of doing so before the Pope. 
Was Berengar beginning to take up the defence of his views 
by visiting other places, or did Gregory wish him to dis- 
continue his lectures at Tours? It is clear that conditions at 
Angers were now sufficiently favourable to permit a quiet 
retreat there for Berengar, ifhe had desired it. Fulk of Anjou 
had not yet taken up his brother’s hostility towards him. 

At this time one of the earlier symptoms of the dispute 
reappeared. There was for a moment a danger lest the cause 
of Berengar should again be adopted by the civil authorities. 
Philip of France was drawing the attention of the Curia more 
and more upon himself, by outraging public feeling and by 
breaches of Church law. He was gluttonous and lazy, but the 
free use which he made of his marriage vows drew rebuke 
after rebuke upon him until he was finally excommunicated 
at the Council of Clermont (1094) by Urban II, where 
Berengar’s teaching was also condemned.? The King en- 
deavoured to secure the support of Berengar,? who, in the 
dispute over the appointment of Radulf to the archbishopric 
of Tours, was really one of Philip’s opponents. But enemies 
often draw together under the stress of a common affliction, 
especially if it arises from the same source. Inthe royal action 
we may see an indication that Philip was aware that Berengar 
was again losing ground with the Curia,‘ and that his following 
in Anjou and Touraine was again growing. Philip would not 
have applied to an isolated heresiarch. But Berengar himself 
removed any anxiety that a new political complication was 
about to spring from the eucharistic controversy. He replied

to the King at length, but definitely upheld the Church’s 
attitude on the points raised by Philip. He declined to be 
drawn into a discussion on the theory of the Eucharist, and 
warned the King against continuing in his misdeeds. He also 
made use of the opportunity to rebuke the royal action 
concerning the archbishopric of Tours. 


The words of the apostle are ‘ Let a brother remain in the 
vocation to which he is called.’ God has called you to direct 
the government of the kingdom. On what you ought to do in this 
matter your coronation oath was not silent. If you have kept this 
oath inviolate from that time, you will at length obtain a peaceful 
kingdom and renown. For the rest certain are not silent that the 
royal dignity ought to devote greater attention to the Lord’s Table, 
more application to the fulfilment of righteousness, more joyfulness 
in giving alms, more recourse to the Church at the regular hours 
of prayer. . . . Concerning the practice of righteousness, what 
pertains to the King’s person, pertains to his dignity. As for works 
of charity to be cheerfully done, that concerns not only the royal 
sublimity, but all those who, at the judgment day, are to be placed 
on the right hand. ‘The Lord Himself teacheth saying, ‘ When the 
Son of Man cometh He will say, Come, ye blessed children of my 
Fathets .. 42° .was hungry and ye fed» me.’ ..... As to. other 
works of mercy the King’s watchfulness should study this, that he 
ought to do more who has received more from the Lord. . . . As 
for prayer, we have the prescript of the Lord . . . and the gospels 
advocate short prayers. Augustine says that in the primitive 
Church, people went morning and evening to church, and that 
the Egyptian hermits used ejaculatory prayer. . . . Prayer is not 
to be urged against the claims of other good works, a maxim 
especially applicable to kings, and all who assist in the adminis- 
tration. But monks and canons are to persevere in the rule which 
they have chosen. I intended later to deal with my first point 
which concerned partaking of the Sacrament of the Lord’s Table. 
The Lord says ‘ He who eateth my flesh and drinketh my blood 
abideth in me, and I in him,’ and the apostle says ‘ Let a man 
prove himself, and then eat of that bread and drink that cup. He 
who eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh condemna- 
tion to himself.’ Augustine says ‘ Remembering your stations and 
maintaining your vows, approach the flesh and blood of the Lord. 
But if a man knows himself to be otherwise let him not come.’ . . . 
As to relations with women at festival seasons, he says ‘ No one 
wants to come to church in a soiled garment, then why has he 
boldness to approach the altar with a soul besmirched by wanton- 
ness? If one ought to blush to touch the Eucharist with soiled 
hands, how much more to receive it with a polluted soul.’ Hilary 
says that infirm souls, grown old in sin, cannot receive the 

N 


178 BERENGAR 


Sacraments of the new grace, for the rent becomes worse, the new 
wine and the old bottles perish. ‘The reason is twofold, for because 
of the age of their sins, they cannot bear the virtue of the new grace. 
Cyprian says that no sinner ought to arrogate to himself the authority 
or use of the Sacraments. Jerome says ‘ Woe to the evil man who 
approaches the Table of the Lord, who, with a mind full of craft, 
with a heart besmirched with filth, does not fear to share in the holy 
oblations of the mysteries of Christ.’ Augustine draws a distinction 
shewing that those who are under penance for crimes, of whom the 
apostle says ‘ Those who act thus do not attain to the Kingdom of 
God,’ do not approach the Lord’s Table . . . as much as those 
who for crimes should not cease rigorously offering sacrifices of 
alms, fasting, and prayers themselves, and supplications. Con- 
cerning those who think a man ought to communicate frequently, 
even daily, and those who think less frequently, though both act 
legitimately, Augustine thus states the case. . . . On the contrary 
someone may say that if the wound of sin is so great that such 
medicines are to be postponed, each ought to be removed from the 
altar by the authority of the bishop, lest each freely comes or stays 
away at his own will. . . . Perchance he decides more correctly 
between them who advises that each shall above all remain in the 
peace of Christ, and that each shall do according to what he faith- 
fully believes he ought. I apologise for the prolixity of my letter, 
but the royal commands are responsible for this. I am coming 
to the end. I will tell you the words of Augustine. He said to 
Boniface, a Roman Count, ‘ May conjugal modesty, sobriety and 
frugality adorn your behaviour. ‘To act well and not to abstain from 
unlawful things is a conspiracy of error. . . . You complain of the 
heavy fight.’ . . . Take arms in your hands, let prayer smite the 
ears of your Maker, for when fighting occurs, God, having opened 
the heavens, sees, and gives a righteous victory to the side at which 
He looks. Rule justly, claim nothing in your own strength, boast 
rather in the Author of virtues, and you will fear no enemy. Fare- 
well! May God long preserve your royal dignity for our solace and 
consolation, devoted to prayer so long as other good actions are not 
neglected, communicating in the Sacrament of the Altar on the 
fixed solemn and festival days, so far as the aforesaid causes do not 
prevent you, and taking care to perform adequately works of mercy 
to the utmost, and to do justice, and in this way concerning the 
sacrilege against the Church of the blessed Martin, exercise the 
rigour of the royal censure, delaying not at all to the honour of 
Christ and so great a Confessor. 


This admirable epistle is full of the same large-hearted 
wisdom which appears in the letter to the hermits.? Avoiding

bald and crude allusions to the royal misdeeds, he makes quite 
clear his disapproval of the King’s actions. Religious duties 
are not to be neglected, but they are not to be overdone, and 
full allowance is made for the busy preoccupations of a king’s 
life. ‘he wise admonitions concerning prayer and attendance 
at the Eucharist might have been given by a prudent and 
sympathetic modern bishop to an administrator immersed in 
the duties of office. 

The refusal of Berengar to lower the standards of the 
Church, or to be drawn into a political union against the 
Papacy,! did not prevent a renewal of synodical action against 
himself. At Poitiers, on January 13, 1076,7 the legate Gerald 
held a synod at which the Berengarian question was again 
handled. The turbulent outbursts which necessitated the 
intervention of Leo IX on behalf of Berengar’s supporters at 
Vercelli in 1050, and the intervention of Eusebius Bruno at 
Tours in 1054, were repeated. But on this occasion Berengar 
was nearly killed. Not only did he give offence by his 
teaching on the Eucharist ; he appears to have criticised the 
doctrine of Hilary, the great Saint of Poitiers, on faith and on 
the person of Christ.?

which Berengar about this time sent to Herman, Bishop of

Emperor Henry IV. Herman had sent a consolatory letter 
to Berengar and confided one of his clergy to Berengar’s care. 
Berengar sends his greeting to Herman and the clergy of 
Metz and continues : 


I rejoice in God’s propitious comfort shewn to me in the 
arrival of your letter. He strikes and heals, annoying me with 
the endless disturbance of envious men, but none the less not 
disdaining to soften it, by the favour of your kind love for me. It 
is only your kind love which causes your eminence to write to me, 
for I was never, nor ever shall be worthy of such notice. Who 
indeed am I to whom you ascribe the treasures of wisdom? You 
should rather have dealt with me as a sinner. I have received 
brother Peter, son of your love dear Father, willingly. Gladly do 
I see him. It will be for you to secure the help of the almighty 
power of the Lord Jesus, in order to make your decision to send 
him to me, fruitful both to him and to me.! 


If the complaint made by Reginald, Abbot of Poitiers, to 
Lanfranc, now Archbishop of Canterbury, against Berengar 
refers to words spoken by Berengar at the Synod of Poitiers, 
the long reply of Lanfranc to Reginald, Sweyn,? and Henry 
may be dated 1076.3 Lanfranc acknowledges the receipt of 
the Abbot’s letter, and disapproves of his intention to visit 
England, on account of the long journey and perils by land 
and water, and continues : 


Since that schismatic—I mean Berengar—as your letter 
testified, constantly asserts that the blessed Hilary, formerly Bishop 
of your city and people, teaches wrongly in his book on Faith, and 
puts forth unlikely opinions about the Lord Jesus Christ, in his 
book on the divine Trinity, your blessedness ought not to wonder 
that he, who is reported by the truest accounts to believe and teach 
so many and such evil things concerning the Head himself—who is 
reported to speak equally evilly of a member of the Head, is de- 
livered by God’s judgment to a reprobate mind. ‘Truly, whoever 
attaches the stigma of a heresy to Hilary, involves in the stain of 
the same error many orthodox leaders, who have extolled him with 
great praise.’

The disputed teaching arose from a somewhat obscure 
passage in Hilary’s work on the Trinity, in which Hilary 
maintained that although the body of Jesus received the 
blows of the Passion, it did not suffer pain, but was impervious 
like water, fire, or air when smitten by a javelin. The strength 
of the body received the violence of the pain raging against 
it without the sense of pain.’ In defence of Hilary’s view 
Lanfranc appealed to the theory of the hypostatic union, and 
contended that Hilary meant that the human body of Jesus 
received and felt the blows, which the divinity in Him could 
not feel. Probably Berengar was attempting to draw a similar 
distinction, in opposition to the crude theological notions of 
the age.2 The absence of any reference to the eucharistic 
question in Lanfranc’s letter suggests that Berengar had 
publicly raised a new topic of discussion, or that he was 
obeying the injunction of Gregory VII to leave the subject 
alone.*’ On the other hand, the absence of any reference to 
questions apart from the Eucharist, in the only account we 
have of the Synod of Poitiers, was due either to the fact that 
Berengar expressed himself vaguely on Hilary’s doctrine, or 
that he was not understood, or again, that the minds of the 
authorities were too much occupied with the eucharistic 
question to associate Berengar with anything else at the time, 
and if Berengar confined himself to obscure passages like that 
quoted by Lanfranc, the more moderate minds among the 
leading churchmen may have felt that such questions were 
better left alone.

archbishopric by the legate Hugo, and in the following year 
from his priesthood. ‘Three letters of Berengar to Joscelin 
have survived,° and the Scolasticus made use of an opportunity, 
probably between the two condemnations of the Archbishop, 
to send him a letter of condolence : ® 


I would have sympathetically condoled with you in the 
misfortune which recently disturbed you overmuch perhaps, save 
that I remembered the consolation for both of us in the words

1 Marténe and Durand, iv. ro4d. Our chief source for the Roman 
Councils 1078-79 is Berengar’s own account (7bid. pp. 103-109), together 
with the additional passage from an old Gembloux MS., printed by Mabillon 
(Annales, v. 139). Bouq., xi. 531d., and Rieberer, xxi. 48, following 
Marténe and Durand, iv. 102, think this account is wrongly assigned to 
Berengar. Staudlin, ii. 82 ff., thinks it is rightly ascribed to Berengar, 
but is not altogether trustworthy. He summarises Rieberer’s objections 
against Berengar’s authorship: (1) This document does not contain 
Mabillon’s additional passage. (2) The Bishop of Pisa died October 25, 
1080, and not ‘ by an unaccustomed death ’ as Berengar suggests. (3) The 
Bishop of Padua lived till ro90, and so outlived Berengar, who alleged 
that he died after being run through with a sword. (4) Peter Damiani 
is spoken of as if still alive, but he was dead by 1072. (5) Damiani’s 
writings do not bear out Berengar’s statement that he favoured Berengar’s 
views. 

Staudlin rightly urges on the contrary: (1) The document has been 
attacked in order to clear Gregory VII from the suspicion of heresy. 
(2) It does not necessarily imply that Damiani was alive, and even if 
Damiani did not actually support Berengar in his writings, Gregory could 
still have appealed to him (iufra, p. 186). (3) It only reports what is 
said of the Bishop of Pisa. (We may add that the time after his death in 
1080 was not too late for Berengar to have written his report, and so his 
statement concerning the Bishop of Pisa may be quite correct.) (4) If 
Ughelli’s report (Italia Sacra, iii. 364, in Muratori, Rerum Italicarum 
Scriptores, vi. 108d) of the death of the Bishop of Padua is correct, 
Berengar’s statement is only an error in the report which reached him. 
(But we may note that it is not the kind of error he usually repeats.) (5) The 
absence of Mabillon’s passage does not invalidate the document. It 
contains internal marks of genuineness. It is entirely in Berengar’s style 
and manner and tone of thought and character. 

Among modern critics, Reuter, i. 122 f., and Schwabe, p. 122, accept 
it, the latter as a biased statement. Schnitzer, p. 99 n. 2, accepts it as 
genuine, but thinks that its statements are frequently untrustworthy. 
Ebersolt, p. 151, accepts it. It may be added that the trustworthiness 
of Berengar’s statements in the De Sacra Cena, notably in the case of the 
reordinations, which has been established by modern writers, enables us 
to place more confidence in the Acta Concilit Romani than was possible in 
the case of earlier writers.

This announcement was received with applause, especially 
when Gregory pointed out that it contained nothing to which 
anyone could raise objection. It met the requirements of 
faith, especially the needs of less sturdy minds to whom milk 
rather than strong meat should be given, a statement which 
had the authority of Augustine, who said: ‘ That which you 
see on the altar is bread and wine as your eyes tell you, but 
faith insists that the bread is the body of Christ and the wine 
is His blood.’ Berengar, announced Gregory to the assembly, 
was no heretic, his teaching came from the holy Scripture 
and not from his own heart. Peter Damiani, who was not 
inferior to Lanfranc in scholarship or spiritual worth, had at 
Rome declined to agree with the teaching of Lanfranc on the 
Eucharist,1 and the Pope maintained that Damiani’s opinion 
rather than that of Lanfranc should be accepted, especially as he 
was even more painstaking in the study of sacred writings.” 

Gregory thought that the violence of the opposition had 
been checked, especially as he had caused books to be collected 
beforehand by the bishops, abbots, and clergy, and had ordered 
selected passages from the works of Augustine, Jerome, and 
Ambrose to be read out. Many of the leading clergy ex- 
pressed satisfaction with Berengar, and among them the 
Bishops of Porto, Sutri, and Terracina ;* Cardinals Atto of 
Milan and Deusdedit; Peter the Roman Chancellor, ‘ the 
kind and humble-hearted brother beyond the Alps’; Fulk,

learning at Rome was famous, and Bonadies. The names 
of many others Berengar could not remember.4 But his 
enemies were not silenced by the Pope’s obvious desire to

of opinion in the Council. Moreover, the animosity of

ecclesiastical politics exerted its influence. Gregory had

humiliation of the Emperor Henry IV had taken place at 
Canossa on January 25, 1077, and a large party among the 
clergy were supporters of the imperial policy, even if anti-

The opposing faction now urged that the matter should be 
adjourned until the Lenten Synod of 1079, hoping thereby, 
as Berengar says, to gather more of their supporters in Rome, 
when it would be easy to upset the Pope’s plans. Possibly 
in order to pacify these people, Gregory announced that on

Jesu Christ, thou just Assessor, 
King of Kings and Lord of Lords, 
Reigning ever with the Father 
And the Sanctifying Flame, 

Deign to answer my petition, 
Listening of thy clemency. 

Thou from heaven hast descended — 
To the Virgin’s humble womb, 

So receiving human body, 

Thou hast visited thy slave, 

To redeem our human nature 
Through thine own, thy precious blood. 
Asking that thy glorious passion— 
O! my God, I cry out now— 
May defend me without ceasing 
’Gainst the peril gathering round, 
So that I may ever steadfast 

In thy service stand my ground. 
Ever with me be thy power, 

Ever with me thy defence, 

Lest the onrush of the foemen 
Break and overturn my mind ; 
Lest it damn my mortal body 

By a fraudulent device.

A few days before the Lenten Synod assembled the Pope 
summoned Berengar into his presence, together with the 
Bishop of Porto. Gregory informed Berengar that he believed 
that his teaching on the Eucharist had the authority of 
Scripture, but that, following his custom, whenever he was 
troubled about a decision which had to be made, he had 
determined to appeal to the Virgin Mary. A few days before 
he had asked a certain pious friend of his to fast and pray, 
and then to intercede with the Virgin concerning Berengar’s 
teaching. All this had been done, and the Virgin had said 
that nothing was to be believed concerning the doctrine of 
the Eucharist, save what was taught by Scripture, and that 
Berengar’s teaching was not contrary to Scripture. Berengar 
reports that Gregory had informed him of this incident so 
that he might have the greater confidence in the Pope,! but 
obviously behind the account lies an attempt made by Gregory 
to secure the most compliant attitude possible from Berengar. 
The emphasis in the story is laid on the statement that the 
norm for eucharistic doctrine was the Scripture. It conveyed 
a hint to Berengar to make no appeal save to Scripture. The 
Pope’s anger, when Berengar reported the incident in the 
Council, proves that Gregory was not attempting, by this 
device, to overawe the popular mind by an appeal to a 
miraculous intervention of the Virgin. He resorted to 
another and less dangerous measure in order to influence 
the minds of the cardinals and the Roman clergy. A fast 
was imposed on them, so that God might reveal to them the 
true doctrine of the Eucharist. He sent Cardinals Atto and

The addition of the word ‘substantialiter’ troubled 
Berengar. It seemed to pin him down to the interpretation 
of his adversaries. He seized the document, but after hastily 
reading it through perceived that it would bear his own inter- 
pretation, and that by the insertion of a saving clause, ‘ saving 
the substance of the bread,’ ® he could circumvent its verbal 
meaning. He promptly said that he was ready to read the 
formula. But after he had done so the opposing bishops, 
who saw through his device, charged him with reading it 
according to his own interpretation and not theirs, and they 
clamoured that he should swear an oath, affirming that he 
accepted its meaning in the same sense as they. ‘This demand

Berengar’s action had brought on a crisis which Gregory

intellect, not of spirit. In a literary debate he was a match 
for any of the controversialists of the day, and the strength 
of his arguments had half convinced Gregory. But when 
brought face to face with his enemies in the heated atmosphere 
of the Council chamber, he lost his wits, and after flounder- 
ing before the final onslaught of foes who knew how to repress 
a retreating enemy, he collapsed into utter submission. With 
full knowledge of his own weakness had he prayed

The chief significance of the Council of Rome (1079) was 
the final defeat of Berengar after thirty years of conflict; it 
was not merely the shattering of his long-tried confidence 
in Gregory, but the surrender of religious enlightenment by

day, the welfare of the Church demanded the sacrifice. The 
enemies of Gregory, headed by Henry IV, were gathering for 
the final stage in the first great campaign between Papacy and 
Empire which Gregory had inaugurated. Since the day of 
Canossa the cause of Henry had steadily improved.? Yet the 
reform of clerical life and the freedom of the Church from 
lay-interference, which at that day was seldom beneficial, 
especially in the exercise of patronage, depended entirely upon 
the success of Gregory’s ecclesiastical programme. It is one 
of the tragedies of history that the policy by which that 
programme was being worked out threw itself across the 
dogmatic reform, headed by Berengar, which called for equally 
powerful support from the chief pontiff of the West, a result 
due partly to the fact that the zealots of practical reform were 
the grand reactionaries of orthodoxy, and so were opponents 
of the new eucharistic theory, and partly to the fact that in 
Berengar statesmanship was entirely lacking. If he failed to 
manifest the martyr’s firm will and flaming zeal, he had the 
prophet’s insight and clearness of vision, and showed the 
perseverance of the artist in nurturing the creation of his 
brain. For twenty-five years there was always a possibility 
that Berengar and Hildebrand might be linked together in an 
enterprise in which the deficiencies of each might be made up > 
by the gifts of the other. If that union had been established, 
the reform of dogma would have been sponsored instead of 
repressed by the early medieval Popes, and the development 
of European civilisation might have been antedated by five 


enemy’s book. Gregory’s change of front is more easily explained by his 
fear of the imperialist party among the bishops.

CHAPTER XI 
LAST YEARS AT TOURS 


AFTER his return to Anjou in the autumn of 1079,! a revulsion 
of mind overtook Berengar, similar to that which he experienced 
after the Roman Council of 1059. He now wrote a spirited 
defence of his behaviour before the Councils, and poured out 
his feelings against Gregory, although not in the abusive terms 
used of Nicholas II. He complained of the Pope’s fickleness ? 
and sudden madness,? which allowed Gregory to be over- 
thrown by the calumniators of truth. But unlike the earlier 
attacks on Leo IX and Nicholas II, this account does not 
appear to have been written for the purpose of propaganda, 
but rather to ease his mind by a confession of his own weakness, 
and as an appeal to the sympathy of posterity.® ‘ Almighty 
God, who shewest thy almighty power chiefly in forgiveness 
and mercy, have mercy on me, thou Fount of Mercy. I confess 
my great sacrilege. Pardon my wretchedness, restore to me 
the joy of thy salvation, before thy Blessed One comes in thy 
majesty, in the company of the angels, in order to expiate 
with fire the great sins which I have committed against Thee.’ 
He appealed to all who read his account: ‘O! my brothers 
in Christ, on whom this document shall chance, extend to my 
aid the strong power of Christian love, see with pity the tears 
of my confession, so that your prayers may propitiate God’s 
mercy for me.’ ® 

His sentiments became known, for on September 30, 1080, 
he was summoned before the Synod of Bordeaux, held by the 
legates Amatus of Oleron and Hugh of Die, in the presence of

brother of the Conqueror, who had been made Earl of Kent,

At Brixen Gregory VII was set aside, by the imperialist

became the anti-Pope, Clement III. Odo made use of his 
great wealth to secure influence at Rome among the cardinals 
and citizens. He caused gold to be distributed freely, and 
ordered a palace to be built for himself in the city. All his 
life he had been a liberal benefactor of poor students, and 
some of his protégés had been educated at Tours, where the 
liberal thinking of Berengar seems to have appealed to Odo, 
who was also a man of independent mind. There was another 
bond between them. They were both enemies of Lanfranc. 
When Lanfranc became Archbishop of Canterbury and the 
confidential adviser of the Conqueror, he not only secured an 
office which Odo coveted, but became a hindrance to the 
ambitious schemes of the Bishop of Bayeux.1 Odo now 
attempted to secure the aid of Berengar by offering to give 
him his assistance. But Berengar had already declined to 
lend support to the political schemes of Philip of France, and 
he now refused the aid offered by Odo. 


Blessed be the Lord God Almighty, the Father of mercies 
and all consolation, the God who slays and makes to live ; who 
pierces through and heals, who has frustrated your enemies, both 
those who instigated and those who attacked, from the expectation 
of their malignity so that they should not cause thee to fall, who 
with an almighty hand raised thy worth above their worthlessness. 
In order therefore that you may never show yourself ungrateful for 
such benefits, may the same Father of mercies drain the pit of 
corruption from the depth of your heart, so that you may love 
Him uncorruptly, . . . that He may make you as an arrow in the 
hand of the mighty, a son of the proven, worthy of Himself, 
whom, having been placed at the helm of the Church, and pro- 
moted from strength to strength, He orders to ascend to His people 
that is ready. For the rest, as for the fact that your worship is 
moved to restore my affairs, I being beneath all compassions of the 
Lord, wait as suppliant, though not with perfect humility, upon 
the kindness of His almighty Spirit, lest my sin becomes greater 
than for me to merit forgiveness, lest He destroy my soul with 
sinners and my life with the blood-thirsty. . . . I drew away from
