In 1082, through the intervention of Lanfranc, Odo was 
arrested by the Conqueror in the Isle of Wight, when about to 
embark on an expedition to Rome, accompanied by the Earl 
of Chester and many armed men. He was imprisoned and 
remained in confinement until William’s death.2. Berengar’s 
reply indicates that he was weary of the conflict, and in 
a chastened frame of mind had withdrawn from the public 
prosecution of his case. Soon after going back to-Tours he 
retired to the island of Come in the river near the city. 

After the death of Gregory VII on May 25, 1085, he 
wrote to Archbishop Joscelin of Bordeaux : 


The sudden death of our Gregory disturbs me not a little, 
but so far as I appear to have known the man, I am certain of his 
salvation, no matter what may be the prejudiced opinion of those who, 
according to the Lord’s saying, ‘strain at a gnat and swallow a 
camel.’ ‘In Christ Jesus,’ saith the apostle, ‘ circumcision is 
nothing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature.’ That he was 
such, so far as I knew him, I trust to the divine mercy. Barnabas 
departed from Paul, so that he could not remain with him 
according to the outward man, but no less, according to the inward 
man, did Barnabas remain in the book of life. The divine mercy 
does not so relate itself to men, that it abandons, for a few light 
offences, those who are not wanting in the highest and as it were 
universal things. Any such course would be considered most 
unjust even amongst men. But if they alleged ‘ Whosoever ye 
shall bind, shall be bound,’ I say that to bind is not to bind indis- 
criminately and generally. Otherwise, the Lord will seem to have 
commanded any sins or misdeeds when He said ‘ Whatsoever ye 
will that men may do to you, even so do to them,’ if the words 
‘ye will’ are to be taken indiscriminately and generally. But to 
will is not to will foolishly and perversely. ‘I will put a curse 
on your benedictions,’ saith the Lord through the prophet to

Lord says ‘ Righteousness removes unrighteous bonds.’ Gregory

This letter reflects the condemnation of Gregory by his 
enemies at the Synod of Brixen, an incident which made a 
greater impression on the people of the time than historians 
have allowed. It reflects the calmer spirit which Berengar 
had developed since he went into retreat. His comments on 
Gregory’s action in the Lenten Council of 1079 did not run 
to the extreme lengths of his abuse of Leo IX and Nicholas II, 
and now that the great Pope was dead he was able to look back 
on the happier incidents of their relationship, even as Barnabas 
might have looked back on some of the milder periods of his 
relationship with S. Paul. 

The island of Céme, on the river Loire, near Tours, 
belonged, in the early part of the eleventh century, to Hugh, 
the Cellarer of S. Martin’s cathedral church. Herveus the 
Younger, of Buzancy, the Treasurer of S. Martin’s, who had 
restored the cathedral in 1001,2 built a little church on the 
island in 1002 in honour of SS. 'Céme and Damianus,? and 
lived there for some years in seclusion. When he was recalled

consent, to twelve monks of the Abbey of Marmoutier (1012),*

expression mark his appeal to the Deity in the Acta Conciliu

Your petitions are commands, your order is compulsion, 
your prayers are my chariot. You recently urged that I should 
write something to you by which devotion might be incited, ardour 
sharpened and attention directed. I confess that I fear to inflict 
upon doves flying in the free air the wings of the body of a pig, 
and it is presumption to haul out aninfirm elephant. I am in the 
mire and you urge that I should purge you, when it were more 
fitting for me to be raised up by your hands, than that you should 
be excited by my eloquence. But humility which is the chief of 
all virtues, opens your mouths, so that you seek instruments ? of 
warfare from him who knows not how to strike enemies, but only 
to declare against them. A horse runs, but it is written ‘ There is 
no harm in subduing a fleeing horse with the spur.’ And the same » 
man in another place, elegantly enough says ‘ The horse about to 
race of its own accord will go swiftly to the honours of the palm, 
if you urge it strongly.’ A warlike trumpet stirs up the strong 
man to battle ; a wounded lion rises more swiftly to anger; lynxes 
sleep when they are satisfied, after they are hungry they possess 
boldness for preying. ‘The ant instructs man to salvation or labour. 

Ye are the horses of God. Ye are called to a race. Christ 
is among the spectators, your bridle is silence, the spurs which 
stimulate you are fear and love. ‘Therefore it is necessary for those 
who join in the contest (to know) from whence they begin the race, 
how they should run, and whither they ought to run. From what 
do you run? From the flesh. How? Through righteousness. 
Whither? To God. This is the right course—from the flesh, 
through righteousness, to God; from Egypt, through the desert, 
to the land of promise ; from vice through virtue to a reward ; 
from nature through activity to happiness ; from the world, without 
the world, beyond the world. Indeed, ye ought not to remain 
in this in which ye were born, but ye shall go three days journey 
into the wilderness. What is solitude ? Heaven. Why? Because 
it is solitary and pure from all malice. A journey of three days 
is necessary for heaven. The first journey is to neglect the 
law of the flesh, the second is to adhere to the law of the spirit, 
the third is to see the great Spirit. Whence the prophetic word 
says elegantly enough—‘ Rise, shine, Jerusalem!’ The first (thing) 
is to rise up; afterwards to receive light. The soul lies on the 
pallet of conscience, overcome with sleepy inactivity. If it wishes 
to shine, it rises, and so the glory of the Lord is oriented. So, 
my brothers, ye begin to run, casting aside the world with its own ; 
ye are come to the desert since the Lord is not in a commotion ; 
ye are come to the desert that ye may see the hissing of fine gold !

Ye are come to the desert not that ye may cleave to riches, but 
that ye may fight with sin; ye are come into the desert since Jesus 
was led by the Spirit into the wilderness. Ye have fled from the 
crowd, and Christ fled, lest they should make Him king. Ye have 
fled, but the enemy follows. Fly until the enemy ceases. The 
flight does not end until life ends. There is not in the world a 
place so deep below the earth, so high above the mountains, so 
hidden in a wood, so encircled by the sea, to which sin cannot come. 
There is not a cell so enclosed but that sin can approach. Whence 
Seneca says ‘Although ye cross the waste of the sea, although 
ye leave the cities of the earth, sins follow you wherever you go.’ 
Is the hermit alone in his cell? Sin lies outside the door, seeking 
a lodging with an alluring address. ‘I,’ she says, ‘am your beloved 
whom ye cherished in the world, who came with thee to the table, 
who slept with you in your little bed, without whom you did 
nothing. Why have you done this wrong that you wish to leave 
me? I have followed your footsteps, and do you think to hide 
without me in a cell? I hold the bond? of your father Adam, 
signed by your hand. ‘That charter is death to which you sub- 
scribed while you sinned. I am not proud, I am not disdainful, 
I was with you in the world, when you ate meat, when you drank 
wine, when you? satisfied yourself to excess. I shall be with 
you in the desert when you feed on bread only, when you taste 
water, when after moderate feeding, you still remain hungry. 
I was with you when you were in a crowd, when you slept on 
fine linen. I shall be with you when you think you are alone 
in your retreat, when you lie down in your hair-shirt. Not 
only is purple in hell, not only silk, but the hair-shirt and per- 
chance wool. You have chosen rather to descend into hell with 
sack-cloth and ashes, with a large tonsure and great hunting 
boots,’ as if by such things reverence may be offered there, 
than crimped, beautified, bathed, and satisfied with elegant food. 
You have a certain hermitage of mine. The flesh which you 
bear is my sister. She was born with me, suckled with me. 
Do you want to die without me? So long as the flesh is 
flesh, so long shall I be in thy flesh. When flesh ceases to be 
flesh, it shall be liberated from my demands. Behold I knock 
at the door. Open! flesh to thy beloved. Why are you within 
and I without?’ So flatters sin, and such patronage it offers to 
its cause. ‘The anchoret receives sin forsooth with magnificent 
hospitality, and so it frequently visits its host. But if sin is re- 
ceived with a sad face, it does not come so often into the cell. Here 
is the only guest whom Christ orders to be shut out, to whom no 
one ought to show a joyful face. If you conquer the flesh by 
abstinence with the proud—here is sin. If you are conquered

Pride is the sin common to demons and hermits. If demons were

through some fissure? He must have a dog at the door of the 
cell which shall constantly bark against sin, lest while he sleeps 
the thief is able to enter the house. That dog is the invocation 
of grace, that barking-dog is attentive prayer, which forbids the 
pure heart to sleep. The dog is faith in grace alone. The apostle 
had this dog when he said ‘I know nothing by myself, yet am 
I not hereby justified’ (1 Cor. iv. 4). The apostle also praised 
this saying, “ Pray without ceasing ’’ (1 Thess. v. 17). When this 
dog barks wrong flies. I do not advise that you trust in yourselves 
as Julian? the heretic exhorted the virgin Demetrias. ‘ There 
are,’ he said, ‘ lawful fundamentals of warfare, that a celibate may 
know his own strength, and that sort is most valuable in exhorting 
an army, which warns every soldier concerning his own strength.’ 
I think otherwise. The fundamentals of Christian warfare are 
that each may know his own weakness, and wholly leaning on 
grace, he may know that he can do nothing by his own strength, 
save evil. This is the pillar of those who struggle, this is the 
only consolation of the fallen—to venture nothing in himself, but 
all in grace. Therefore grace, seeing the weakness of those who 
fight, and the greatness of the danger, cries ‘ Fly from the middle 
of Babylon, and let each save his soul.’ The hand bold for battle 
seeks flight with the timid, since it is better to escape by flying, 
than to be conquered by resisting. ‘The warfare of God is different 
from the warfare of the world. In the warfare of the world flight 
is called * disgraceful. In the warfare of God flight is praised 
as industry. Why do you fear to fly when your Emperor says 
‘Fly !’—‘ Fly from the middle of Babylon.’ In Babylon is the 
beginning, the middle, the end. The beginning of Babylon is 
suggestion, the middle of Babylon is pleasure, the end of Babylon 
is labour. He does not say ‘ Fly from the beginning of Babylon,’ 
since no one can avoid being tempted, and where there is no 
suggestion there is no battle. So without a conflict there is no 
victory, and where there is no victory there is no crown. And 
so suggestion tempts that the triumph may receive the conqueror. 
He does not say ‘ Fly from the neighbourhood of Babylon,’ since 
he who has fallen in duty is already wounded, has already broken 
his legs, is already crippled. He who is crippled by broken legs 
can be carried, he cannot fly. But‘ Fly from the middle of Babylon,’ 
so he can openly say ‘ Fly pleasure and suggestion will not harm,

And, again, ‘ Save your souls’ (Jer. xlviii. 6). We saved our souls

The leaf which the wind seizes is not rooted in the tree. He whom

for both. The bed is the blessing of God, in which God sweetly 
rests with those obedient to Him. In this bed the devil wishes 
to recline through pride, and to have as great a part as God. 
But narrow is the bed, so that the other falls, since although 
Divinity receives many to be made like God, He receives no one 
to be equal with God. And the other falls. Whoever the other 
may be, he is relinquished. ‘The other is he who is not one with 
God ; he who adheres to God is one in spirit. Therefore he who 
does not adhere is ‘ the other.’ He desires unity, and God refuses 
otherness,! since conjunction is in unity, and division is in other- 
ness. So the bed of blessedness is? sufficient for one, but so 
narrow that it does not open to another, and the small coverlet 
cannot open to both. What is the small coverlet save charity, 
which is an element of the goodness of small things, in which all 
the members of perfection are enclosed. The blessed Isaiah calls 
charity the garment of praise, which Christ wore, since He is to 
be praised, who by charity alone acts well. The coverlet cannot 
cover both, since charity cannot bind together the humble and 
the proud. ‘These, most beloved, we have fashioned for you with

a hasty hand, and charity, which was latently fervid, did not blush

If Berengar makes no allusion in this long and beautiful 
epistle to his own controversy, or to his enemies, that was 
because no reference to the current dispute of the time would 
have been fitting in a letter of advice to hermits. But the 
high spiritual tone and mellow wisdom of his monitions are 
the fruit of his own chastened outlook, matured by the calm 
and humble life of prayer and alms-giving which he was now 
living at Come. With few wants of his own, he gave away 
the bulk of his possessions to the poor.2 A late report says 
that he made some attempt to obey Gregory’s injunction to 
reconvert those who had been misled by him, but that his 
old scholars were too widely scattered to enable him to 
succeed.? But of this there is no reliable evidence. Nor is 
there any conclusive evidence that he had surrendered his 
own convictions on the eucharistic question ; but when he 
died on the Feast of the Epiphany, 1088,* he passed away in 
the odour of sanctity after a long life of perfect health.’ It is 
reported that shortly before his death he said that the Lord 
Jesus had appeared to him, as a sign that glory was laid up 
for him on account of his penitence, but he none the less 
feared punishment for his sins.6 ‘Thoughts of the Epiphany 
were clearly passing through his mind at the time. They 
buried him in the cathedral church of S. Martin at Tours, 
but Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours, an old pupil of Berengar,

Laudatory notices of Berengar were natural at Tours and 
Angers, where, even at the height of the controversy, he had 
always possessed friends. But tributes to his catholicity were 
soon forthcoming from distant parts, the result of nearly a 
decade of submission beneath the wing of the Papacy. ‘The 
monk Clarius, a member of the Abbey of Fleury, near Sens, 
wrote ten years after his death that ‘he finished his life as 
a faithful and true Catholic.’2 Richard of Poitiers, a monk 
at Cluny, a contemporary writer, reports that ‘he erred in 
the faith, but afterwards corrected his error.2 William of 
Malmesbury, the leading English historian of the next century, 
records that although he had erred in youth he was regarded 
as a saint when he came to graver years.*. ‘The anonymous 
chronicler of Melk reports that, although not convicted at 
heart, he made the usual statement of Catholic belief in the 
Sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord and Saviour, 
and confirmed it in some versicles. 


Constat in altari carnem de pane creari 
Ipsa caro Deus est ; qui negat hoc reus est.°

prevarication and the clearest deceit.1_ From his writings it 
is evident that his intérpretation of the Eucharist was com- 
pletely free from the materialistic conceptions common to 
writers of that age. If the charge of prevarication is to be 
considered, it lies rather against his adversaries. ‘There are 
passages in their writings, especially in those of Lanfranc,? 
where the spiritual interpretation of the doctrine is couched 
in terms almost as lofty as those of Berengar, but they nullify 
these phrases in their teaching when they come to explain 
the meaning of their words. 

If Berengar occasionally used language which seemed to 
embody some of the current orthodox conceptions, he 
seldom failed to explain his meaning in spiritual terms. ‘The 
evangelical thought was ever present to his mind: ‘ ‘The words 
I say unto you, they are spirit, they are life, the flesh profiteth 
nothing.’ When in the De Sacra Cena he claims that the 
physical-realism of Paschasius and Lanfranc was execrated 
by the greater part of the Church,? he gave way to exaggera- 
tion. In the Benedictine houses, which were the nurseries 
of at least one-half of the clergy of the day, the teaching of 
Paschasius in one form or another was predominant, and the 
Paschasian realism had been used to heighten the materialistic 
teaching of the Mass-cultus, so that the illiterate worshippers 
were helplessly under its influence. Yet Berengar’s was not 
a solitary voice crying aloud. In Paschasius’ time, even in 
the Benedictine monasteries, strong opposition to Paschasius’ 
teaching was to be found, and this attitude, forcibly re- 
presented then by Ratramn, was preserved right down to 
Berengar’s era,* especially in cathedral schools like ‘Tours. 
Down to 1050, at least, Berengar was supported by the best 
of the clergy at Tours. 

The dispute with Lanfranc was largely a dispute between 
seculars and regulars, between the old cathedral schools and 
the new Benedictine theology, and the wide-spread opposition

If Berengar had a clearly perceptible following in his own 
day, and on into the twelfth century,®? he created no sect. 
His old scholars did not succeed in converting a single little 
town or even village in France.4 If Berengarianism never 
reached the dimensions of a schism, three causes co-operated 
to prevent this development, which at one time appeared 
probable. Firstly, Berengar was a student and a man of 
letters. He was not an organiser, and beyond the qualifica- 
tions needed to maintain and popularise a great cathedral 
school, he had no capacity for leading men, or even for rally- 
ing them to his standard. Secondly, the future lay with 
the realists, and the: capture of the Benedictine houses made 
the victory of a modified Radbertian doctrine a certainty. 
Thirdly, the message of Berengar was rather for the clergy

and monks, and even among them it appealed only to the 
learned. For the ‘mob’ of illiterate priests and monks he 
always maintained the greatest contempt.1 Any movement 
for the reform of dogma must indeed begin with the 
theologians. It must be disseminated in the study. Until 
it has established itself there, little opportunity is open for 
its publication to the masses. The success of the Reforma- 
tion was due in the first instance to the literary work of Luther, 
and to the spread of the movement among the theologians and 
thinkers of north-western Europe. In the early Middle Ages 
the attempt to popularise a spiritual interpretation of the 
Eucharist was met by the barrier set up by the Mass-cultus, 
by increasing refinements in ritual, by the development of 
the legends which were used through the medium of preaching 
to emphasise the actual presence of the body of Christ on the 
altar. The crude materialism of some of these stories 7 made 
impossible a lofty spiritual devotion in the minds of simple, 
illiterate worshippers, whether noble or peasant. In days 
when men have not been trained to think—and the medieval 
Roman Church discouraged independent thought—only those 
ideas which are presented through the senses have any chance 
of being permanently absorbed. ‘This has been the weakness 
of the sacramental theory from the beginning. Yet it cannot 
be abandoned, and the words of institution sanction it, but 
when divorced from the attendant evangelical principle ‘ The 
words I say unto you, they are spirit, they are life,’ the theory 
defeats its own end, and instead of raising human life up to 
the level of God, it buries the divine in the body of materialism 
and leaves religion grovelling in the dust of earth. 

The story of Berengarianism illustrates the fate which 
overtakes ideas when unsupported by a dominant personality 
for their publication. Berengar was not a Luther. His

temperament was not qualified for the rough-and-tumble of

before principle and lose no opportunity of advancing them-

thought. His personal influence was exerted rather in the 
class-room than the council-chamber. Before the shallow 
but confident criticism of zealots like Humbert, or experienced 
pleaders like Lanfranc, he was unable to make an impression. 
That his ideas made an appeal when quietly considered is 
proved by the attitude of Hildebrand, and by the long list 
of distinguished clergy who were counted among his friends. 
But he had no force of personality sufficient to impress the 
minds of adversaries. Within his smaller academic sphere, 
in the presence of the generous open-mindedness of young 
-men when listening to intellectual genius, the spirit of 
Berengar felt no restraint. Here was he master of himself. 
Here could he successfully plant his teaching and draw the 
love of those who listened. 

In addition to his views on the Eucharist, Berengar has 
been charged with several other heretical conceptions. It 
was alleged that he denied the efficacy of infant baptism and 
the indissolubility of marriage, that he denied the Virgin- 
birth and the palpability of the Resurrection-body of Christ. 
But his teaching on baptism in the letter to the hermits 1 and 
in the De Sacra Cena, his warning letter to Philip of 
France against adultery,? and his advice to Eusebius Bruno 
on the marriage of widows,* dispose of the allegations of 
Theoduin,® who records a mere rumour that Berengar was 
unsound on these matters.

Virgin-birth ® has arisen through a misunderstanding of his

of Christ. In Germany, according to Ratramn, the curious

On the doctrine of grace, his letter to the hermits presents

of Rhegium—‘ Co-operate with God for your salvation.’ ? 

In all matters of practical morality and ecclesiastical 
discipline Berengar supported the Cluniac-Hildebrandine 
reforms,® although only once does he hint at one of the abuses 
against which the reforms were directed.4 By instinct and 
by nature he was a man to whom the policy of the reformers 
was obviously right, and needed no statement from him for 
its furtherance. This gave him great credit with moderate 
and practical minds like Alexander II and Gregory VII, 
although men like Berengar, whose sympathies were with 
the movement, but who avoided trenchant proclamation of 
it, were not so few as might be supposed. In every era of 
reform there is a large body of silent men who occupy a 
central and non-vocal position, and whose interests are 
frequently abandoned by reformers and reactionaries. Even 
in the eucharistic controversy we do not read that Berengar 
demanded recognition for his views, save when compelled by 
direct attack to state them. His correspondence is mainly 
occupied with the affairs of his friends. The elements of 
the Berengarian eucharistic doctrine could not be recon-

in his attitude to the great and powerful men among whom 
he moved. No single letter has been preserved appealing 
for the support of kings and barons.1 He preferred to have 
his case judged by the authorities of his Church. He was 
indifferent to the attitude of the lay-magnates.2 On the 
contrary, when they applied to him, even when his interests 
seemed to demand compliance with them, he did not fail to 
rebuke them for their weakness or selfishness. The letters 
to King Philip and Odo of Bayeux are models of polite but 
honest integrity. ‘They were but the manifestations of his 
own inner life. No breath of slander was ever uttered against 
him, save against his charity, and that was vindicated by the 
supreme Pontiff? To tenacity of purpose, as real as that of 
Lanfranc, he added the kindly consideration of Anselm. He 
was the prince of schoolmasters of that age. Even Lanfranc’s 
success as a preceptor was criticised by Anselm, and the latter 
erred on the side of indulgence. Young men were sent to 
Berengar from all parts of Europe, and even the writers of 
legend of a succeeding age could not conceal his popularity 
as a teacher. 

All these qualities serve partly to explain his bitter polemic 
against Humbert and Lanfranc. He makes no reference to 
the writings of Durand and Guitmund, possibly because they 
had not overstepped the limits of controversial courtesy. 
Their terminology and method merited the respect of another 
scholar and man of letters. But in Humbert and Lanfranc 
he saw not only the arch-schemers of a selfish reactionary 
policy, possessed of a zeal which did not comprehend the 
implications of that which they criticised, or the trend of their 
own views, and was ready to sacrifice all new manifestations of 
truth, all exercise of reason in support of things as they were,

intransigeance of the Roman formulae of 1059 and 1079. So 
Berengar came into the lists with the sword of the pen, and 
smote these foemen with the full weight of an indignation 
which was not stirred by other men. 

In greatness of moral indignation Berengar has never 
been surpassed. It was his one great passion, and if it 
frequently swept him away from the restraints of sober 
utterance and broke his reasoned argument into shafts of 
disconnected polemic, who shall say that the inspiration was 
ignoble ? When we estimate his contribution to the progress 
of the Evangelical principle, we shall find it not so much in 
the appeal to Scripture as the final authority for belief— 
although he never loses an opportunity to quote the Bible— 
but in the demand for freedom whereby the individual may 
open the books of Scripture and there judge for himself the 
meaning of God’s Word. ‘The Evangelical principle of the 
freedom of private judgment was originated in the Middle 
Ages by Berengar. But he did not uphold a mere appeal to 
the letter of Scripture—that was more frequently adopted by 
writers on the other side. Berengar saw that the final test lay 
in the interpretation, and that that must be made with the assist- 
ance of reason, which in turn was a divinely inspired faculty.? 

Yet Berengar is not to be numbered among the great 
scholastics, still less among the founders of Nominalism.? 
If the influence of Aristotle can be traced in his thought, 
he owed far more to the Neo-Platonists,? and certainly no 
systematisation of theology by the aid of Aristotelean 
categories can be found in his writings. Only if the term 
“ scolasticism ’ be stretched backwards, so as to include the 
earlier application of dialectics or reason to the interpretation 
of Scripture, can he be included among the scholastics, but 
some authorities dispute this broad usage of the term.* His

In the next century the name of Berengar was used 
to illustrate crude ideas of demoniacal possession, and as 
an excuse for further elaboration of the Mass-cultus. A 
Berengarian legend developed. ‘The Scolasticus was charged 
with dabbling in necromancy when a young man, but the 
clumsy romancer makes use of the story to explain why 
Berengar wrote the Fuste Ffudex. One night the devil 
carried him from Tours to Rome. Here a certain boy, a 
clerk of noble family, was committed to his care. One day 
during the absence of the Scolasticus the pupil read his books 
on necromancy, and was killed by the devil. On his return 
Berengar compelled the demon to enter the body of the dead 
boy, so that he walked about and sang with the others in the 
choir, until a rival necromancer exposed the fraud and showed 
that the boy was really dead. Berengar was then condemned 
to death, but taking refuge in a church he composed the 
Juste Fudex, and, singing it with lamentation, was set free 
by divine intervention.?

Some Roman Catholic writers associated the origin of

Its observance spread gradually. Durand of Mende, who 
wrote his Rational in 1284, does not mention it.’ The 
processions, which became the principal feature of this feast, 
were not originated at the same time as the liturgical festival.

That the teaching of Berengar was followed during the 
next two centuries by a growing cult of the Sacrament was 
only a natural expression of the Catholic reaction,? although 
we need not attribute to his influence the elaborate sequence 
of consequences drawn up recently by Biginelli.2 Among the 
ceremonies which are said to have been protests against 
Berengar’s influence are included the procession on Palm 
Sunday, started by Lanfranc,* and the elevation of the host 
and chalice. But Lanfranc nowhere states that the elaborate 
ceremony introduced by him into his Benedictine Constitu- 
tions > was related to the Berengarian controversy. More 
probably it was an attempt to emphasise liturgically the 
evangelic event commemorated on Palm Sunday. No refer- 
ence to the elevation of the host occurs in the ‘ Ecclesiastical 
Offices ’ of John, Bishop of Avranches, written in 1068,° nor 
in the letter of Ivo of Chartres to Matilda, Queen of England.’ 
The earliest reference to this practice is associated with 
Cardinal Guy, who in 1140 ordered a bell to be sounded when 
the host was carried abroad, so that the people might adore.® 
Again in 1203, Guy, the Cardinal-Bishop of Palestrina, when

Otherwise he might indeed have adopted, quite early, an 
attitude similar to that of Humbert, though without 
expressing himself in the domineering terms of that typical 
rigorist. On the other hand, he might well have been won

whole intellectual outlook of the Church and for a develop-

the Scot and Ratramn had attempted to lay down against the 
sensual and paganising interpretation which Paschasius Radbert 
left as a hereditas damnosa to the medieval Church. If 
Hildebrand in later years had been less insistent upon the

the final revolt of Germany and the north-western nations 
against the politico-religious system founded by Hildebrand, 
might have been forestalled. In a word the Reformation 
might have been staged in the eleventh century without the 
disastrous results to the unity of Western Christendom which 
were inevitable five centuries later, results which necessitated 
the hundred years of religious wars preceding the Peace of 
Westphalia (1648). From the ninth century sprang the 
perversion of dogma which ended in the commercial travelling 
of Tetzel and all the huckstering of religious privileges in the 
fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.1_ From the eleventh century 
sprang the practical ecclesiastical system which gave these 
abuses a long life, and made possible their ramification into 
every cell of the European religious body. But in the eleventh 
century with the call of Berengar, a voice was heard which 
might have rolled back the gathering clouds. ‘To quote his 
own words, repeated more than once to Lanfranc: ‘ A light 
shined in the darkness, but the darkness comprehended it not.’? 
In the spiritualising and purifying of dogma offered by the 
system of Berengar as a contribution to the work of the 
administrative and moral reformers, Hildebrand and his school 
might have obtained an inspirational impetus which would 
have kept the practical reforms in a state of healthy develop- 
ment, and prevented their becoming involved, and so degraded, 
in the political maelstrom of medieval Europe. But the day 
of opportunity for the medieval Papacy to become the in- 
augurator of spiritual as well as practical reform was allowed 
to pass. When it seemed to have reappeared in the fifteenth 
century, in the era of the Conciliar movement, it was but a 
fictitious dawn. ‘The Church was too far sunk in corruption 
and decrepitude to arise for the reform of head and members, 
and the primacy of Peter passed for ever from the sphere 
of practical possibility. The Papacy was compelled to rest 
content with a Counter-Reformation which turned the Roman 
Church into one of the sects, or at the most into a mere Italian 
and therefore national interpretation of Catholicism. The

eucharistic theory of Berengar—to which in later centuries the 
reformed Churches returned, whether they knew it or not— 
and indeed they did not know of his De Sacra Cena until 
modern days—freed from some of its crudities, might have 
been adopted at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215). In this 
case Protestantism would have been checked by a surer remedy 
than Innocent III thought he had applied when he embodied 
Transubstantiation in the first decree of the Council. But it 
would have been checked by a process of absorption, not of 
inhibition, and an Evangelical-Catholicism arrayed in the 
beauty of some of Rome’s finer garments, without the dour 
cerements which were wrapped around the Evangelical tradition 
by the zealots of Geneva, might have supplied vital religion 
to a united European church. When the medieval Papacy 
refused to mount on the wings offered by the teaching of 
Berengar, its development became more and more a worldly 
policy of defence against not only innovation but progress. 
It concentrated more and more on the mere wrappings of the 
body of religion, neglecting the spiritual call of saint and 
thinker alike.

PART II 


CHAPTER XII 
BERENGAR AND THE STREAM OF TRADITION 


We have seen that Berengar’s teaching exerted an influence 
far into the twelfth century. If he did not create an organised 
following, and if the Berengarians of the next age have left 
behind no formal treatises on the Eucharist, yet their influence 
was sufficient to call forth widespread literary activity from the 
orthodox thinkers. In the first stage of the controversy the 
orthodox writers were occupied mainly with the conception 
of the real presence, and the work of Durand of Troarn 
occupies the chief place during this period. In the second 
stage of the dispute the theory of Transubstantiation was 
elaborated by Lanfranc and Guitmund, and then certain 
questions arising from the implications of both these great 
doctrines were discussed by the orthodox apologists of the 
later part of the eleventh and the first half of the twelfth 
centuries. Moreover, Berengar’s own teaching left its mark on 
some leading writers whose orthodoxy has never been 
impugned. An equally important question arises at the other 
end of the history of this dispute. Did Berengar’s protest 
issue from a new and solitary voice crying out for the first 
time in the eleventh century, and was he the originator of the 
dynamic symbolism which is associated with his name? Our 
references to John the Scot and Ratramn will have indicated 
that Berengar did not stand alone, but some further discussion is 
necessary to show that he completed rather than started a long 
line of spiritual teachers who held views similar to his own. 

The Augustinian tradition had never ceased to operate in 
the Western Church. While the influence of Ambrose was 


1 Cf. Riickert, pp. 25 f., 50; Schréckh, xxiii. 437 ff.; Vernous, Deux 
Trattes, p. 4 ff. 


228 BERENGAR 


present in the Gallic and Spanish liturgies,1 and formed the 
main strand in the Roman liturgies (Leonine, Gelasian, and 
Gregorian), yet Augustinian symbolism produced a marked 
effect upon the structure of the Roman service books.2 As the 
centuries advanced the influence of Augustine grew and, 
together with the teaching of Ambrose, became the source of 
the eucharistic teaching of the pre-scholastic era,? and it was 
the growing influence of Augustinian eucharistic doctrine 
which created the first eucharistic controversy in the time of 
the Carolings.* 

This double strand of teaching was emphasised by Batiffol 
in former editions of his work, L’Eucharistie,> which have 
now been expurgated by the Roman authorities. In the 
edition of 1905 Batiffol wrote: ‘C’étaient deux courants, non 
point contraires, mais cependant distincts, et entre lesquels 
se partageaient les Occidentaux . . . Augustin maintenait le 
crédit de la “ praesentia spiritalis’ . . . Ambrose s’accordait 
mieux avec le réalisme traditionnel.’® » He continues by 
affirming that this dual current was maintained down to the 
time of Charles the Bald without exciting disquietude in 


anyone.’ The Carolingian renaissance found the doctrine in 


a state of indecision, and two parties sprang from the attempt 
at solution. Of course this passage does not appear in later 
editions of the book, and in an article in the Revue du Clergeé 
frangaise ® he contradicted his earlier considered opinion by 
saying that the teaching of Berengar had no root in tradition.

But if the Eucharist has the external body and blood of the 
Lord and the internal ‘ life,’ yet the body and blood are the 
bread and wine, which remain in the sacrament and can be 
eaten by the unfaithful,* a statement which constitutes an 
important antecedent for one of Berengar’s main contentions. 
Jonas of Orleans (d. 843) says that the presence of Christ | 
depends upon the condition of the receiver, and is mediated 
only to those who receive worthily.® A similar idea was held 
by Maxentius of Aquileia (811-833), who said that the eating 
of the body of the Lord consisted in abiding in Christ through 
grace.6 ‘Theodulf of Orleans says that the Eucharist effects 
a mystical union with Christ by means of a passing into the 
body of Christ,’ but the comparison which he draws between 
the Eucharist and Baptism shows that his interpretation is 
symbolical, although the symbolism is not bare. The bread 
and wine while ‘signifying’ the body and blood of Christ 
yet receive the ‘ dignities’ of the body and blood of Christ, 
through the power of the visible offering of the priest and the 
invisible consecration of the Holy Ghost,’ an explanation 
which, again, foreshadows Berengar’s teaching that consecra- 
tion produces the effect of the body and blood of Christ in 
the Eucharist. 

This dynamic symbolism, which stresses the effectiveness

was developed by Candidus of Fulda (d. after 865) and 
Christian Druthmar. ‘The eucharistic body and blood, writes 
Candidus, represent Christ’s body and soul. The blood 
symbolises His soul,® and he conceives of the consecrated

The part played by the name of John the Scot in the 
Berengarian controversy necessitates a fuller treatment of 
the eucharistic teaching of that writer, especially as John 
the Scot was a prominent figure in the first eucharistic con-

fundamental ideas of Alexandrian Neo-Platonism, and from 
him came down, as from a peak in the line of tradition, the

which the material elements are symbols, is formed or pre- 
pared in the Church. But there is no local or temporal 
presence of Christ in the Eucharist.t His flesh has returned 
to spirit, into God, and cannot be comprised within form or 
sex, or become part of the flux of time, or be contained in 
any place.2 The process of salvation operated by Christ 
through the Eucharist is effected by His divinity. 

Our participation in Jesus in Communion depends upon 
faith,? so that the apotheosis of the believer demands an 
accessory subjective condition. In the Neo-Platonic sense 
the enlightenment of men is achieved through the earthly 
lights, which are images of the spiritual light, and especially 
of the true light which lighteneth every man coming into the 
world.*’ A mystical union is thus effected with God, which 
is the result of the operation of grace.5 The wisdom of God 
descends through grace, a Theophany is the agent of the 
enlightenment.® 

Across the stream of this strongly-flowing spiritual 
symbolism, which constituted the eucharistic interpretation 
of most writers in the Gallic Church at the end of the eighth 
and beginning of the ninth century, a reactionary barrier was 
now flung by Paschasius Radbert. Granted that the Gallic 
liturgies were formed under the influence of Ambrosian 
realism, yet the trend of eucharistic thought during this era 
was directed by the spiritual dynamic symbolism of Augustine. 
The only reinforcement for realism, received by the 
Carolingian Church during the preceding hundred years, was 
derived from the gradual introduction of the Roman liturgies

sacramental process is not a miraculous change; it is not a 
miracle but a mystery.1 Yet all this, when read side by side 
with the testimony of the series of symbolical writers already 
considered, only proves conclusively the strength of the 
Augustinian symbolical tradition in the Carolingian era, and 
suggests that when the controversy is regarded in its wider 
aspect, Paschasius, and not Berengar, was the innovator. 

The reply of Ratramn, another member of the Community 
of Corbey, one of the Benedictine abbeys which had for fifty 
years been the centre of the Augustinian interpretation of the 
Eucharist,? represents the reaction of contemporary theology 
against the new interpretation of Ambrosian realism put out 
by Radbert.2 Ratramn wrote his book, De Corpore et 
Sanguine Domini,* under a commission from Charles the 
Bald. ‘The Emperor submitted to him two questions: In 
the Communion, is the body and blood of Christ received in 
a mystery which is perceived only by the eye of faith; or 
actually,® so that the body and blood are seen by the bodily 
eye? Is the eucharistic body that which was born of the 
Virgin Mary, suffered, died, was buried, rose again, ascended 
into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father? Plainly 
the Emperor had Radbert’s treatise in mind. 

Ratramn answers the first question by a sustained and con- 
sistent criticism of realist doctrine, and seeks to interpret 
Ambrose from his own point of view. Nothing is more absurd 
than to receive the bread as flesh, and to say that the wine is

Continuing his positive statement, Ratramn draws a 
contrast between ‘ figura’ and ‘ veritas.’ A figure or symbol 
must connote by its form the process or reality which it 
indicates, thus bread and the feeding of the Eucharist indicate 
by their form spiritual feeding on the body of Christ. ‘The term 
‘bread’ does not indicate the substantial body.* ‘ Veritas ’ 
is a Clear statement about a thing, as when we say Christ was 

born of the Virgin, suffered, was crucified, dead and buried.® 
The symbol has substantial reality. ‘The substance which 
the bread and wine had before consecration, they possess after 
it.6 He then makes use of Augustine’s distinction between 
the sacrament and the thing of which it is the sacrament (res 
sacramenti). But this ‘thing,’ or the sacramental content, 
or reality, is not the body of Christ in the realist sense of an 
actually present spiritual substance, covered by the accidence 
of the eucharistic species. Accidence plays no part in his 
philosophy.’ The body and blood are only so called figura- 
tively. The sacrament indeed symbolises the heavenly body 
of Christ, but its actuality, as in Berengar’s teaching, is a value.

Thus if the Ratramnian symbolism has a content, the

The concept of Metabolism or Transubstantiation finds 
no place in the doctrine of Ratramn, save in some of his 
terminology,’ which was doubtless due to the influence of 
Ambrose. ‘Transubstantiation is impossible in the light of his 
theory of substance, which, when used of an invisible thing, 
in contrast with the visible, he defines as an invisible virtue, or 
power of the divine Word, in comparison with the visible 
thing.? So the invisible eucharistic substance is a virtue, not 
a real presence. In a similar way he describes the eucharistic 
‘ veritas ’ and ‘ natura’ as the inward virtue of the sacrament, 
in contrast with ‘ essentia ’ or the material elements," although 
he does not goso far as to emphasise the Aristotelean distinction 
between substance and its mode of appearance. Substance, 
nature, essence, ‘ veritas’ in his system are simply ‘things’ in

Radbert’s teaching was criticised, according to his own 
statement,® by several writers, and its innovating character is 
illustrated by the attitude of Rabanus Maurus (d. 856), the 
scholarly Bishop of Mainz. Rabanus was the author of many 
voluminous theological works, but, like John the Scot, does 
not appear to have written a special treatise on the Eucharist.‘ 
Although Rabanus has been judged to be strictly orthodox by 
most Catholic writers,’ yet, like Ratramn, he declined to admit, 
with Paschasius, the identification of the eucharistic body with 
the body of Christ received from the Virgin. ‘The Eucharist, 
he says, is a sign, as Augustine taught.’ The bread and wine 
remain after consecration, but they have a mystic value or effect.8

They unite the faithful with Christ, and signify mystically

His theory of the sacramental process excludes the con- 
ception of a substantial presence of Christ in favour of an 
invisible ‘ thing ’ or eucharistic ‘ virtue ’* in the Augustinian- 
Platonic sense.* Consecration produces the effect of the body 
of Christ, and in this sense the bread becomes His body.°® 
The elements pass over into the sacraments of the body and 
blood of Christ. 

Perhaps Rabanus’ teaching should be described as a dualism 
in which the symbolic conception plays the leading part, while 
his language is couched in the terms of Ambrosian realism. 
If he refers to the body of Christ extended on the cross, and 
the consecrated body extended on the altar, indicating that 
both are present at the Eucharist,® it would be an exaggeration 
to classify him with those who in later days set up the theory 
of Consubstantiation. He interprets the dynamic symbolism 
of Augustine as a process by which the mystic presence of 
Christ produces a real effect upon the communicant who 
receives worthily, not as a ‘ presence ’ in the realist sense, and 
still less as the result of a change of substance.’ 

Yet the teaching of Rabanus illustrates the enormous 
impression made by Paschasius,® even on those who criticised 
him ; indeed, some of the writers of that era were thrown into 
confusion, with the result that the eucharistic teaching of the 
next generation resolved itself into a dualism, in which no 
clear distinction between realism and symbolism was reached.

any truth in the allegation that Berengar began to question the 
realist theory while at Chartres, possibly the statement of 
Fulbert that the substance of bread and wine remained in the 
Eucharist had some influence on Berengar’s thought. But 
Fulbert retains the doctrine of the inward presence of the

the substance of Christ’s body, but without removing their

Throughout the two hundred years preceding the Beren- 
garian controversy, the spiritual interpretation of the Eucharist, 
in the terms of dynamic symbolism, expressing a change of 
value in the elements after consecration, which produced an 
effect upon worthy recipients—an interpretation based upon 
Augustinian teaching—was maintained. It is true that the 
tide of this doctrine was on the ebb, and in the first half of the 
eleventh century had receded so far that, when Berengar’s 
teaching became known, it was condemned as heretical. But 
the orthodox attitude had been largely created by the spread 
of realism under the influence of Paschasian doctrine, and this 
development cannot shake the conviction that, when Berengar 
appeared, he did not come as an innovator, but as the vindi- 
cator and latest prophet of a stream of tradition which had 
flowed steadily from the time of Charles the Great to that of 
Henry III.

Paschasius wrote his work for the benefit of Saxon monks at 
Corbey.2 So early as the time of Oda, Archbishop of 
Canterbury (942-959), the view was widely held among the 
Saxon clergy that consecration did not change the substance 
of bread and wine. The consecrated elements were only a

CHAPTER XIII 
SOURCES OF BERENGAR’S TEACHING 


THE development of Berengar’s theory of the Eucharist issued 
from the critical bent of a mind sharpened by habits of 
philosophical inquiry. Dialectics or logic supplied an instru- 
ment of inquiry which was eagerly seized by an intellect 
naturally prone to probe behind the demands of tradition and 
ecclesiastical authority.1_ For the use of dialectics he claimed 
uninterrupted freedom.? This did not constitute a new 
method in the investigation of eucharistic doctrine. It had 
been used by Ratramn in the ninth century,® and again by 
Heriger of Lobbes in the tenth. But to Berengar it was more 
than an instrument of inquiry, it formed the fundamental 
principle of theological investigation.® 

In such a mind the extravagant realism of Paschasius, 
which was interpreted to illiterate people through the medium 
of the gross stories reported by that teacher,® could not fail to 
arouse opposition. Nor was Berengar dealing with an academic 
question of mere historical interest. ‘The orthodox theological 
disquisition of his day is instinct with Paschasian thought, 
and even the legends, which came probably from the East and

In response to the prayer of a presbyter of blameless life, 
an angel on one occasion appeared and transformed the bread 
on the altar into a boy, whom the presbyter received with 
trembling hands, pressed him to his bosom, and kissed him

the elements were actually the body and blood of the Lord. 
‘Unless I see the thing, I will not believe,’ he cried. They

went to the church where, in the midst of a celebration, they 
saw a boy lying on the altar. When the priest was about to 
take the bread in his hand, an angel descended from heaven 
and sacrificed the boy with a knife, allowing his blood to fall 
into a chalice. He then cut up the limbs of the boy into small 
pieces, one of which, covered with blood, was handed to the 
unbelieving priest, who then confessed that he was convinced. 
Immediately the flesh became bread.°®

Then comes the famous story of a Jewish boy who was at 
school with Christian boys, and one day went into church 
with them during the mysteries, and communicated with the 
other boys. When his father heard what had taken place, he 
became enraged and thrust his son into a burning furnace. 
His mother raised the townspeople, who rushed to the house 
and rescued the boy, and pushed the father into the flames, 
where he perished. When asked how it was that he remained 
unharmed, the boy said that the lady who carried a little boy in 
her bosom in the church, where he had received the bread, 
had covered him with her robe.? 

Tales like these, which were reported also by Guitmund,® 
had been popularised among simple monks, clergy, and people 
in western Europe for two hundred years, and however a 
writer like Lanfranc may have attempted to refine away the 
crudities of realism, that interpretation of the Eucharist was 
clearly presented to the great body of church people through 
the medium of these tales. It was natural that sooner or 
later a revolt against the theoretical conceptions from which 
they issued should occur. Probably from early youth the 
mind of the young Berengar had been provoked by the 
legends. In this contingency we may perhaps see the 
foundation for the rumour of his critical attitude to Fulbert 
when a student at Chartres.4 His gloomy view of the con- 
dition of the Church in his own day appears repeatedly in 
the De Sacra Cena® He saw in the condition of the 
times the fulfilment of Apocalyptic prophecy. ‘ In the times 
in which it has pleased God that we should be born we see 
the overthrow of religion, the sun turned into darkness, the 
moon into blood, when all confess that they know God, but 
deny Him by their conduct, crying “‘ Lord! Lord!” but 
flying from obeying His commands.’® ‘The passage confirms

the report that Berengar wrote a commentary on the

Throughout the controversy Berengar’s method was 
well known to his critics. Gozechin charged him with 
attempting to solve the supra-rational by the aid of the rational 
faculty,! and Lanfranc complained of his attempt to under- 
stand everything through the medium of reason. Guitmund 
sarcastically referred to his petty reasoning.? But if by this 
method, and influenced by a mental reaction against popular 
forms of realist teaching, he quite early reached the conclusion 
that the current theory of the real presence was untenable,‘ 
he allowed several decades to pass before his views were 
committed to a formal treatise, and even then he was driven 
by the necessity of undertaking a polemical defence against 
his enemies. 

A passage in the Epistle to Ansfroi, written about 1050, 
suggests that he did not begin a thorough investigation of 
the historical antecedents of eucharistic doctrine until after 
his general theory had been conceived. He admits that he 
had only recently made a careful study of S. John’s teaching 
on the Eucharist, and that the inquiry had thrown a flood of 
light upon his mind.® It does not follow that up to this 
point he had paid no attention to New Testament teaching 
on the doctrine, but probably, like some other investigators, 
he was not hitherto convinced that the sixth chapter of 
S. John referred to the Eucharist.6 Yet the statement in the 
letter to Ansfroi shows that he had made no close examination 
of Radbert’s De Corpore et Sanguine Domini at that date, for 
in that work Paschasius so closely scrutinises the teaching 
of S. John that any careful reader of his book must have 
been compelled to examine the relation of S. John to the 
controversy.

Ascelin, and Adelmann ; short extracts from his little treatise,

the sacrament.1_ This emphatic criticism of the dogma of 
a change of essence is elaborated in the lengthy epistle to 
Adelmann, written somewhat later, between the Councils of 
Tours (1054) and Rome (1059).?, He says that the bread sur- 
vives and its substance is not annihilated (per assumtionem) 3 
and Paschasius and Lanfranc ‘rave’ when they allege that 
the bread and wine, after consecration, through a breaking-up 
or annihilation of their substance, pass materially (sensualiter) 
into a particle of the flesh and blood of Christ.4 If this 
preliminary objection to the theory of a change of essence 
stands, the whole of their case falls. There is no evidence 
whatever that the flesh of Christ is materially (sensualiter) 
present on the altar.® 

Herein lies the fundamental principle of the whole 
Berengarian criticism of the Catholic dogma of Transub- 
stantiation. It is contrary to the evidence of the senses. 
The bread and wine are there. They can be seen and 
touched. Secondly, reason compels an admission that it 
is contrary to the law of nature that one thing can be changed 
into another without the breaking-up or annihilation of its 
original elements. When the wand of Moses was turned into 
a serpent, or the serpent back into a wand ; when Lot’s wife 
was turned into a pillar of salt, and the water into wine at the 
wedding at Cana; when water and food are transmuted into 
the flesh and blood of the whole animal creation—a breaking- 
up of the one substance takes place before the other can come 
into existence. The latter does not exist before the former 
has ceased to exist. Supposing it were possible for the bread 
on the altar to be transformed materially, through a breaking- 
up of itself, into the flesh of the Lord, then a change would

has existed for ages in immortality in a state of perfection. 

It is hardly necessary to point out that the modern theory 
of the indestructibility of matter does not affect the argument 
of Berengar. The redistribution of elements, on that theory, 
is so complete as to be equivalent, for philosophic and rational 
definition, in that era of thought, to the annihilation of sub- 
stance which Berengar criticised. He admits the possibility of 
such a change of the substance of bread, but it must be trans- 
muted into a substance which had no previous existence,” and 
this, in the case of the body of Christ, is shown to be absurd. 

The doctrine of a change of essence was not only contrary , 
to reason and natural law, it was contrary to Scripture and 
the teaching of the Fathers. Paschasius taught that a little 
portion (portiuncula) of the flesh of Christ is broken with the 
hands and ground by the teeth of men. Against that folly 
(ineptum istud) must be urged the statement of the evangelist, 
who reports that what the Lord gave to His disciples was 
bread, saying ‘Take bread,’ z.e. this thing. S. Paul em- 
phasises the same truth when he says ‘ 'The bread which we 
break is the body of Christ.’ 3 

Thus not only the physical terminology of Radbert, but 
the scholastic realism, which was being developed in his own 
day and which conceived of a change of substance in a philo- 
sophic sense, was refused by Berengar. His detailed criticism 
of the philosophic theory of the change appeared in later 
years, but during this early period he had at least reached a 
denial of the real presence. But he does not deny that after 
consecration the bread and wine have the religious value of 
the body and blood of Christ for the believing and reverent 
recipient. ‘This is the first point which occupies his attention 
in his reply to Adelmann.

sacrament and the consecrated elements, which are ‘signs, 
figures, similitude, pledge "that is to say, symbols—and this

of day. The ‘thing’ of the sacrament, the internal grace,

The similitude or figure lies in the elements, for as Augustine 
writes in the Epistle to Boniface, ‘If the sacraments have 
not the similitude of the things of which they are sacraments, 
they are in no sense sacraments.’® His idea is that the con- 
secrated bread and wine which feed physically have the value 
and hence the similitude of that which feeds spiritually—the

and understanding, with the religious value of the body and

other. In this context Berengar does not mean by ‘ faith and

realism of contemporary orthodox thought, he yet maintains

soul with spiritual life. But the eucharistic experience is 
operated through a subjective medium. To faith and under- 
standing the consecrated elements become ‘the thing of the 
sacrament,’ the body and blood of Christ. Herein lies no 
theory of an objectively real presence.

they come within the survey, realism fades away. As the 
Catholic writer Geiselmann says, if Augustine did not exert 
the same influence as Ambrose upon orthodox writers in the 
pre-scholastic era, that was because he was involved in the 
dynamic and spiritual tendencies of Basil, Gregory of 
Nazianzus, Tertullian, and Cyprian.1 But he carried the line 
of thought very much farther than any of these writers would 
have gone. He draws a clear distinction between a material 
sign and its spiritual significance. A sacrament is not that 
which it represents. It is bread and wine to the senses, but it 
has the significance of the body and blood of Christ for the 
soul. It exerts a dynamic influence upon the soul of the 
faithful recipient. Its effect is the same as if the spiritual body 
and blood of Christ were actually given. Within these limits 
the change wrought by consecration upon the elements is 
confined. In the Berengarian terminology of Augustinian 
dynamic symbolism, they are changed not by destruction of 
the original material elements, but by the addition of spiritual 
significance. The sacrament is the body of Christ for th 

inner man only. It is not in itself an objective quantity. It 
has a spiritual significance.? Its effect depends not on the act 
of reception, but so far as a man is spiritually a member of 
Christ. ‘The pious receive the sacrament visibly, but the 
thing of the sacrament invisibly. The impious receive only 
the sacrament 4 (z.e. the elements). So he overcomes a con- 
tradiction into which Augustine was driven during the 
controversy with the Donatist schismatics, when the theory 
of the ministry, put out by him, based upon apostolic suc- 
cession, caused him to contend that good and bad alike 
received the grace of the sacrament, on the ground that

CHAPTER XIV 
BERENGAR’S EARLIEST CRITICS 


CRITICAL friends and enemies of Berengar did not rest content 
with the bare statement and denial of his doctrines, but in 
long letters and formal treatises took up the discussion, and 
began the philosophic grounding of orthodox eucharistic 
teaching, which was one of the results of the Berengarian 
controversy. Ascelin says ‘ So long as I live, by the help of 
God, I will hold certainly and indubitably in the sacred places 
of my heart, against all who attempt to enter with violence, 
that the bread and wine on the altar, by the power of the 
Holy Ghost, through the ministry of the priest, are made true 
body and true blood of Christ.’1 This can be proved by 
Scripture, if a wrong interpretation is not put upon its state- 
ments. John the Scot maintained that what was consecrated 
on the altar was not the true body and blood of Christ.2. This 
could be refuted from the writings of the Fathers, and especially 
from the Gregorian Sacramentary. ‘May thy sacraments 
perfect in us, O Lord! what they contain, that what we take in 
form, we may receiveintruth.’? ‘ Contrary to what is Catholic,’ 
John the Scot denied this, and said that those things (namely 
the body and blood) ‘ are received in form not in truth.’ 4 

It is to be noticed that the use of ‘specie’ in the two 
quotations differs. For Ascelin and the Gregorian Sacra- 
mentary ‘specie’ means the form of the material elements. 
For John the Scot (or Ratramn) it means the form or appear- 
ance of the body and blood, which is all that the sacrament 
contains. Symbolism is emphasised in the latter case and 
realism in the other.

Ascelin continues: ‘ For the rest, with Paschasius and 
other Catholics, I not only discern, but I venerate and hold 
that the true body and true blood of Christ are received by the 
faithful at the altar beneath the forms of bread and wine.’ 4 
‘I do not do this, as you say, contrary to the law of nature,” 
for by nature I mean no other than the will of God.’ ? Nature 
is not the cause of things, the will of God is the cause of 
nature itself and of everything born in nature. The will of 
God is so effective and powerful that anything can come into 
existence by His mere act of volition.* ‘ All that God wills 
He does.’ He wills that the bread and wine on the altar 
prepared by the consecration of the Holy Spirit, through the 
ministry of the priest, may be mightily created as His true 
flesh and blood, and by being created daily, may be mystically 
offered. This He Himself clearly shows in the words of 
institution, saying ‘ Take, eat ; This is my body.’ 

Up to this point Ascelin’s language and meaning are 
expressed in the Radbertian sense. But he wanders into 
obscurity in attempting to define the significance of ‘ body ’ 
in the words of institution. ‘ Lest they perceive lightly or 
think of “body” without discrimination,’ the faithful are 
called members of Christ. He clearly defines ‘ body’ and 
says ‘ which is offered for you.’ So with the cup ‘ which is 
poured out for you.’® Ascelin stumbles between the idea 
of the body of Christ as the members of the Church on the one 
hand, and as the historical body of the Incarnation on the 
other.” His confused language suggests that the body of 
Christ is received by itself, that is by its own members, or the 
company of the faithful—that reception depends upon faith.

are composed of material and immaterial, mortal and immortal 
substances, if we believe that the divine and human nature 
came together in one person.’ In this statement, firstly, 
Ascelin avoids the Radbertian doctrine of a change of essence.® 
His thought is rather that of Heriger of Lobbes, who had 
already given expression to the idea of a unifying process of the 
bread with the body, rather than a change of essence.® It is 
also possible to see here the beginning of the later doctrine 
of impanation, or coming of Christ into the bread on the 
analogy of the Incarnation.’ Secondly, a curious confusion 
of thought is apparent. He speaks of both substances, meaning 
the bread and body, being material and visible. This really 
goes farther than the Radbertian doctrine in the direction of 
a physical presence of Christ in the Eucharist, and it is indeed 
not what Ascelin means. His allusion to the body and soul

Radbert when he met the criticism of Ratramn.? 

But this want was supplied by Adelmann in a letter to 
Berengar, which has the dimensions of a treatise. Adelmann 
begins his positive statement by a quotation from S. John vi.: 
“I am the living bread which came down from heaven. 
Whosoever eateth of this bread shall live for ever: the bread 
which I shall give is my flesh, for the life of the world.’ 
Adelmann notes that Christ says ‘I will give,’ not ‘I have 
given,’ that His words refer to the Eucharist which was yet to 
be instituted, and not to the feeding of the five thousand, 
which was past. Christ began to give His flesh on the day 
before He suffered, as the words of institution indicate. Ifthe 
words of institution are not credited, then either the veracity 
of Christ is questioned or the words cannot be genuine. But 
cannot He whose word at the beginning created the light 
from nothing, also say of the bread ‘ This is my body,’ so that 
it becomes so? And could not He whose authority turned 
water into wine, by the use of the same authority vocally 
mediated, turn wine into His blood ?? Here is the Radbertian 
doctrine expressed in its naked metabolism. 

The change takes place by the agency of the human 
ministry through which Christ Himself operates. He had 
said ‘ Without me ye can do nothing’ and ‘ Behold! I am 
with you always, even to the end of the world.’ This presence 


is possible by reason of His divinity or uncircumscribed nature

in His twofold Person, which enables Him to be wholly |

Yet Adelmann applies it not only to explain the eucharistic

Because Christ remains always with men, He baptises men 
through men, and consecrates whatever is consecrated through 
men.? Through the hand and mouth of the priest Christ 
both baptises and creates His body and blood. That which 
He once did passibly in Himself, He does daily and impassibly 
through those to whom He gives power to become the sons 
of God. 

Adelmann is groping for the conception of the Eucharist as 
a sacrifice, but he swings back in the direction of a symbolical 
interpretation. ‘The words ‘ This do in remembrance of me’ 
are the most sure pledge of His love to the disciples and of 
obedience to God.* ‘The sacrament is not visibly transmuted 
into the form of flesh and blood ® because we walk by faith 
and not by sight. If the sacraments showed outwardly the 
things that are within, the faith by which the just liveth would 
be not only idle, but altogether non-existent. This was a 
loftier conception than that of Paschasius, who, like Ambrose, 
explained away the appearance of bread and wine as a con- 
cession to human weakness, which could not tolerate the sight 
of flesh and blood. Faith is exercised in believing what is not 
apparent. ‘The life-giving sacrament lies hidden in power 
beneath the material species, as the soul in the body.® 

Adelmann was the first of Berengar’s opponents to make 
use of psychology, a weapon which Ratramn had directed

against the Radbertian system. He classifies the modes of

the apprehension of the relation between numbers and sounds, 
or the ideas of incorporeal things which can only be under-

of perception he refers to another, which, however, he terms

cesses of perception. We can approach God directly, not by 
a natural process, but by the grace of God, and this is faith. 
Now the Christian sacraments cannot be discussed by human 
reason. ‘They must be discussed by faith, that is by a divine 
gift (munere).? Thus, in Baptism when perception and reason 
apprehend nothing more than water, faith descending within, 
sees the life-giving power there, and simply gazes.2 Thus 
he combines mysticism with his psychology. But the human 
soul always gushes forth, especially in those who through 
philosophy and empty fallacy, seek to discuss meticulously 
the causes and reasons of everything.t So although, like 
Lanfranc, Adelmann ostensibly despises dialectical methods, 
he not only, like the Archbishop, adopts the method, but 
arrives at a much more reasonable and lofty conclusion. 
Without direct reference to the Eucharist, he admits that the 
material of water survives in the baptismal sacrament. The 
incorporeal soul is born again through corporeal water,® and 
the process by which the spiritual gift or grace of God is 
apprehended is the process of faith, which itself is a gift of 
God. The spiritual gift is received rather subjectively than 
objectively. Was Adelmann at times unconsciously under the 
influence of Berengar’s teaching, or did the Radbertian 
materialism only gradually stifle the more spiritual intuitions 
of the thinkers of the eleventh century ? 

But he falls back finally into the metabolism of the ninth- 
century writer. Faith, after all,is rather a mantle which covers 
up the metabolic process in the Eucharist from the scrutiny 
of human gaze, than a torch leading on to spiritual perception.

The early defenders of Paschasian doctrine made no 
attempt to explain, still less to develop, the dogma of a change 
of essence in the Eucharist. In his long epistle to Berengar 
this subject was treated by Hugh, Bishop of Langres.1 He 
begins with a criticism of the dynamic symbolism of Berengar,? 
based upon information obtained from him at a personal 
interview. If Berengar, whom he compliments as the most 
acute of men, had examined the nature of things, and had not 
scrutinised the opinions of the Fathers with a distraught and 
prejudiced mind, it would have been impossible for him to 
describe the sacrament as the body and blood of Christ and 
yet to say that it is incorporeal.* 

Schwabe claims that no other contemporary grasped so 
clearly Berengar’s meaning or expressed it so concisely.> But 
while Hugh does not stumble about among the implications of 
the Berengarian doctrine, proceeding directly to its centre, 
and dealing frankly with its content, yet his apprehension of 
Berengar’s meaning appears to be only one degree clearer than 
that of other orthodox writers. He perceives that the funda- 
mental principle of Berengar’s teaching is that the nature and 
essence of the bread and wine are not changed, and that the 
body of Christ has an intellectual existence only, by which is 
meant that it is incorporeal °—that is to say, it has no real 
existence in the sacrament. 

Hugh’s criticism starts from an entirely different angle 
from that of Berengar. It springs from the doctrine of the 
change of essence. ‘'The body which you say is incorporeal 
Christ offered palpably.’” If the nature and essence of the 
bread and wine remain unchanged after consecration, no change

Hugh states the physiological problem of realism which its 
_ metaphysics never solved. On his premises the body of Christ 
is not destroyed, because the bread is translated into itself and 
so becomes indestructible, a manifest denial of physiological 
processes. Berengar conserved the indestructibility of the 
body of Christ by denying that it was in the bread. 

On this unsafe foundation Hugh of Langres developed his 
positive theory of the real presence. ‘ What is incorruptible 
cannot be destroyed. Fire is not destroyed when smitten, nor 
the air by a flying arrow.1 Nor is the body of Christ made 
less by the repeated communions at human altars, any more 
than the light which feeds the eyes.’ ? Quoting Ambrose? he 
identifies the eucharistic body with the flesh and blood born 
of the Virgin: ‘from this very material the fruits of the 
sacrament proceed.’ This bread feeds us with so great a 
power that we are incorporated with Christ to the very marrow 
and are suckled in faith. By this means we become the sons 
of God. By this immortal food we are increased, while He 
is not decreased.* 

Thus the superstructure which Hugh erects is much firmer 
than his foundation. When his theory of the real presence is © 
separated from his denial of the existence of the nature of the 
bread and wine after consecration, it represents a big step in 
the advance of orthodox doctrine. If the sacrament possesses 
the effectiveness of the body of Christ as the dynamic 
symbolists maintained, then, Hugh argued, the body of Christ 
must be present in the sacrament as a working or effective 
principle. Whereas Radbert had only reduced the function of 
symbolism for the theology of metabolism, Hugh deliberately 
separated himself from it, and laid the foundation for the 
elevation of the Eucharist, in a special manner, above other 
sacraments. So he apprehends the sacramental content

the Aristotelean doctrine of substance and accidence is applied

species in the sense of accidence becomes the final conclusion.® 

The book of Durand of ‘Troarn, De Corpore et Sanguine 
Domini,’ is the first exhaustive treatise on the Eucharist 
which appeared in our period. It makes use of more orthodox 
phraseology than the lengthy epistle of Hugh of Langres, and 
while, like all medieval writings which discussed the theory 
of the Eucharist, Durand’s book suffers from repetition and 
some verbosity, it marks a farther stage in advance upon the 
development of the doctrine of Transubstantiation presented 
by Hugh of Langres.

latter. Eve was made ‘ similar ’ to Adam, but none the less 
she had the same nature and the same condition. She had 
flesh like Adam. So also, although the bread and wine are 
a similitude of the flesh and blood of Christ, yet the sacramental 
elements are really His body and blood.? In the same way, 
if Christ is said to have been made in the similitude of a man, 
He actually possesses manhood.? But this is to explain sym- 
bolism in the alleged Greek sense.4 The symbol is actually 
that which it represents, a conception foreign to Berengar’s 
teaching. 

He perceives that the manna was a bare symbol of the 
Eucharist, because the manna really was what it appeared to 
be. It did not represent something other than it really was. 
When the apostle said that manna was a figure of the Eucharist, 
he was referring to mere similarity between the manna and 
sacramental bread, not to any similarity of inward reality.® 
A ‘ figure ’ may possess the form of the reality, as the writer 
to the Hebrews said when he described the Son as the image 
of the Father’s being.6 Butif the conception of ‘ figura ’ rules 
out that of substance, then the Son is not what the Father is. 
Similarly, if the sacrament, which likewise is called ‘ figura,’ is 
only a shade (umbra) it has no reality.’ But if on the contrary 
the Son, who is called a ‘ figure,’ is yet of the divine substance, 
so can the word ‘ figure’ be used of the sacrament without 
contradicting its reality. The Eucharist is then a figure of the 
Divine Substance, and the manna is a figure of this figure, the 
one is reality, the other is a mere similarity.®

Durand’s conception of symbolism is thus merely nominal. 
In the most favourable light it represents an old Greek idea, 
but when laid bare it proves to be but little removed from the 
Paschasian realism. Although something different appears to 
human eyes, although as a type it is not denied that it usefully 
signifies something different, the sacramental element is 
actually nothing else substantially than the true flesh and blood 
of Christ. So he really inverts the significance of eucharistic 
symbolism. 'The elements being substantially body and blood, 
are only the symbols of bread and wine, and there is a sense in 
which symbolism constitutes a hindrance to the conception 
of the real presence.?. This inversion of the significance of 
symbolism, by setting up the elements as symbols of the bread 
and wine, has been noticed before in the old Gallic liturgies and 
in Amalry’s teaching,? and it will occur again in the phraseology 
of Lanfranc.* 

If Durand’s criticism of symbolism breaks down, his 
positive contribution to the development of the doctrine of 
Transubstantiation is more successful. The real flesh and 
blood of Christ are available to us through the process of the 
Incarnation,®? which makes possible a communion with His 
flesh,* so that we remain naturally in Him, and thus we feed 
on the divine.’ Durand’s argument reverses the significance 
of the Incarnation for the purpose of eucharistic feeding. In 
the hypostatic union of God and man in Christ, the divine 
Christ assumes flesh, but in that union man also, by way of 
the sacrament, is united with Christ. We are made the throne 
and kingdom of the divinity, we are transfigured from the 
human into the divine, and are led from the carnal to the 
spiritual. The cause of our life is the presence of the

The climax of the orthodox defence of the Ambrosian- 
Radbertian doctrine of the identification of the eucharistic 
body with the historical flesh of Christ was reached in the 
definition of belief submitted by Humbert to Berengar at the 
Roman Council of 1059, where the ‘ true body and blood of 
Christ ’ were stated to be materially (sensualiter) present in 
the Eucharist when they were actually handled and broken by 
the priest and ground by the teeth of the faithful. No more 
gross statement of the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist has 
ever been made. Not only have later Catholic writers sought 
to explain away the crude realism of Humbert, by resorting 
to the theory of the ‘ communicatio idiomatum,’ or by limiting 
the conception of the breaking of the body to the eucharistic 
species,* but later definitions of the dogma have frankly 
reduced the terminology of Humbert. This does not mean 
that the development of Catholic dogma ceased with Humbert. 
The theory of Transubstantiation had still to be developed. 
It was not a leading subject of inquiry among orthodox 
writers during the first phase of the controversy, although the 
fact of a change, and some discussion of its method, was noted 
by them under the stress of Berengar’s criticism, which had 
already raised the point,® and he, like his opponents, does not 
lay emphasis upon it until a later stage in the dispute. The 
first phase of the Berengarian controversy was occupied by 
the orthodox writers with establishing the doctrine of the real 
presence.
