CHAPTER XV 


BERENGAR’S ‘ OPUSCULUM ” AND LANFRANC’S REPLY 


Second Stage of the Controversy. 


Soon after the Council of 1059 Berengar assembled his 
opinions on the Eucharist, and published them in the form 
of a ‘ little book ’ which Lanfranc said he had received ‘ to be 
destroyed,’ 4 doubtless under the order. of the Roman authori- 
ties, who had condemned all Berengar’s writings. The time 
when this treatise was written is indicated by internal state- 
ments, which show that one of Berengar’s objects in writing 
it was the refutation of Cardinal Humbert, and the recantation 
of the oath which the latter had drawn up for him to swear 
at Rome in 1059. Only fragments of the treatise survive. 
They have been preserved in Lanfrane’s De Corpore et 
Sanguine Domini.2. Sufficient remains to show that Berengar’s 
views had become more definite since he wrote the long epistle 
to Adelmann, and in the ‘Opusculum’ we have the main lines, 
or at least a series of texts, for his longer work, the De Sacra 
Cena. 

The opinion of Paschasius and Lanfranc that the substance 
of bread and wine does not remain on the altar after consecration 
is madness.? If they say that the bread and wine of the altar 
are only sacraments, or only true body and blood of Christ, 
in either case, he contends, they admit that the bread and 
wine remain ;* just as when Scripture says that Christ is the 
chief corner-stone, the statement does not do away with Christ, 
but unreservedly asserts that He ‘is.’5 Not every statement 
remains valid if either of its premises is removed,® so that 


1 Migne, 150, 415b. 2 Ibid. 407-426. 3 Ibid. 412d. 
4 Ibid. 414d. 5 [bid. 415d. 8 Ibid. 416d. 


286 BERENGAR 


both predicate and object in these statements must be main- 
tained. The subject bread and wine remains, whether it is 
predicated of a sacrament or of the true body and blood of 
Christ.1_ Thus Humbert, in spite of his denial, cannot escape 
the conclusion that the bread and wine remain in the con- 
secrated elements.” 

As in the epistle to Adelmann, his constructive theory is 
derived from Augustine. A sacrament is a ‘ sacred sign.’ 4 
A sign is something beyond the form (species) which it conveys 
to the senses, causing something different from itself to enter 
into perception.® But sacraments must have the similitude of 
the things of which they are sacraments, otherwise they 
cannot be sacraments. ‘The signs of spiritual things are 
visible, but invisible things are honoured in them. The species 
which has been sanctified by consecration may not be 
degraded to ordinary use.” 

Consecration produces an effect on the bread and wine. 
They become the agents of spiritual life.® It gives them a 
religious value, but they do not cease to exist ; while remaining, 
they are changed into something else. A new significance is 
added to them, that of the heavenly body of Christ. A sacra- 
ment has two parts, it is prepared from two things, the visible 
and the invisible, the sacrament and the thing of the sacrament. 
The latter is the body of Christ and would be visible if it were 
before the eyes, but as it is raised up in heaven, sitting at the 
right hand of the Father until the end of the world, as 
S. Peter writes, existing in Christ’s Person as God and man,”® 
it cannot be recalled. From one point of view the sacraments 
are the body and blood of Christ, as baptism is faith,! for the

But Lanfranc has broken off Berengar’s statement with

these words refer to other things, and nothing which refers to 
something else can be that to which it refers. So it is not the 
body of Christ.* 

Berengar’s idea of consecration at this period is made clear 
by his use of the term ‘conficitur.’> The elements are 
prepared, or are given the significance of the body of Christ, 
which is in heaven, and not in the sacrament. At this early 
stage he was content to do little more than repeat the criticism 
directed by Ratramn against the theory of a change of essence. 
He does not yet expound it dialectically.6 While no doubt the

have brought out more clearly, and with better sequence,

in concluding that Lanfranc has preserved the most important 
passages. As all these extracts are repeated, and most of them 
expanded, in the De Sacra Cena, they call for no further 
comment here.

Eusebius makes no contribution to the development of the 
Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist. His letter, which only 
repeats the language of earlier writers, probably represents 
the attitude of many contemporaries to the dispute, an attitude 
which had been maintained by uncontroversial minds in the 
Western Church since Radbert and Ratramn raised the 
question in the ninth century. It represented a vague mystical 
realism. ‘The words of institution showed that the body of 
Christ was present, but the method of the presence was quite 
unknown. If Berengar had not asked Eusebius to allow a 
public disputation on the doctrine of Ambrose,? it is probable 
that Eusebius would not have attempted to define his own 
belief. The epistle is to be interpreted not so much as an 
indication of a change in the doctrinal attitude of Eusebius, 
but rather as a refusal to give Berengar any further practical 
or political support. To Eusebius Berengar was a subject of 
political rather than doctrinal interest. It is probable that the 
doctrinal statement given in the letter represents the views 
held by Eusebius from the beginning of his relations with 
Berengar. If he accorded to Berengar any doctrinal latitude, 
that was because the whole question was for him too deeply

The dialectical formulation of the orthodox opinions 
begins with Lanfranc’s treatise. This was, of course, inspired 
by Berengar’s lost treatise, although it is probable that the 
Scolasticus did not direct an elaborate dialectical attack, such 
as appears in the De Sacra Cena, against his opponents, in

lation of Radbertian doctrine, the method was still dis- 
regarded, as we shall see, by many orthodox writers. A 
school of anti-dialectical,! as well as dialectical,? writers 
appeared. 

Although the day has long gone by since it was sup- 
posed that Lanfranc’s book was the last word in the dispute 
between himself and Berengar, yet some writers, and among 
them Schnitzer, Endres,? and Geiselmann, discuss the De 
Sacra Cana before the De Corpore et Sanguine Domini# 
Perhaps the dogmatic theologians have some justification for 
grouping Berengar’s main ideas around one nucleus, but the 
historical sequence of events and of thought, which is 
Schnitzer’s concern as a historian, is thereby disarranged, a 
result the less desirable because Berengar does not appear 
to have produced a thorough formulation of his scheme of 
thought until after Lanfranc’s book appeared. . 

Lanfranc’s distrust of Berengar’s critical method dated 
from the time when, quite early in his career in France, he 
listened to Berengar’s lectures at Tours.® But he was too 
sound a scholar not to perceive the value of dialectics for 
orthodox theology, within certain well-defined limits, and the 
caution expressed in his letter to Domnald, Bishop of Dublin,®

Lanfranc starts from the general proposition that faith is

Like Durand of Troarn, Lanfranc reverses the symbolism 
of the Eucharist. The sacrament is called bread by the usage 
of Holy Scripture by which things are often called by the 
names of those things by means of which they come into 
existence.? The terms ‘ species’ and ‘ similitude’ are words 
used of the things which existed before, and from which the 
body and blood of Christ are prepared.* It is usual to give 
certain things the names of those things from which they are 
prepared, although being changed into another nature they 
cannot now be those things by which they are proved effective.® 
The divine pages call the body of the Lord bread, by a sacred 
or mystical method of speech, either because being prepared 
from bread it retains some of its qualities, or because it 
ministers to the soul and substance of eternal life, or because 
it is the bread of angels. So the consecrated elements are

by which the doctrine of the real presence was rescued from 
the hands of headstrong zealots. From the beginning, the 
main body of Catholic doctrine had been expressed in less 
extravagant terms than those drawn up by Humbert in 1059 ; 
but Lanfranc was the first writer to resort to a rational ex- 
planation, yet rather in the form of the separation of ideas 
and the definition of terms than by systematising his con- 
clusions. Hence much had to be done by those who followed 
him.

CHAPTER XVI 
BERENGAR ‘ON THE HOLY SUPPER’ 


IN his own day Berengar was a defeated man, but no career 
illustrates more completely the wisdom of never admitting 
defeat. From this unconquerable attitude sprang the De 
Sacra Cena, which has enabled a later generation to rescue 
the teaching of that persevering controversialist from the hands 
of his enemies, and from the gossiping letter-writers of his 
own age. Ifthe campaign for a plain and sensible interpreta- 
tion of the words of Scripture and sayings of the Fathers was 
lost by Berengar in the eleventh century, when the realists 
passed over him in their advance to final victory in 1215, the 
date when Transubstantiation became the official dogma of 
the Church, yet by handing on the De Sacra Cena Berengar 
has shown how well developed the evangelical theory of the 
Eucharist was in the early Middle Ages. 

But if the contents of his book have placed succeeding 
generations under an obligation of gratitude to him, its form 
constitutes for all who read it a labour and a penance. As 
a disquisition it is amorphous, as a composition it entirely lacks 
the qualities of the beautiful epistle to the hermits. The 
elliptical and frequently almost untranslatable syntax, the 
disorderly treatment of topic after topic, pursuing no sequence 
of ideas, and guided by fits and starts of emotional recollection 
rather than by methodical thought—the mind occupied for a 
few moments with a subject springing forth from the welter of 
badly correlated notions which crowded his brain, then seizing 
upon another—the book will always be a cause of despair, save 
to the most patient of readers. Being agitated, his Latin style 
became disorganised. Perhaps his most trying trick is the con- 
stant use of the double negative. Often he appears to have been 


BERENGAR ‘ON THE HOLY SUPPER’ — 301 


thinking in his mother-tongue, and writing in Latin, without 
taking care to translate his syntax as well as his accidence. 
Again, the constant repetition of statement and quotation, the 
doubling back upon themes already worn threadbare, suggest 
not only excessive excitement of brain, but a composition put 
together at intervals during a period of persecution when the 
writer was never sure of an opportunity for protracted work. 
He seems to have forgotten what had already been written, 
and the book is the output of a mind which did not naturally 
unburden itself, or discharge at leisure the ideas which it 
struggled to throw out. He wrote in haste and fear lest 
destruction should overtake him before his great apologia was 
completed. It is even possible that the only MS. which exists 
is his own unrevised and uncorrected copy. As a polemical 
work it was written with one eye upon the adversary. It rebuts, 
point after point, the shafts of the enemy, and this constitutes 
the only method of composition observed by its writer. ‘That 
Berengar intended his work to go forth to the world in its 
present form is inconceivable. If he had been allowed 
opportunity for leisurely composition he might have produced 
a classic work on the doctrine of the Eucharist, for if amorphous 
and unmethodical, the De Sacra Cena is its own trumpeter, 
and contains in its uncorrelated paragraphs ideas and explana- 
tions which in themselves are quite clear. The process of 
drawing them forth and setting them in as orderly a sequence 
as may be amounts almost to editorial revision. 

However defective Berengar’s earlier studies of Holy 
Scripture on the doctrine of the Eucharist may have been, 
this omission was amply filled by the time the De Sacra 
Cena was written. It abounds with references both to the 
Old and New Testaments. Whoever goes contrary, he says, 
to the gospels and epistles, and indeed to any of the ‘ authentic 
Scriptures,’ does not do well.1 The weight of authority of the 
prophetical books,? the gospels and epistles is not to be 
refused.2 The Holy Spirit speaks in the Scriptures.t He 
denies that he has thrown aside the Scriptures,> and he

in dialectics, for this is equivalent to taking refuge in reason, 
and he who does not take refuge in it surrenders his honour, 
and cannot be renewed from day to day in the image of God. 
Augustine said that dialectics is the art of arts, the discipline 
of disciplines. Itcanlearn; it can teach; it not only desires to 
create people who know, but does it.2. A man of spirit would 
rather prefer to perish, if he had the option, than to yield to 


tradition.® 
At the same time Berengar maintains that Lanfranc has 


exaggerated his use of dialectics. To make use of dialectical 
terminology for the explanation of truth was not to take refuge 
in dialectics as a final court of appeal. Christ Himself did not 
refuse to make use of this method when He said ‘If I by 
Beelzebub cast out devils, by whom do your sons cast them 
out ?’ and ‘If David in the Spirit called Him Lord, how is 
He his Son?’® Reason is predominant and independent of

the authority of tradition.t Yet, as Harnack has said, in

of negative illuminism ’ against authority, but in order that 
authority, or the true tradition of the Church, might be

Berengar’s criticism of the theory of Paschasius, Humbert, 
and Lanfranc strikes at the root of all realist interpretations 
of the Eucharist. He refuses to admit their denial that the 
material elements remain on the altar after consecration,? and 
he denies their assertion that the real substantial body and 
blood of Christ are present after consecration.* His criticism 
therefore advances along two avenues. Paschasius and 
Lanfranc urged that although the substances of bread and wine 
do not remain on the altar after consecration in their original 
elements,” yet they are present in their visible form ® and retain 
the colour of bread and wine.’ Berengar replies that the 
qualities of colour, flavour, and smell cannot be separated from 
their substances.’ If the original elements or substances dis- 
appear, the qualities which the senses apprehend cannot remain. 
It is as absurd to maintain that the substance of bread can 
be changed into the substance of the body of Christ and yet 
retain the colour of bread, as it would be to allege, on the 
contrary, that by changing the colour of a man’s face into that 
of an Ethiopian’s the substance of his face could be changed.? 
By the evidence of the senses the colour of the elements 
remains,/® and they themselves can be seen.! We have, in 
addition, the evidence of the words of institution and of the 
Fathers. At the Supper Christ broke material bread and spoke 
of material bread. When He used the words ‘ Eat of this,’

supporter of truth, a statement which Lanfranc had criticised

of his remark. Although Humbert denied, and had compelled 
Berengar to deny, in the terms of the oath of 1059, that bread 
and wine remained on the altar after consecration, yet in what-

escape from an admission of the existence of bread and wine 
in the Eucharist. Whether he affirmed that the bread and 
wine which are placed on the altar are, after consecration, 
sacraments ; or the bread and wine which are placed on the 
altar are, after consecration, true body and blood of Christ ; 
or, again, the bread and wine which are placed on the altar are, 
after consecration, only true body and blood of Christ—in 
each case, Berengar contends, Humbert has admitted the 
survival of the bread and wine.1 

The proposition must stand as a whole in its subjective and 
predicative terms. Humbert sets up as a subjective statement 
‘the bread and wine which are placed on the altar,’ together 
with its predicate, ‘are true body and blood of Christ’ or 
‘only true body and blood of Christ.’ If, then, he afterwards 
denies either term he overthrows his own case.” In the earlier 
treatise Berengar had driven home this argument by affirming 
that not every proposition could stand if part of it were over- 
thrown, and Lanfranc had succeeded in destroying his case by 
pointing out that this was a particular, not a general, premise, 
so that his conclusion was invalid. Berengar rather lamely 
now tried to cover himself by alleging that a similar usage of 
the words ‘ not every ’ was to be found in the Vulgate.* Yet 
the quotations which he offered are not convincing, and he

rock was Christ’ does not predicate the divine man. In the

food, element, raiment, ornament are not particulars (solitaria). 
Particulars are the names of specific objects which are 
differentiated from other things—such as earth or bread—which 
have no reference to anything save themselves, and cannot be 
extended so as to comprise many other things, unless, for 
example, the term ‘ earth’ is equated with ‘ element,’ when 
it can be applied to earth, water, etc., or when bread is used 
inthe sense of food. ‘ Element ’ and‘ food ’ are general terms— 
so also is the term ‘ sacrament ’—which, while connoting to the 
mind a certain thing possessing a special name, yet imparts to 
the recipient something which is common or general with 
other things.} 


There is indeed a nominalistic ring in this phraseology, but , 


when Berengar’s developed theory of the sacrament is examined 
a vague Platonic realism appears to lie behind his thoughts. 
He quotes Augustine’s letter to Faustus, in which the former 
refers to a ‘ mystical becoming ’ at consecration, not a creative 
action,” and Berengar conceives of the body of Christ as 
existing in idea, in heaven, on the Platonic theory. This body 
becomes effective and so available for men in its sacramental 
counterpart or type. ‘The consecrated eucharistic elements 
have the value of the body of Christ for the salvation of the 
soul.? It is their function to concentrate attention upon the 
body of Christ, which cannot be touched with the hands, 
since it remains in heaven.* This approximation to Platonic 
idealism ° is the nearest approach made by Berengar to sacra- 
mental realism, and embodies a realism of a more refined 
character than that conceived by Lanfranc and other con- 
temporaries on the orthodox side. Even the resurrected flesh 
of Christ which sits at the right hand of the Father is super- 
substantial, as Ambrose and Augustine said.®

He denies that the statement ‘ the bread and wine of the 
altar are only sacraments’ was made by him. On the contrary, 
his contention is that when it is stated that the bread and wine 
are sacraments there is no abolition of the bread and wine, 
but another name is applied to their natural designations, a 
name which is quite unconnected with their nature—the name 
‘sacrament.’ ‘Their particular designation is exchanged for a 
general term, or, at least, a general term is thrown around their 
particular designations, without obliterating the specific sub- 
stances of bread and wine.! If this is realism, it consists 
rather in the terminology than in the content of Berengar’s 
thought. It_does not pass beyond idealism, for the ‘ parti- 
culars’ bread and wine are retained. They make generally 
effective the body of Christ which has an ‘ideal,’ a real- 
heavenly existence. 

- This appears to be the distinction drawn by him between 
the ‘sacrament’ and the ‘thing of the sacrament.’? If a 
sacrament exists, it cannot reasonably be denied that the 
thing of the sacrament (res sacramenti) exists. To be a sacra- 
ment and to be ‘only’ (solum) cannot be demonstrated of 
anything.* ‘The term ‘sacrament ’ (sacramentum) describes the 
‘ particulars,’ the consecrated bread and wine. The ‘res 
sacramenti’ is the heavenly body of Christ, a universal 4 
applicable to all who receive the sacrament worthily. He never 
identifies, in the realist-metabolist sense, the sacrament with its 
spiritual content. If the terms ‘ body ’ and ‘ blood’ are used, 
as he admits they may be,® with reference to the sacramental 
body of Christ in heaven, they can only be used in a figurative 
sense, which is the only usage sanctioned by Scripture.®

The application of the concept of accidence to the unessential 
or contingent qualities of matter belongs to the era when 
Scolasticism was fully developed. Berengar’s teaching marked 
a step in advance, and the intermediate stage was supplied by 
Alan of Lille.® 

According to Berengar everything has two properties. It 
is one thing in that which it is. It is another thing in the 
sense in which anything is. The distinction between particu- 
lars and universals was not far beyond the horizon of Berengar’s 
thought. His meaning is that everything is one thing in its 
special identity, and another thing so far as it shares its 
‘materia’ or substance with everything else—so far as it is 
universal. 

His next proposition has the appearance of a logical quibble. 
‘ Nothing can exist subject to the contingency of ceasing to be 
itself.’>- But his meaning is that special identity cannot be 
separated from substantial existence. ‘ If you say,’ he argues, 
‘that Socrates is righteous, you have stated him to be some- 
thing, but he cannot be righteous if he ceases to exist.” ® Aman

may be a stern Cato in character, but he cannot have the

If my finger is destroyed by fire its straightness (col- 
lineatio) can still survive in a finger modelled of wood or stone, 
but this argument does not bear on the question, because the 
statement is concerned with two different objects—my finger 
and wood or stone ‘—and this is equivalent to admitting that 
specific qualities cease to be if the materia or substance is 
destroyed. ‘The statement directly negatives his proposition 
that nothing can exist subject to the contingency of ceasing 
to be itself, and, on the contrary, admits that specific qualities 
may be shared by different objects. 

Yet when applied to the sacramental process his argument 
is valid. For to allege that through consecration the original 
essence (pristina essentia) of the bread and wine has dis- 
appeared, and that they only exist in appearance (specie), is 
unjustifiable, for that cannot exist which is no longer in the 
substance in which it was.8 The substance being destroyed, 
qualities which accompanied it, such as colour, cannot survive.?®

in the nature of the iron which Elisha caused to float like

existed before the change, and the woman and the rod ceased 
to exist after it.2 Metabolism in these instances can be ex- 
plained either as the change of a disposition into a condition, 
or the promotion of a lower condition into a higher, or through 
the destruction of one condition and the institution of another. 
Expressed in other terms, these three modes of change may be 
said to take place—through the total destruction of the original 
object ; by a change of condition while the original element is 
preserved ; or by the merging of two existing things without 
destruction or new creation.* 

Matter can change its form. Gold becomes a ring, brass 
becomes a dish, marble can be shaped into a pear, and wood 
into a bow, but the original material remains in each case.° 
So, then, consecration does not annihilate the substances of 
bread and wine, nor does it bring into existence, by a process 
of creation (generatio), the body and blood of Christ.6 The 
body of Christ can be no longer clothed with matter or flesh, 
since ‘ Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more’ and 
‘now know we Christ no more after the flesh.’7 God does 
not create Christ’s flesh from bread by a miracle, as Lanfranc 
alleged; such a view brings God into contempt, for it implies 
that Christ’s body can be wounded again, when the sacrament 
is eaten.) The body of Christ has been in existence for a 
thousand years, it cannot therefore come into existence at con- 
secration.?, Berengar does not speak of a body present in the 
Eucharist, but of the heavenly Word operating in the bread 
and wine.’° The change in the elements is not a simple 
conversion (conversio) of one substance into another,! but a 
hallowing of the bread and wine so that they may possess the 
potency and effectiveness of the body and blood. They are 
no longer merely the elements which nature formed, but are 
also that which blessing has effected. Their conversion is

contends that even Lanfranc, who attempted to define the 
mode of the conversion, did not make his meaning clear.* 

The process of consecration, in which the divine Word is 
the effective principle,? operates in a mystical way.2 The 
faithful feed on the body of Christ and drink His blood through 
a mystery,* a mystery which was destroyed by Lanfranc’s 
theory when he alleged that the body of Christ is actually 
broken by the hands of the priest.5 The mysteries supply us 
with the effect of salvation, and the pledge of salvation we 
receive through the office of the priest.° Thus the sacramental 
theory of Berengar—his conception of the process of conse- 
cration—embodies the mystic symbolism of Alexandria and 
other Greek centres, but, unlike the Greeks, he distinguishes 
between the symbol and that which it symbolises. 

In contrast with realist ideas, it will be noted that his 
chief contribution to the history of the controversy was the 
emphasis which he laid upon the survival of the substance 
of bread and wine after consecration. This obvious fact of 
experience was indicated by Ratramn, but the extravagant 
language of contemporary metabolism made it necessary for 
Berengar constantly to draw attention to it. But he did not 
remain content with a mere memorialist interpretation. 
Through the mystery of consecration a change takes place in 
the effectiveness of the elements, and through this operation 
they become a sacrament, the pledge of salvation and the 
medium of spiritual life. The consecrated or sacramental 
bread and wine have a religious value. The ‘thing of the 
sacrament,’ its spiritual reality, is the body of Christ which is 
in heaven, and does not leave it until the end of the age. The 
body of Christ is thus the ideal archetype of the consecrated 
elements, which may be called ‘ body and blood,’ but only in 
a figurative, tropical, or symbolical sense. ‘The consecrated 
elements symbolise a spiritual body which really exists, 
and so far as it is represented to us in the sacrament it is 
made available to us for spiritual purposes. It is, however,

Berengar’s system does not involve a theory of Transub- 
stantiation, only a conversion of value or efficacy. The 
conversion of a sinner does not involve the destruction of his 
mortal life.6 If Peter Gerald becomes a bishop, after conse- 
cration he is different in character, not in substance.’ As 
Cyprian said, a young man who has been enticed away from 
virtue by a woman, but who repents and leaves her, can say 
‘You are the same, but I am now different.’® ‘There is no 
equation between a conversion of substance and a change of 
substance. The consecrated bread and wine and the glorified 
body of Christ are in different categories. There can be no 
displacement of the substance of the one without displacing 
its accidents. The metabolism by which food is changed into 
human flesh and blood cannot be applied to the sacrament. 
For the rest, he leaves the relationship between the consecrated 
elements and the heavenly body of Christ wrapped in mystery. 
He makes no attempt to solve the problem by postulating 
a eucharistic body of Christ distinct from a heavenly body.

Luther rejected the theory of Berengar and maintained 
that he was rightly condemned by Pope Nicholas II. Certainly 
Berengar’s doctrine is not the Lutheran theory of Consub- 
stantiation.» The substance of the body of Christ is not 
present with the substance of bread and wine in the Eucharist. 
If there were a consubstantial sacramental union, the process 
would involve a thousand thousand bodies of Christ on the 
altar every day, a result which Berengar denies. He nowhere 
states that there are two substances in the Eucharist, and it was 
an impossible conclusion to his thesis. The sacrament con- 
sists of one substance only—that of bread and wine. His 
interpretation of the Augustinian ‘thing of the sacrament ’ 
does not set up a concomitance, but a mystical archetypal 
entity which the sacrament makes available. In Berengar’s 
system the Platonism of John the Scot was again active. ‘The 
believer effects a contact with the ‘sacrament’ or objective

holding that Christ’s body was in heaven and could not

Berengar claims that his teaching has the support of 
Augustine, Ambrose, Hilary, and Gregory the Great.1 He 
also refers to Jerome * and Cyprian,® Leo the Great,* Faustus 
of Riez,° and Fulbert.6 ‘This appeal to tradition, which 
supplements the authority of Scripture, is made within defined 
limits. A text is not to be taken in isolation. What is obscure 
is to be interpreted by a comparison with other passages.’ 
Ambrose and Augustine are the writers chiefly quoted by him, 
and most of his quotations are taken from Ambrose,® who 
supplied the chief armoury for the weapons of his antagonists. 
He admits that he does not always quote Ambrose verbatim, 
but contends that the doctrine of a change of essence does not 
appear in the teaching of that writer, yet he was only able to 
arrive at this conclusion by a partial use of his own principle 
of interpretation. He selects Ambrosian statements which are 
relevant to his own theory, and disregards the rest. Ambrose 
teaches that the effect of the words of institution in consecra- 
tion is to supply the elements with a new significance, without 
causing their material existence to cease.® If Ambrose alleges 1°

Moreover, Berengar was able to strengthen his appeal to 
Ambrose by quoting the Ambrosian De Sacramentis, which

to be what they were,* but he has said that they are ‘as’ 
(qualia) they were.® If the elements become body and blood, 
then the offering of bread and wine by Melchizedek to 
Abraham could not have taken place, for Melchizedek did 
not offer flesh and blood, which did not yet exist.®

which is broken’ (hoc . . . fractum), show that the Lord 
offered bread to the disciples, and He spoke of bread which 
was ‘ broken for many,’ not of a body which ‘ was offered for 
many.’ So also, when the Word of Christ approaches that 
which before (antequam) was bread, so that it becomes body, 
the writer does not mean that bread has ceased to be, for the 
Word supplements and does not destroy the bread. The use

The strength of the grip maintained by tradition upon the 
medieval mind is further illustrated by Berengar’s contention 
that there was no conflict of ideas between the teaching of 
Ambrose and that of Augustine.’ Criticism was in its early 
stages. It was exercising its weapons in assault. It had not 
yet perceived that in dialectics a consistent victory includes 
a process of surrender, and that, when an appeal is made to 
authority or tradition, neither side can claim the undivided 
allegiance of the alliance. Berengar was attempting to devour

According to Augustine, although the bread and wine ‘ by a 
certain consecration become mystical for us,’? and to the eye 
of faith are now the body and blood of the Lord, yet the 
elements of bread and wine remain.? The realists maintained 
that Augustine supported their view, yet in his Sermo ad 
neophytos he made it clear that the substances of bread and 
wine are not wanting, and they are called bread and wine by 
a literal, not by a figurative description. What is seen on the 
altar is bread and wine—bread made from many grains, and 
wine from many berries,> as also Cyprian originally taught.® 
They have the similitude of the things of which they are 
sacraments.’ Augustine distinguishes between two things in 
the Eucharist—that which is seen, and that which is grasped 
by the mind (intelligitur). That which is seen has material 
form (speciem habet corporalem), that which is apprehended 
by the mind has spiritual fruit (fructum habet spiritualem). 
The sacrament is veritable and temporal.® Sanctification is a 
process related to the thing itself, not merely to its qualities.? 
Even if Augustine allows that the bread and wine by a mystical 
consecration become body and blood, it cannot be concluded 
from his teaching that he obliterates their substance, so that 
the sacrament became, as Lanfranc maintained, merely a 
symbol of the bread and wine.!° Whenthe Lord commended 
His body and blood to the disciples, He did not mean that the 
elements of the bread and wine were annihilated. One can 
neither commend nor consecrate what does not survive.1?

which possesses the authority of the prophets and apostles, 
of the Lord of the prophets and apostles, and of the great 
Fathers of the Western Church. He has made out his claim. 
The realists of the pre-scholastic era had used the sources of 
authority to support a philosophic theory of the sacramental 
change, which in turn was an attempt to substantiate the 
crude realism of the Mass-cultus. Philosophy in their hands 
became a mere handmaid to ceremonial. So the teaching of 
Berengar took the form of a protest, and issued in a demand 
for eucharistic reform. It constituted a call to return to 
Augustine, whose teaching, as Luther proved, was the point 
at which the medieval church had departed from the true line 
of advance. Back to Augustine, and to a spiritual interpre- 
tation of Scripture—that was Berengar’s note, and even the 
realists never again attempted to define the Eucharist in the 
terms of the formula of Humbert.? Although Berengar failed 
to check the formulation of the dogma of Transubstantiation, 
his protest bore fruit in the form of a more restrained 
terminology, and a sounder philosophic grasp in the leading 
writers of later times.

CHAPTER XVII 
ANTI-DIALECTIC CONSERVATIVES 


In the second half of the eleventh century eucharistic doctrine 
was interpreted by three modes of inquiry. Berengar headed 
the dialectic dynamic symbolists and gave scientific expression 
to the tradition of John the Scot and Ratramn. The method 
also claimed an unrestricted use of dialectics for the explana- 
tion and vindication of the ancient western Fathers. Lanfranc 
and Guitmund, the dialectical realists, developed the tradition 
of Paschasius Radbert, and while condemning the free dia- 
lectical method of Berengar, none the less conducted their 
inquiry along dialectical lines within clearly defined limits. 
To this they were pledged by the aims and conditions of the 
Benedictine educational revival. Logic was in use in famous 
monastic schools like Bec, as well as in cathedral centres like 
Tours, and one of the objects of the educational revival was to 
break away from the mere study of grammar and patristic 
texts, and to train the intellect for a philosophical defence 
_of the traditional faith. The process issued in the work of 
Anselm of Canterbury and the scholastics of the twelfth century. 
But whereas Berengar boldly advanced the conclusions to 
which dialectical investigation inevitably led, the school of 
Lanfranc and Guitmund did not go beyond the reconstruction 
of the old system of eucharistic doctrine, and were content to 
limit the use of dialectics to those occasions when it appeared 
to support the traditional statement. Whenever it appeared 
to demand a restatement they adopted an anti-dialectical 
attitude. 

Another coterie of conservative writers, the anti-dialectical 
realists, which included early critics of Berengar, like Ascelin 
and Adelmann, adopted an attitude similar to that of the 


332 BERENGAR 


Eusebian Conservatives in the Arian controversy.! They did 
not follow in the steps of the great leaders of orthodox thought. 
They would have no assistance whatever from dialectics. 
They represented the tone of the older monastic schools. 
Yet, while they refused to make use of the watchwords of 
‘ Athanasius,’ they did not condemn ‘ Arius.’ No attack upon 
Berengar appears in their writings, save in the letter of 
Wolfelm, and reports about Peter Damiani indicate that they 
possessed some sympathy with his ideals. 

The cause of this phenomenon lies away back in the 
conditions of the Carolingian interpretation of eucharistic 
doctrine. We have seen that two strains of interpretation were 
in vogue in that era. In the schools the Augustinian tradition 
was strongly upheld, but behind the sacramentaries and the 
Mass-cultus the realism of Ambrose was in operation. The 
doctrine of Radbert constituted an attempt at once to develop 
and to purify the Ambrosian tradition from its grosser 
manifestations, yet these aims did not check the revival of 
Augustinianism in the teaching of Ratramn, inspired by the 
Neo-Platonism of John the Scot. The controversy of the 
ninth century left the question unsettled. Contemporaries of 
Paschasius and Ratramn were content to adopt elements from 
the teaching of both writers. This was indeed no more than 
a continuance of the method of pre-Carolingian theology, and 
it was the method adopted by the anti-dialectic writers of 
Berengar’s time. If they supported the Ambrosian realism of 
Lanfranc and Guitmund, Berengar was so faithful an adherent 
of Augustine, that, with one exception, they avoided direct 
attack upon him; and if they rejected the use of dialectics, 
which the protagonists on both sides of the controversy 
adopted, they confined their disapproval to a refusal to 
sanction the introduction of dialectics into the curriculum of the 
schools, without expressly attacking those who made use of it. 

No better representative of the conservative anti-dia- 
lecticians can be found than Peter Damiani. Damiani was a 
critic not only of the educational methods of the day,? but of

the worldly ambitions of the great bishops. Thus the profes- 
sional efficiency of Lanfranc as well as his educational policy 
was likely to rouse the antipathy of Damiani. Damiani’s mys- 
tical temperament was unable to appreciate the determined 
methods of the ecclesiastics of Lanfranc’s circle, who realised 
that the reform of clerical life and learning could only be 
secured by a strong and efficient episcopate. Damiani centred 
all his hopes on the reform of the Papacy. Thus there are 
antecedent grounds for the vindication of the report that 
Damiani favoured Berengar against Lanfranc,” and the blame- 
less and self-effacing public life of Berengar, especially his 
devotion to the ideals of hermit-life, were bound to win 
sympathy from Damiani, who spent much of his time in 
advocating the eremitical life,? although without weakening 
in his support of the current policy for the reform of cenobitic 
tie: 

Both strands of Carolingian eucharistic teaching are 
represented in Damiani’s writings, although he lays greater 
stress upon Ambrosian realism.* The eucharistic body is the 
true body of the Lord,°® in contrast with the symbol (umbra) 
of the Old Testament shew-bread. ‘The Eucharist is a 
“mystery of terror,’ from the Lord’s body flames beat on the 
breast of the officiant.6 The mouth of the receiver is red with 
the body of the Lord.’ If necessary the Lord’s body can 
become visible through the aid of a miracle ; and to convince 
a doubting priest, actual flesh can appear in his hands, so that 
his fingers become red with the blood.’ If poured from a 
schools, but Damiani’s efforts were confined to the attempt to remedy 
the illiteracy of the clergy. He criticised their inability to read and write.

The sacramental process consists of a change of the bread 
and wine into the sacrament of the body and blood.? But his 
only explanation of the change is an appeal to miracles. For 
ordinary occasions the actual body and blood remain invisible 
beneath the species of bread and wine.® 

This is the popular eucharistic terminology of Carolingian 
times, reinforced by the mystic realism of Damiani’s tempera- 
ment and assisted by the vivid phraseology of the popular 
preacher, a feature reminiscent of Chrysostom’s teaching. 
It illustrates the extent to which the earlier teaching was 
prevalent in the eleventh century. Its significance is not to 
be overestimated when dogmatic intention is under considera- 
tion. It is relieved by another aspect of Damiani’s teaching. 
The body of the Lord, the sacrificial gift, which is dedicated 
on the altar through the office of the priest, receives the power 
of the Spirit, and thereby gives life and sanctifies. This 
vivifying virtue in the elements can only be received from the 
Holy Spirit, who actually fills them with His grace. If the — 
Holy Spirit is not there, the element is not the body of the 
Lord, but simply bread.6 Yet this doctrine of an infusion of 
spiritual grace, which makes the elements dynamically effective 
in an Augustinian sense, is not correlated by Damiani with his 
conception of the real presence of the body of Christ. Like 
the writers of the previous generation, he did not think out 
his statements to a conclusion. 

In a letter addressed by Wolfelm of Brauweiler to Megin- 
hard, Abbot of Gladbach,’ the writer attacks a statement 
which he attributes to Berengar, that as the resurrection body 
of Christ could not pass through closed doors, it could not be 
actually present in the Eucharist. Wolfelm appeals to the 
Gospel of S. John for proof that after the Resurrection Jesus 
appeared to His disciples after passing through closed doors.® 
The words of institution, uttered by Him who created all

things by a mere verbal command, prove the actuality of the 
body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist, although they still 
remain mysteries.!_ God’s word cannot remain without effect, 
especially as God the Creator and God the Redeemer are the 
same. That which the Redeemer wills must be fulfilled as 
inevitably as that which the Creator orders.2 To the authority 
of the Old and New Testaments Berengar attempts to add 
a third, when he says that if a mouse eats a piece of the conse- 
crated element, Christ does not remain in it. This is the sort 
of folly which Horace rebuked when he said ‘ The mountain 
travailed and brought forth a mouse.’ We thought Berengar 
was placed above the mountains, and would produce some- 
thing great, but all he can do is to bring forth a trifling thing 
of this kind. If the body of Christ, although eaten by the 
elect, returns to heaven and is not impaired in its entirety, 
how much less will it be impaired if reprobate men and even 
a mouse consume the elements, even as the sun, which sends 
its rays into the noisome places of this world, withdraws 
them again to itself without pollution. S. Andrew, according 
to the Church of Achaia, taught that although the flesh and 
blood of the Lamb were sacrificed and consumed, yet the Lamb 
remained whole and alive. But Wolfelm ends by conceding 
Berengar’s point by maintaining that there is a difference 
between worthy and unworthy reception. Christ remains in 
the former casein the recipient, but not in the latter.® Wolfelm 
emphasises the necessity of perceiving with the eye of the 
mind, and complains that Berengar made use of the eye of 
the body only. Wolfelm does not discuss the character of the 
sacramental presence. Chronologically he belonged to the 
anti-dialectic writers of the second half of the century, yet his 
inquiry does not advance beyond that of similar writers in the 
period which closed with Durand of Troarn, but the question 
of the relation of the eucharistic content to unworthy recipients, 
and of cases where an accident caused its consumption by 
animals, was much discussed in later stages of the controversy.’ 

The challenge of Wolfelm was taken up by Manegold 
of Lautenbach, who directed a treatise against the Abbot of

5 Ibid. 4144, c. 8 [bid. 41 3b. ’ Cf. Geiselmann, p. 404. 


336 BERENGAR 


Brauweiler. The body of the Lord was immortal and in- 
destructible before the Resurrection, and by virtue of divine 
power it was this body which He gave to His disciples. This 
He did lest the believers should think that the grace imparted 
to them was due to His bodily withdrawal into heaven. Just 
as His physical condition was no hindrance to the reception 
by the disciples of His immortal and indestructible body, so 
now His withdrawal to heaven is no hindrance to the reception 
of the body received from the Virgin.! 

The process of the sacrament is the work of the invisible 
priest. As in Baptism the minister is only the external 
instrument, while One is standing in the midst whom the 
believer sees but whom the unbeliever does not recognise, 
who really performs the act of Baptism and causes the effect 
of salvation, so while in the Eucharist the priest utters the 
life-giving and sanctifying words, yet the invisible Priest 
changes and sanctifies the elements,? so that the worshipper 
receives, as Ambrose taught, not what nature forms, but what 
blessing consecrates. 

But the chief object of Manegold’s short treatise was the 
confutation of the Berengarian doctrine, although he does not 
nominally attack its author. We are refreshed at the Lord’s 
Table not by the symbolical but by the actual body of the 
Lord.? The use of the phrase ‘ Lord’s Table ’ appears to have 
been inspired by Berengarian terminology. Even though it is 
a table and not an altar, Manegold argues that the body— 
the food—is none the less real. The remains of the anti- 
dialectic writers+ show how few standpoints of defence 
against Berengar’s criticism they possessed without recourse 
to Berengar’s own weapons. Without the aid of dialectics, 
the metabolic realism would soon have come to the end of 
its resources. 

The Augustinian tradition comes to the surface again in

who died at Fulda about 1070.1 Otloh declined the aid of 


dialectical reasoning,? but made a curious use of dialectical 
terms in an attempt to arrive at the mystical sense lying behind 
ordinary language.? Disregarding the conclusions of formal 
logic, he presents his own definition of substance and accidence. 
Objects which come within human experience consist of 
elements (elementa) and things (res). The elements consist 
of everything which, as corporal substance, mankind uses.® 
A thing does not exist as a special substance, but as the 
accidence of a special substance,® such as day and night, 
number, weariness, medicine, plenty, and scarcity.’ Yet he 
does not appear to have included all that pertains to a ‘ thing ’ 
in its accidentals,8 and he is aware that some thinkers use the 
term ‘substance’ for his interpretation of ‘res.’® In this 
confusion of terms and categories Otloh seems to equate 
elements with matter, and substance with form or special 
existence (aliquid substantia), while his use of accidence is 
confined to certain categories, such as number and size, 
without including form. So he is able to define ‘ things’ of 
this kind as natural mysteries.!° 

Another kind of ‘ things’ consists of the mysteries of the 
divine dispensation, comprising the Incarnation, Passion, and 
Resurrection of the Lord.“ These two definitions of ‘ thing ’ 
Otloh applies to the elucidation of eucharistic teaching, and 
obtains thereby a third kind of ‘things ’"—the elements used 
in consecration, oil, salt, water, baptismal water, and the 
eucharistic elements. Through consecration the nature 
mysteries are brought into relationship with the divine dis- 
pensational mysteries. The eucharistic elements have the

The consecrated elements do not remain solely mystical, for 
they receive from consecration the power of effecting salvation.* 
If they are mystical symbols they produce a dynamic effect 
upon the recipient. ‘The medium which creates this capacity 
in the elements is the appeal to the divine name or the 
repetition of the Lord’s words. As without the appeal to the 
Trinity in Baptism, no new-birth and no forgiveness of sins 
takes place, so without the words of institution there is no 
transfiguration of the bread and wine into the life-giving 
mystery of the Lord’s body and blood.® By this process of the 
sacrament the elements are absorbed into a mystery, the bread 
and wine are transfigured into the life-giving body and blood 
of the Lord.® 

There is a distinction between the Eucharist and other 
mysteries of this kind. The latter are only spiritual so far as 
they are consecrated in a spiritual manner, and are received 
by faith only ; but the Eucharist is a living and life-giving 
mystery.’ ‘The difference between the two is that which exists 
between an actual body and its figure.2 So the Eucharist is a 
singular mystery.? While other mysteries only possess saving- 
grace for those who receive them, the Eucharist is not only a

Apart from the system of Berengar, no stronger testimony 
could be produced to the strength of the Augustinian tradition 
existing in the eleventh century. Berengar’s was not a voice 
crying in the wilderness. It is possible that the four sections 
of Berengarian thought described by Guitmund ® represented 
independent developments of Augustinian doctrine, and, if so, 
there can be no doubt that their activity was quickened by 
Berengar, and the work of Otloh shows that away in Germany 
the old dynamic-symbolism was still vocal. Possibly the 
teaching of Otloh inspired the complaint of Theoduin ® that 
the influence of Berengar was rampant in Germany, and if his 
system also possesses elements of the Ambrosian realism, its 
independence is shown by his attempt to establish an anti- 
dialectical description or definition of substance and accidence. 
If he uses realist expressions such as the contrast between 
body and figure, and if he adopts the Ambrosian term 
‘transfigurare,’ these expressions are not allowed to run into 
contradiction with his own dynamic-symbolism. It was the 
attitude of the old Carolingian Augustinian school, and stands 
in contrast with that of Berengar chiefly in its refusal to 
criticise the positive realism of contemporaries.*

CHAPTER XViIlI 
GUITMUND OF AVERSA 


TOGETHER with Lanfranc, Guitmund of Aversa conducted the 
chief dialectical defence of realist doctrine in the early Middle 
Ages.1 Like Lanfranc, he emphasised faith rather than reason, 
but his strictures against the use of reason are less severe than 
those of his predecessor, and he does not make any specific 
attack on dialectics as a science. He begins his treatise 
De Corporis et Sanguinis Christi Veritate? by noting that all 
sections of Berengarian opinion are agreed that the accidence 
of bread and wine remains after consecration,? and this doc- 
trine he proceeds to demolish. By making this denial, the 
Berengarians leave out of account the will of God, for, accord- 
_ ing to the Psalmist, God can do anything that He wills, and if 
God is almighty He can will a change to take place in natural 
objects. ‘To deny this necessity is to assert that He is not 
almighty, which would mean that He is not truly God. As 
the faithful believe in God, they must accept the statement 
that He can do whatever He wills.* 
Guitmund states the metabolism of realism in clearer terms

than any predecessor had ventured to use. The ‘ essentialiter 
mutari’ of Lanfranc is developed by Guitmund into ‘ sub- 
stantialiter transmutari.’! If all the varied objects of nature 
were developed by God out of nothing, how can the nature of 
bread and wine, which already exists, resist being changed 
(transferatur) by the will of God? Berengar must admit from 
his knowledge of medicine that the bread or wine which we 
daily consume is transformed (transformatur) into the flesh or 
blood of our bodies. Then why cannot God, by the majesty 
of His presence and the power of His word, if He wishes, 
change (transformat) the bread and wine of the Eucharist into 
flesh and blood ? Even Plato said that the nature of things is 
what God wills.” 

The fundamental objection to the doctrine of a change of 
essence lies in the contention that such a transformation does 
not take place in nature, and Guitmund admits that when any 
material thing is changed in substance (substantialiter .. . 
transformatur) into something else, it is transformed into 
something which did not previously exist, as when the rod of 
Moses was changed into a serpent, but the bread is changed 
into the body of Christ which already exists.2 The change 
does not create the body of Christ, and Guitmund finally 
disposed of the Radbertian theory of the new creation of the 
eucharistic body at each celebration.* 

Like Berengar, he appeals to the Ambrosian statement 
“they are what they were and are changed into other,’ but 
whereas Berengar stressed the first part of the passage, 
Guitmund makes use of the second, and twists the statement 
to mean ‘ that they may not be in themselves, but are changed 
into other things.’® Through the change the bread becomes 
the body of Christ. That which does not exist cannot come 
within the category of ‘becoming.’ He draws a contrast 
between phenomenal existence and pure ‘being.’ ‘To 
become ’ belongs to the category of being and refers to what 
already is, so that when it ‘ comes into existence ’ it cannot be 
said ‘ to become’ or to begin to be. An original creation was

antecedent to coming into existence or appearance among 
phenomena. It is not a question between ‘being’ and 
‘not being,’ but between something which already ‘is’ and 
then ‘ becomes’ something else. How does that which was 
first created ‘become’ something? By the word of God. 
That which did not lack a beginning could not become 
anything else save by ‘becoming.’! The Arianism of this 
argumentation, when applied to the body of Christ, entirely 
escaped Guitmund’s notice. 

Scripture mentions four methods by which a man comes 
into existence. Firstly, the case of Adam, who was made from 
the earth; secondly, the normal process of procreation ; 
thirdly, the creation of Eve, a virgin woman from a virgin man ; 
fourthly, the reverse process, a man from a woman, the virgin 
Christ from a virgin. The second and most usual of these 
processes, at which no one marvels, is none the less wonderful.” 
But the most wonderful of all, the Virgin-birth, people 
attempt to contradict and refuse ;? although it is really less 
singular than the second and third processes, and is similar 
to the first.4 

So also sacred writings mention four kinds of substantive 
change or effectiveness :®° one by which all things are created 
from nothing ; another by which all things return to nothing— 
although we have no experience of it;® a third in which 
substances change, by nature or miracle, into other substances, 
as the nut into the tree, a seed into a herb, food and drink into 
flesh and blood, or a serpent into a rod ;’ a fourth by which 
that which ‘is’ changes into that which no less is, as when 
the bread and wine are changed into the body and blood of 
Christ,® a process which most resembles the first and is more 
credible than the second or third,® and is analogous to the 
Incarnation.t° ‘The bread and wine of the altar of the Lord 
are substantially changed into the body and blood of Christ."

The body and blood are not bread and wine.!' The whole of

into body or blood, while part remains bread or wine, with the 
object of protecting the body and blood against unworthy 
recipients.” The agent of the change is the word of Christ 
pronounced in the blessing of the priest.’ 

If Lanfranc had established the theory of Transubstantia- 
tion by his doctrine of a change of essence, Guitmund reinforces 
the doctrine with the terminology of Transubstantiation, 
although the actual word was probably not yet coined.‘ It is 
significant that his term ‘substantialiter’ appeared in the 
formula offered to Berengar in 1079. Henceforth the 
description of the change as taking place ‘ essentialiter ’ was 
abandoned by most orthodox writers, probably on account of 
its physical associations. ‘The theory of a ‘ substantial ’ change 
raised the doctrine to a more philosophical plane, but the 
idea was the same. A substantial change is a real change, 
obliterating the substances of bread and wine, transferring 
them into the substances of body and blood. 

Yet Guitmund, like Lanfranc, could not escape the funda- 
mental contradiction involved in the theory of 'Transubstantia- 
tion. Ifa thing is changed in substance it ceases to be what 
it was. If it has not ceased to be what it was, it is not changed. 
In discussing the third mode of substantive change,° he says 
that although this kind of change does not come within our 
experience, it is conceivable to reason, for when specific 
accidents are displaced by others, the only thing that can be 
said is that they cease to be. A thing so far as it exists, exists 
in substance. But when the contrary (accidents ?) supervene, 
it cannot exist in its substance, nor pass over into another 
substance. So it altogether ceases to be, unless one describes 
the process of displacement as a transformation. ‘There are 
indeed numerous examples of things which are essentially 
changed into other things which exist in a similar condition, 
for example, when a white parchment is covered with black ink. 
Thus we can speak of a withdrawal of the accidence, so that 
a thing becomes nothing; or of a change into the approaching

This statement admits Berengar’s contention that accidence 
and substance are inseparable, especially as Guitmund allows 
that flavour and colour and other accidents remain when the 
substances are changed.2 Although asserting that a thing 
exists by virtue of its substance, he grants that if its accidents 
are displaced it either ceases to exist or becomes something 
else. Conversely, if the accidents remain, the substance 
remains, so that Berengar’s argument, that because of the 
existence of the accidents of bread and wine in the Eucharist 
the substance of the same must also be there, remains valid. 
Guitmund tries to overcome the difficulty by postulating a 
fourth kind of change, in addition to that put forward in the 
passage from the pseudo-Augustinian work on the unity of the 
Trinity against Felicianus, on which he is commenting—namely, 
a change from one thing into another which already exists, as 
of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ. 
This is a process which the Lord reserves for Himself, and it 
stands in the same category with the Incarnation.? But, we 
may ask, what then becomes of the accidence of bread and wine 
which falls within Guitmund’s third category? He merges 
his proof in its objective. He uses the object as an illustration 
of itself, and shirking the difficulty lying in his third example, 
from which alone an illustration for his case would have been 
valid, he ends by arguing in a circle in his fourth example,

On the other hand, Guitmund’s theory of the sacramental 
content is a definition of realism in the clearest terms. In 
Book III he presents his own positive statement of the 
doctrine of the real presence. He begins with a proof of the 
proposition that we eat the true body of Christ in its substance, 
not in the Berengarian symbol.? At the words of institution 
Christ bore Himself in His own hands, and, as Augustine 
pointed out, this is the explanation of the saying that David 
was borne in his hands before Abimelech, a passage which 
cannot be taken literally, but which refers to Christ. Yet the 
words ‘ This is my body’ are to be taken literally and not 
figuratively, meaning that Christ bore the substance of His 
body.® Guitmund reverses Berengar’s interpretation of ‘ This,’ 
as referring to the substance of bread. Grammarians and 
dialecticians show that pronouns need not always refer to 
substance. So when Christ said ‘ This,’ He did not mean the 
substance of bread, but the qualities ® of the eucharistic sub- 
stance which appear in the form of bread. ‘This’ has a 
demonstrative, not a relative significance in the passage.’ 
Several other examples are given by Augustine which prove 
that the true body is present. The Ambrosian De 
Sacramentis also teaches that it is the true flesh and blood 
which we receive,°® and this teaching is supported by Leo the 
Great, Cyril of Alexandria,#° Gregory the Great, Jerome,

A similar contradiction arises in his discussion of the 
statement that the body of Christ can be broken into parts 
and ground with the teeth. The body which could be touched

the same time, yet it remains in heaven, just as the thought of

criticism that the realist theory broke up the body of Christ 
into parts and necessitated its presence in many places at once. 
He unfolds the idea that the body of Christ is not only present 
as a whole in each several particle of the host, but that it is 
everywhere present at once. The latter problem had been 
noticed by Radbert and was described by Lanfranc as an 
incomprehensible mystery.®

does not abhor being consumed by an animal. A certain 
decree sanctions the burning of the host on certain occasions 
in order to preserve it from misuse,® but only the accidents

Guitmund’s theory of the sacrament is an attempt to 
combine his own conception of realism with the Augustinian 
sacramental idea. The body of Christ is substantially present 
in the Eucharist, which is not a mere sign or figure.4 The 
symbol, he says, in the Augustinian sense is the consecrated 
element, and in all ecclesiastical authorities, and in the missal, 
‘the bread of the altar is called a sacrament, that is a sacred 
sign,’ ° but it is not a sign of the body, but a sign of the 
Passion of Christ. We do not kill Christ again in the celebra- 
tion of the Lord’s body and blood, but we commemorate His 
death and so signify the Passion, and when Christ is said to 
be sacrificed, no carnal interpretation is to be put upon the 
statement. ‘This misconception caused some to desert Jesus 
when He spoke to them of eating His flesh.’ Augustine says 
that Christ used these words figuratively, but Augustine’s 
meaning is difficult to grasp. In any case it cannot refer to 
the body of the Lord, but to His Passion, so that we may 
imitate Christ and communicate with Him by sharing in 
His Passion. By ‘figure’ Augustine means not sacramental 
presence, but the sacramental act, the celebration of the body 
and blood of Christ. So Berengar’s appeal to Augustine’s 
work, On Christian Doctrine, fails, because Augustine never 
uses the terms ‘sign ’ and ‘ figure ’ of the real content of the 
sacrament. Symbolism is concerned not with the Eucharist, 
but with soteriology, and in this sense the language of the

Himself? He is the sign of our redemption. In a com- 
mercial transaction every price is a sign of that which is 
paid. So Christ is both the price paid for us and the sign 
of our redemption, and as the food of the altar is effective 
for our salvation, we believe it to be significative of our 
salvation.? 

Commenting on Eph. i. 22, he developed another aspect 
of sacramental symbolism. Christ’s own body, which is the 
Church, is the sign, figure, or sacrament of the body which He 
received from the Virgin. The body of the Church, in the 
likeness of its Head,is born in the heart by the operation of the

races.2 In Guitmund’s language the Church is thus born of

distinguishes between a proper (proprium) body of Christ, 
which is the Church, and true (verum) body of Christ, but the 
Eucharist, he says, is seldom or never called openly a sign of 
the latter.®

CHAPTER XIX 
BERENGAR AND THE FORMULA OF 1079 


THE terminology of the formula of belief submitted to Berengar 
at the Roman Council of 1079 reveals the influence of the 
phraseology of Lanfranc and Guitmund. Lanfranc’s treatise 
had been sent to Rome at the request of Alexander II.} 
Guitmund went to Rome in the time of Gregory VII, and was 
made Archbishop of Aversa by that pontiff, and as his book 
was written for general instruction,” it was doubtless well 
known at the Curia. The formula of 1059 had made no 
reference to the Radbertian doctrine of the identity of the 
eucharistic body with the historical body received from the 
Virgin. In the formula of 1079 this was clearly expressed. 
After consecration the eucharistic body is the true body of 
Christ which was born of the Virgin and was offered for our 
salvation and hung upon the Cross.? Yet the body of Christ 
sits at the right hand of the Father. In the formula of 1059 
the sacramental body was defined by the terms ‘ verum ’ and 
‘in veritate.’* In 1079 it was described as being the ‘ proper 
nature ’ and ‘true substance’ of that body.® In the earlier 
formula Humbert defined the change with the simple state- 
ment that after consecration the bread and wine become the 
true body and blood of Christ. In 1079 Guitmund’s 
terminology was definitely adopted, the bread and wine are 
substantially changed into the true and proper and life-giving

really exist, and are not mediated merely in the sign and virtue

which described the body of Christ as being materially 
(sensualiter) present and not only sacramentally *—truly broken 
by the hands of the priest and ground by the teeth of the 
faithful—was avoided in 1079, yet the phraseology * as well as

usage of the Church. It only remained to embody it in the

mystical statements of Damiani’s genuine writings makes the 
same authorship impossible. 

Berengar did not leave the formula submitted to him at 
Rome in 1079 unchallenged. His last recorded work is an 
account of the proceedings of the Council, and contains an 
apologia for his action on that occasion, and a criticism of the 
formula submitted to him. He begins with a characteristic 
quotation from Augustine : ‘'That which you see on the altar 
is bread and wine, as your eyes tell you, but faith demands 
that the bread is the body of Christ, and the wine is His 
blood.’ ® This, however, does not involve a substantial 
presence of Christ. The word ‘ substantialiter ’ was inserted 
in the formula at the spring Council of 1079, contrary to the 
understanding which Berengar had secured with the Pope in the 
previous autumn.’ He accepted it with a mental reservation, 
believing that he could ultimately turn it against his enemies.®

The sacrament does not lose, through a corruption of substance,

first begin to be by the generation of the substance which it 
already possesses.? 

The argument of his adversaries is really a negation of 
their theory. The formula of 1079 used the words ‘ through 
the mystery of prayer.’ But a mystery necessitates two things, 
that which is exposed and that which is hidden. That which 
is exposed in the Eucharist is the sacrament; that which is 
concealed is the thing of the sacrament.2, His meaning is that 
if the eucharistic content is substantially present, the mystery 
is destroyed, and he nowhere says that ‘the thing of the 
sacrament’ is hidden im the sacrament. He admits that a 
conversion of the bread and wine into the body and blood is 
according to Scripture,? but only in the sense that he has 
already explained,* and we have seen that in the De Sacra 
Cena he uses the term ‘conversio’ in the sense of a new 
orientation supplied to the bread and wine, and. not with any 
metabolic significance. Whatever is consecrated does not lose 
what it was, but is carried over into something better than it 
was. Both terms of the proposition are to be preserved—the 
subjective term ‘ bread and wine,’ and the predicative term 
‘body and blood.’® He contended that the caution inserted in 
the formula ‘ not only through the sign and virtue of the sacra- 
ment ’ was wholly unnecessary, because no one could postulate 
the sacrament of the altar without the corresponding ‘ thing 
of the sacrament.’® Even in allegorical language there 
must be an existing equivalent of the illustration used. 
The use of a term like ‘Scundapsus’? is admitted to be 
meaningless.8 

But the existence of the ‘ thing of the sacrament ’ does not 
necessitate its actual presence in the sacrament. When our 
Lord blessed the bread and wine He raised them in dignity, 
so that beyond the natural substance which they bring to the 
body they may be efficacious for the help of the soul, thus

setting them up as a sacrament of His body and _ blood. 
Consequently, in the Berengarian system a real presence is not 
required because all that is of religious value is present in the 
consecrated elements in the sacrament, in contrast with the 
body of Christ in heaven. The virtue of the sign indeed lies 
in the thing signified,” the body of Christ in heaven, but, as 
he shows in this passage, the sign, or consecrated elements, 
only possess an acquired ‘ dignity,’ following upon consecra- 
tion, which gives to the bread and wine the efficacy or value 
of the body and blood for the fulfilment of the redemptive 
purpose. This is not a theory of the real presence. 

In the light of this explanation is to be read his comment 
on the statement of the formula concerning the true nature 
and substance of the body of Christ. He denies that these 
words had any justifiable reference to his own views, because 
he had maintained that the bread and wine of the altar were 
not ‘ just anything,’? but the proper body of Christ, not 
phantasmal as the Manichees say, but true and human. 
Probably Berengar is rebutting a charge of Docetism with 
reference to the Person of Christ, and his mind had, for the 
time being, directed its attention from the eucharistic question. 
Yet this passage has given rise to the contention that he held 
the doctrine of the real presence. But when the apologia is 
read as a whole it is clear that his convictions were the same 
as when he wrote the De Sacra Cena, and as the Acta 
Concilu Romani was written as a recantation of his oath at 
Rome in 1079, this single passage cannot be produced as a final 
contradiction of all the rest of his recantation. 

His apologia closes with an appeal for divine mercy for his 
weakness in aliowing the term ‘ substantialiter’’ to be added 
to the definition which he had agreed to on All Saints’ Day, 
1078, and he commends the apologia to his readers as a con- 
fession made with tears, and asks for their prayers to propitiate 
the divine mercy on his behalf. This strong emotion is 
inexplicable if any of his statements in the Acta are to be

interpreted as an admission of the doctrine of the real presence. 
Berengar was too acute a thinker to fail to perceive that if the 
only point at issue between himself and the authorities of the 
Church was his contention that the substance of the bread and 
wine remained, an effective compromise was possible at that 
date, when the doctrine of Transubstantiation was not so 
unreservedly demanded by the Church as at a later era. The 
criticism of Lanfranc and Guitmund pivoted on the other 
point raised by the controversy—his denial of the real presence ; 
and it was so far as he realised that the addition of the word 
“ substantialiter > in 1079 constituted something more than a 
mere denial of the presence of the bread.and wine after conse- 
cration, and introduced the presence of the body of Christ in 
the substantial sense defined by the realist thinkers, that his 
final statement betrays so strong a sentiment of regret. 

The question of the real presence had been prominent 
from the beginning of the controversy. During the early 
period, which closed with the appearance of Durand’s De 
Corpore et Sanguine Domini, the orthodox defence was 
almost entirely preoccupied with asserting’ and proving the 
reality of the sacramental content, though no doubt Berengar’s 
consistent refusal to admit the disappearance of the bread and 
wine drew Lanfranc’s attention to the sacramental process. 
In the second part of the dispute the battle was carried over 
to Berengar’s field, and the theory of the change, first expressed 
in terms of essence (Lanfranc) and then in terms of substance 
(Guitmund), was developed. ‘The question of Transubstantia- 
tion was the chief preoccupation of the orthodox writers 
during this period. The Berengarian objection that the 
elements of bread and wine were sensually perceptible was 
met by the theory that only the accidence remained after 
Transubstantiation had taken place. Moreover, the theory of 
Transubstantiation affected the conception of the real presence. 
To Durand the presence remained a mystery, hidden in the 
sacrament. ‘The new theory of a substantial change enabled 
the later metabolists to define the presence as the eucharistic 
substance, hidden from sight, but clearly perceptible to the 
intellect, and really existing.’ So late as the time of Theofrid,

Abbot of Echternach, 1081-1110, the denial of the real presence

Paderborn, have readjusted the balance of Catholic criticism, 
and estimate, like the writers of the eleventh and twelfth 
centuries, the teaching of Berengar as a denial of the doctrine 
of the real presence, as well as that of 'Transubstantiation.

CHAPTER XX 
REALISM IN THE TWELFTH CENTURY 


THE idea of ‘ the thing of the sacrament’ as a real presence, 
and the doctrine of Transubstantiation as the mode of the 
sacramental change, were admitted to be the orthodox interpre- 
tation of the Eucharist before the end of the eleventh century. 
During the next century attempts were made to relate the new 
definitions with the rest of Catholic theology, and especially 
to connect it with the doctrine of the Incarnation.1 The 
eleventh century was occupied with the philosophic or scientific 
definition and interpretation of the doctrine. The twelfth 
century conducted its theological grounding or foundation.? 

This theological tendency is well emphasised in the 
Exposition on the Canon of the Mass, written by Odo, 
Bishop of Cambrai (d. 1113). Odo identifies the eucharistic 
body with the Logos, and with the reasonable soul and human 
flesh which the Logos united with itself at the Incarnation.* 
So he defines the host as God.4 This represents a marked 
advance upon the teaching of Hugh of Langres and Durand, 
who somewhat vaguely spoke of the sacramental reality as 
identified with the divine-human personality of Christ. 

Odo attempts to overcome the antinomy between the 
location of the risen body of Christ in heaven and the 
eucharistic presence on many altars—an antinomy which 
Berengar had indicated—by describing the Resurrection-body 
as being manifest and open, while the sacramental body on 
earth is covered and hidden from the senses. Yet both are

The founder of the Carthusian Order, Bruno of K6ln 
(d. 1101), was a former pupil of Berengar, but his eucharistic 
teaching, which appears in two of his writings, was influenced 
by that of Anselm of Canterbury. The sacramental body and 
blood signify the salvation of body and soul. The blood being 
the centre of the soul quite properly signified the soul,? 
although Christ is not divided by the two substances, for the

Unlike Odo of Cambrai, Bruno relates his theory of the sacra-

Anglican sacramental theory. Spiritual grace can only be 
mediated through a material channel, and he makes use of an 
Augustinian concept ? when he says that a purely spiritual 
form can only be received by angels, not by men.* 

The body of Christ is present in the sacrament in an

Although the systematisation of theology did not take place 
until the second half of the twelfth century, indications of a 
desire to embrace the whole theological field in one sweeping 
glance are not wanting in the first half of that era, and we 
have seen that even earlier the tendency appeared. It was 
deflected for a time by the eucharistic controversy, which 
concentrated upon one point of reference. But Hugh of 
Langres and Durand, by fixing the effecting principle of the 
Eucharist in the divine Word, showed the way towards the 
comprehension of sacramental doctrine within the doctrinal 
system of the Incarnation. This was indeed a revival of the 
ancient method of Irenzeus, although no trace of the influence 
of Irenzeus upon metabolic eucharistic teaching of the eleventh 
and twelfth centuries is to be found. A definite stage in this 
development was marked when Anselm of Canterbury (d. 1109) 
embodied the doctrine of the Eucharist within his theology of 
the Atonement. 

In order to save human nature, which was dead in body 
and soul, God must become incarnate in body and soul.® So 
Anselm perceives in the bread and wine the body and soul of 
Christ. The blood is the seat of the soul,’ according to the 
Old Testament idea. To complete his description of the 
atoning process, he describes the water which is mingled with 
the wine as the equivalent of the water which flowed from 
the side of Christ, and this, in turn, symbolises Baptism and 
its effects.§

an entirely original interpretation. The writings of Guibert

eleventh and twelfth centuries, when the practical implications

subject with considerable independence of attitude, and always 
with freshness in expression and novelty in illustration.

CHAPTER XXI 
ALGER OF LIEGE TO GREGORY OF BERGAMO 


ALGER was scolasticus of Liege until 1121, when he joined the 
community at Cluny, and died there before 1128. He wrote 
a lengthy work, the De Sacramentis Corporis et Sanguinis 
Domini,+ in three books, which ranks with the treatise of 
Guitmund in Catholic estimation. Alger follows Guitmund in 
the plan of his work and in method of treatment, although on 
some points he arrives at more definite conclusions than the 
earlier writer. Peter the Venerable, the ninth Abbot of Cluny, 
who died in 1156, maintained that Alger discussed the doctrine 
better, more fully, and more perfectly than his predecessors 
Lanfranc and Guitmund.? This praise is too fulsome, 
especially as the influence of Guitmund upon Alger’s book 
appears in every part of the work. Like Guitmund, he begins 
by stating that he proposes to deal with current heresies, and 
mentions six types of heretical teaching. Some say that the 
bread and wine are not changed, and that the Eucharist is only 
a sacrament like Baptism or the Chrism, that it is not the true 
body of Christ, and can only be so called figuratively.4 Others 
say that Christ was impanated in the bread, as He was 
personally incarnate in the flesh.® Others, making use of the 
Adoptian heresy, describe a change not into flesh and blood, 
but into that of ‘ any son of man holy and acceptable to God,’ 
not into the flesh and blood of Christ.6 Others say that the 
change cannot be effected by the consecration of an unworthy 
priest.’ Others, again, who believe in the change, allege that
