objections are discussed in detail throughout the work, but 
Alger’s chief aim in writing was the refutation of Berengar. 
He reminds his readers that at the Council of Rome in 1059 
Berengar confessed his belief in the real presence of the body 
of Christ before Pope Nicholas and the hundred and thirteen 
bishops,’ and he quotes the oath in full.* 

Alger belongs to the school of orthodox dialectic writers. 
He uses the syllogism,® and his method includes statement, 
demonstration, and proof. But he is ready to abandon the 
assistance of dialectics when it conflicts with orthodox opinion,® 
and he criticises the conclusions of the dialecticians freely.’ 
With Anselm of Canterbury and other contemporaries, he 
begins with a broad theological view of his subject, and seeks 
to relate it with the whole doctrine of the Incarnation. He 
treats the Eucharist from the standpoint of theology and is not 
content with the defence of mere dogma. In this way he 
supplements the teaching of Guitmund, and perhaps for this 
reason his work impressed the Abbot of Cluny more than that 
of Lanfranc or Guitmund. The Eucharist is part of the great 
process of reconciliation with God, effected by the Incarnation 
and Atonement.’ In the Eucharist the Church is united and 
made concorporate with the body of Christ, who restored 
fallen man by uniting human nature with Himself through 
the assumption of flesh at the Incarnation.#® We receive His 
flesh and blood beneath a mystery, and by this means we are 
one with Him. As the Father is in Him, and He is in us, the

Alger’s theory of the sacramental process or change of the 
substance of the elements into the substance of flesh and 
blood was in harmony with the current theory of Transub- 
stantiation.? He states the theory in the form of a syllogism. 
Whatever is changed into another thing surrenders either 
its accidence or substance. When the bread and wine are 
changed into the body and blood of Christ all the accidents 
remain, therefore the substance of bread and wine ceases to 
be.* ‘The general premise that everything contains the nature 
and truth of those things from which it is prepared does not 
apply to the sacrament, which does not contain the truth and 
nature of those things from which it is prepared, since it 
contains truly and naturally the body and blood of Christ, and 
truly and naturally the form of its original elements.2 Then 
he confuses the categories of spiritual and material. A visible 
body of Christ is not phantasmal. If the sacrament of Christ 
is prepared from a phantasy and truth, the preparation of the 
sacrament is neutralised, for no preparation can be effected 
from something and from nothing.6 ‘The dialecticians say that 
if the substance of bread and wine is changed into that of the 
body of Christ, its qualities, such as colour and flavour, will 
not be those of bread, for they must remain fundamentally 
with the substance of the bread. But this result is achieved 
in the sacrament by a miracle. God causes the accidental 
qualities to exist in the sacrament in themselves, a condition

Alger frequently defines ‘sacrament’ in Augustinian 
terms,* but draws a contrast between ‘sacrament’ and 
‘mystery.’ A sacrament is a visible sign signifying something. 
A mystery is something hidden, which is signified by the 
sacrament. So the mystery is something hiding and hidden, 
and a sacrament is a thing at once signifying and signified.® 
A sacrament is not a description merely of the former, but of 
both—of the sign, and the thing signified,® since the term * body 
of Christ’ is used both of the sacrament and of its content.’

If the Berengarian criticism drove the orthodox writers to 
make a thorough examination of the implications of Augustine’s 
great distinction between ‘sacramentum’ and ‘res,’ so also 
Berengar influenced their treatment of symbolism. When Alger 
says that the priest in the Canon describes the sacraments as 
the body of Christ, he refers to their form which is a similitude 
or figure of the body.2 When Christ is called both truth and 
figure, is the statement equivalent to saying that a man is body 
and soul? Verbally the comparison may stand, but the meaning 
is different. ‘Truth and figure are not made personally one in 
Christ, but the body of Christ is called truth and figure, as 
one can speak of the truth and the portrait of a man, although 
the figure—bread—is more consonant with the truth of the 
body of Christ than a picture with a man, for it not only 
represents it as a sacrament, but contains it, and is sub- 
stantially converted into it.t Yet the symbolism must be 
confined to the accidence of the bread and wine—beyond that 
point the realists would not advance towards Berengar—the 
actuality of the body was always present in the substance.° 
In common with other orthodox writers he sees in the 
ritual features of the sacrament a symbolism of the Passion,® 
yet this is rather a symbolism of action’ than of feature.

About 1130 Abbaud, abbot of an unknown monastery, 
devoted a short treatise to the question of the fraction of the 
eucharistic body.? Geiselmann 3 sees in his work the influence 
of Humbert’s formula, but the problem was bound to arise 
in an era when different implications of realist doctrine in- 
creasingly attracted attention. His theory of the fraction is 
based upon the proceedings and words of institution. Through 
the medium of benediction the Lord made the bread His body. 
It was His own body which He broke and gave to the disciples, 
a process rendered possible by the fact that His body already 
existed in an immortal condition. The fraction in the 
Eucharist does not injure the integrity of Christ’s body which 
is already in heaven. Indeed the antinomy is solved because 
the body of Christ is both palpable and yet spiritual. If it 
came forth from the closed womb of the Virgin, it could also 
pass through closed doors.’ Although this body is divided 
into many parts and is consumed by men, yet it remains 
always whole.® 

If in the sight of God a thousand years are as one day, 
so with Him a thousand places are as one place. He who is 
always wholly present and who is everywhere, cannot come 
within the category of spatial extension. Local absence does 
not cause Him to be absent, ‘ local length ’ does not lengthen

His final argument embodies, as Geiselmann shows, the 
Berengarian contention that the accidence cannot be separated 
from the substance. Abbaud says that as the whiteness or 
rotundity cannot be separated from the body of Christ, so the 
eucharistic elements themselves are not broken, save so far as 
the real body is broken. His argument was directed against 
those who alleged that the fraction took place only in the 
accidence. He insists that the body itself is actually broken. 
He declines to discuss further this aspect of the problem, but 
he clearly sees that the argument led to the conclusion that 
the body of Christ is multiple. 

The fluid condition of orthodox teaching during this era

(d. 1139-40). Under his theory the conclusion of Abbaud would 
be impossible, since Stephen refused to admit a change of the 
elements into the divine nature. ‘They change, said he, into 
a human substance.®

Like Alger and Abbaud, Hildebert attempts to remove the 
antinomy between the location of Christ in heaven and His 
presence on earthly altars—a favourite problem in the first 
half of the twelfth century. He bases his teaching on the 
Incarnation, and illustrates it with a number of felicitous 
antitheses. As the divinity of Christ first came to us from the 
heavens, so now from thence comes His humanity. ‘The 
Incarnation did not separate Him from His heavenly divinity, 
so the Eucharist does not separate Him from His heavenly 
humanity. As the divinity came through His humanity, so 
the human sacramental presence comes through His divinity. 
God came at the Incarnation manifestly or perceptibly through 
the humanity, and now the glorified humanity comes hiddenly 
(occulte) or imperceptibly through the divinity.®

present on different altars, it is not differentiated in time or 
place, it is wholly present on each altar.’ Hildebert tries to

In the eleventh and twelfth centuries the discussion on 
the eucharistic question was conducted chiefly by French and 
Norman writers, who were the leaders of intellectual as well 
as practical reform. But gradually the area of activity was 
widened. The Tractatus de Veritate Corporis Christt,’° an ex- 
tensive work written by Gregory, Bishop of Bergamo, who 
was killed in 1146, belongs, in some important matters, to 
an earlier stage of the controversy. His definition of the 
eucharistic body, and his theory of the change, are sometimes 
expressed in the language of the earlier period. He expounds 
a threefold significance of the sacrament, which resembles the 
teaching of Guibert of Nogent, and his book was written to 
meet the revival of Berengarianism which took place during 
this epoch.1! A sign of the wider theological outlook of the 
twelfth century is to be seen in the fact that he begins with 
a statement of the doctrine of God.” Dialectics find no place

one with the Father. The conception of communion as the 
effective principle of union with God recalls the teaching of 
Herbert of Losinga.

In his description of the eucharistic process Gregory uses 
the language of Ambrose, Lanfranc, and Guitmund alike. 
The bread is transformed 1 into the true body of Christ, it is 
converted into its essence,” the bread and wine are substan- 
tially ? converted. He examines seriatim the terms ‘ species,’ 
‘mystery,’ ‘sacrament,’ and ‘figure,’* and concludes with the 
realist inversion of symbolism that the bread and wine are 
present only in similitude ° or appearance.® 

We have seen that Gregory makes use of the Ignatian 
doctrine of the ¢dapyaxov or medicine of the soul, which im- 
plants the principle of eternal life.’ So also he introduces the 
Greek conception of mystery derived from pvorns, or the Latin 
secretus, meaning one who is initiated into holy things. The 
ovppvorat or ‘ consacerdotes,’ or ‘ consecretales,’ are they who 
are acquainted with the secret thing. ‘The secret or hidden 
thing is the mystery. He also describes the more general 
usage of the term ‘ mystery,’ signifying the sacrament which 
represents the divine Passion,® and also our union with Christ 
through the mystical sacrament.1° 

Gregory classifies three principal sacraments—Baptism, 
Confirmation, and the Eucharist ,—and four lesser sacraments— 
ordination, marriage, the sacraments of Scripture, and the 
oath 14—a description which shows that the era of the 
systematists was near. A sacrament is, as the Greeks say, 
something other than that which is seen, a sacred thing apart 
from that which the senses perceive.!? But the term has a wider 
range. In every sacrament three things are to be observed : 
the consecrated species or ‘ thing which is the sacrament ’ ; 4

CHAPTER XXII 
THE SYSTEMATISTS AND THE FOURTH LATERAN COUNCIL 


Towarps the middle of the twelfth century a new era in 
medieval religious thought begins with the age of the 
systematists. The great teachers of western Europe embody 
their eucharistic teaching in the ‘Sententiae’ or ‘Summae,’ 
which displaced the formal treatises on specific topics of 
the pre-scholastic era. If we may accept the conclusion of 
Bliemetzrieder } that Anselm of Laon was the author of the 
Sententiae Divine Pagine, then the new era begins at the 
commencement of the twelfth century, for Anselm died in 
1117. But it is possible that the Sententiae were compiled by 
one of his pupils.” 

This period covered the first phase of the systematisation 
of Church doctrine, and was separated by the Lateran Council 
of 1215 from the age of Thomas of Aquinas, who carried the 
work of the Summarists to the highest pitch of its develop- 
ment. The influence of Berengar continued to haunt the 
minds of orthodox writers. Rupert of Deutz (d. 1135), in 
the De Divinis Officits, a systematic treatise on theology 
and religious practice and ceremony, approaches closely to

Berengar’s teaching that the sacramental process does not 
involve the destruction of the substance of bread and wine. 
There are two substances in the sacrifice—one divine, the other 
earthly. ‘The earthly substance can be seen corporally and 
locally. ‘The divine substance is the invisible Word, ‘ which 
in the beginning was God, and was with God.’ The Word 
which had accepted human nature, and which remained in the 
flesh, took the substance of bread and wine, and joined the 
bread with His flesh, and the wine with His blood.! This 
theory of impanation was severely criticised by William of 
S. Thierry (d. 1153), who warned Rupert that it could be 
interpreted as Berengarianism.? 

In the middle of the century Folmar, Provost of Triefenstein, 
corresponded with Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg, and gave 
expression to the views of Berengar and Ratramn.® Similar 
opinions were held by a clerk named Gerland, and were 
refuted by Hugh Metellus, a Canon Regular. Abelard 
(1079-1142) admitted that the controversy over the problem 
whether the eucharistic bread was only a figure of the body, 
or was in substance actual flesh, was not closed,® and Abelard 
was described by Walter of S. Victor as another Berengar.® 
Moreover, Hugh Metellus is reported to have attributed to 
him teaching which was an echo of Berengar’s doctrine. 
Peter Lombard (d.1160) challenged the formula submitted 
to Berengar by Humbert in 1059. ‘The formula had said that 
the actual body of Christ was broken by the hands of the 
priest and torn by the teeth of the faithful. ‘To this Peter 
refused to assent. Only the accidents are broken and consumed,

This work answers some of the Berenianan criticisms. 
When the priest Coo the words ‘ Hoc est corpus 
meum, Hic est sanguis meus,’ the bread and wine are changed 
(convertentur) into the flesh and blood. One substance was 
changed into another in Old Testament times, and Christ 
changed water into wine, so why could He not change (mutare) 
bread into flesh.? It is less difficult to change something into 
another thing than to create something from nothing. The 
process of the change is miraculous.? Beneath each species of 
bread and wine the body and blood of Christ are consecrated.4 
Creation takes place when a natural object is constituted ; 
sanctification occurs when it is consecrated; and a thing is 
rendered life-giving when it is transubstantiated.®° Creation 
is a primordial cause, consecration is a sacramental cause, 
and vivification takes place when the bread and wine pass 
over into flesh and blood. ‘Through the blessing of Christ 
the bread is transubstantiated into flesh, and the wine is 
transubstantiated into blood.’

human altars as an incomprehensible sacrament. The Logos

CHAPTER XXIII 
BERENGAR AND THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND 


WE have seen that the teaching of Ratramn was widely spread 
in England during the latter part of the tenth and beginning 
of the eleventh centuries, through the medium of A#lfric’s 
writings. A solid foundation had been laid for the reform of 
English sacramental doctrine if the work of Lanfranc had not 
prevented the dissemination of Berengar’s teaching in England 
during his pontificate. Lanfranc’s influence cut across the 
natural development of English thought, for the popularisation 
of Ratramnian doctrine by Ailfric represented an accommoda- 
tion to English ideas, as well as an effort to reform dogma in 
circles where Radbertianism had taken root. Ifthe Continental 
Reformation of the sixteenth century embodies a return to 
Augustine, the Anglican Reformation constituted a return to 
the simpler and more robust conceptions of the Anglo-Saxon 
Church, and both movements took up the strands of doctrine 
at points where they had been deflected from the true and 
natural course of development. 

No trace of Berengar’s teaching can be found in the writings 
of English theologians until the fourteenth century, partly 
because of the predominating influence of Lanfranc’s De 
Corpore et Sanguine Domini, and of the decree of the Fourth 
Lateran Council, and partly because of the general destruction 
of Berengar’s works. The first appreciative tribute to Berengar 
in England appeared in the De Eucharistia Tractatus Major } 
of Wyclif (d. 1384). Berengar’s teaching undoubtedly in- 
fluenced Wyclif towards a denial of the doctrine of Transub- 
stantiation.2. The substance of the bread and wine remains

As his sacramental ideas matured Wyclif approximated 
more and more closely to Berengar’s teaching on the nature 
of the sacrament. By virtue of the words of Christ the bread 
has the name of the body of Christ.2 The consecrated elements 
are an effectual sign of the Lord’s body. In the De 
Eucharistia he deals specifically with Berengar’s teaching. 
In the ‘ Confession’ of 1059 Berengar could only interpret the 
terms ‘body’ and ‘blood’ figuratively and tropically,® for 
neither the bread nor its accidence can form the body of 
Christ.6 A distinction must be drawn between what is literal 
and what is figurative,’ and he condemns the popular belief 
that the sacramental sign of the body of Christ is actually 
Christ Himself as faithless and blasphemous, but contends 
that the clergy and bishops are involved in it.8

difficulty made worse by his own disinclination to abandon 
realist terminology. He alleges that Berengar corrected his 
original opinion and admitted that the bread and wine are 
both sacrament and the body and blood of Christ.® Berengar’s 
‘Confession ’ must be rightly understood, and when properly 
read it has the authority of the Scriptures and the Fathers 1° 
and is the orthodox faith of the Church; it would have been 
accepted in Wyclif’s own day, although it was officially 
condemned in Berengar’s time.1! Yet the attitude of the 
authorities in that era should not be questioned, otherwise the 
whole fabric of faith would come under suspicion.” 

Wyclif, like Berengar, was anxious to make some con- 
cession to realist terminology—although he went much farther 
in the direction of a realist definition of the sacrament than the

eleventh-century reformer. With Berengar he clearly affirms 
that if the bread and wine are a sacrament and the body and 
blood of Christ, they have that character in sign not in essence.} 
In one passage he gives open expression to the subjective 
dynamic symbolism of Berengar. ‘The aim of the sacrament 
is the indwelling of Christ in the soul, so that a layman who 
recalls to mind the body of Christ in heaven has acquired more 
effectually the presence of the body of Christ than the conse- 
crating priest, and equally really, though in a different mode.” 

Wyclif criticised an impanationist interpretation of the 
formula of 1059, current in his own day, which stated that the 
species of the bread and wine were neither sacrament nor body 
of Christ, but contained the body of Christ beneath them.’ 
He describes the De Corpore et Sanguine Domini of Lanfranc 
as ‘ineffective invective,’* and charges Lanfranc with mis- 
representing Berengar’s argument,® and declines the necessity 
of a further discussion of Lanfranc’s work on the ground that 
it refers to Berengar’s opinions before 1059, and so was not 
relevant. In spite of the futility of this contention, his attitude 
to Lanfranc’s teaching at least proves that whatever view 
Wyclif held on the doctrine of the real presence, it was not 
that of the great orthodox writers of the Church, a conclusion 
which is the more necessary when it is recollected that he 
declined to interpret the presence ‘ substantialiter’ in the 
language of Guitmund. 

Little or no influence has been exerted by Wyclif upon 
the development of eucharistic doctrine in later times. The 
Hussite movement, which owed much to Wyclif’s teaching in 
other fields of doctrine, retained the dogma of 'Transubstantia- 
tion, and there is no record of any important effect produced 
by Wyclif upon the sacramental doctrine of the English 
Reformers.

Ridley’s theory of symbolism springs from the Augustinian 
principle that a sacrament must have the similitude or likeness 
of the thing of which it is a sacrament. He emphasises its 
dynamic character by making use of the three traditional 
principles of value, union, and faith. ‘ This similitude in the 
sacrament of the Lord’s Supper is taken in three manner of 
ways.’ It ‘nourishes ’—and Bertram is again quoted—it 
unites and joins many in one, and causes those who by faith 
make the right use of the sacrament to become the body of 
Christ. The designation ‘body and blood’ is ‘ figurative 
speech,’ as the Fathers declare, and ‘ most plainly Bertram.’ * 
The natural substance of bread and wine is the true natural 
substance of the holy sacrament of the blessed body and blood.°® 

To the proposition that ‘after the consecration there 
remaineth no substance of bread and wine, neither any other 
substance than the substance of God and man,’ Ridley replied: 
“We may no more believe the bread to be transubstantiated 
into the body of Christ than wine into His blood.’ ® He closed 
his defence with a glowing tribute to Ratramn : ‘ This treatise 
whosoever shall read and weigh, considering the time of the 
writer, his learning, godliness of life, the allegations of the 
ancient fathers, and his manifold and most guarded arguments, 
I cannot (doubtless) but much marvel, if he have any fear of 
God at all, how he can, with good conscience, speak against 
him in the matter of the sacrament. This Bertram was the 
first that brought me from the common error of the Romish 
Church, and caused me to search more diligently both the 
Scriptures and the writings of the old ecclesiastical fathers in 
this matter.’ ”

At his formal degradation at Oxford on October 15, 1555, 
the day before he was martyred, ‘in the town ditch ’ opposite 
Balliol College, Ridley urged Brookes, the Bishop of Gloucester 
and Master of Balliol, to ‘read and peruse the little book 
of Bertram’s doings concerning the sacrament.’1 Hooper, 
Bishop of Gloucester, who went to the fire in the same year, 
described Berengar as ‘a good and godly man .. . who 
taught and wrote that the corporal presence of Christ’s body 
could not be in the sacrament. . . . Against the which error 
one John Scot and one Bertram wrote a book of the same 
matter. ... .’ But he over-emphasises the part played by 
Lanfranc in Berengar’s condemnation.’ 

Some twenty years earlier the reactionary Bishop Fisher 
of Rochester criticised severely Berengar’s teaching, and 
compared it with that of Ccolampadius.*? He notes that 
Berengar was compelled to accept the orthodox belief by 
Nicholas II in 1059, and quotes the Confession,* a detail to 
which Cranmer drew attention in 1550, although Cranmer 
condemned the doctrine of the ‘ sensible’ presence of Christ 
maintained by the oath, and pointed out that Berengar ‘ was 
constrained ’ to make the confession.® John Sutton, Canon of 
Worcester and Lincoln (1565-1629), in his Godly Meditation 
on the most Holy Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper (1630), 
refers to the Berengarian controversy, but declines to discuss 
it.6 ‘The French writer Rotier attacked Berengar’s teaching,

Among the Caroline divines, John Cosin, Bishop of Durham 
(1660-72), paid a tribute to Ratramn, John the Scot, and 
Berengar.2 Cosin’s book was probably the first publication in 
English to estimate favourably the teaching of Berengar.2 He 
says that Berengar 


stood up valiantly in defence of that which 170 (sic) years before, 
was delivered out of God’s Word and the holy Fathers, in France 
by Bertram, and John Erigena, and by others elsewhere, against 
those who taught that in the Eucharist’ neither Bread nor Wine 
remained after the Consecration. Yet he did not either believe 
or teach (as many falsely and shamelessly have imputed to him) 
that nothing more is received in the Lord’s Supper, but bare Signs 
only, or meer Bread and Wine; but he believed and openly pro- 
fest, as S. Austin and other faithful Doctors of the Church had 
taught out of God’s Word, that in this Mystery, the souls of the 
faithful are truly fed by the true Body and Blood of Christ to life 
eternal. Nevertheless it was neither in his mind nor his doctrine, 
that the substance of the Bread and Wine is reduced to nothing, 
or changed into the substance of the natural Body of Christ or (as 
some of them would have the Church believe) that Christ himself 
comes down carnally from heaven.‘ 


The vague realism which Cosin sees in Berengar’s teaching 
is counterbalanced by another passage in which the Bishop of 
Durham connects Berengar’s theory with Augustinian sym- 
bolism : ‘ He did not therefore by this his Doctrine exclude 
the Body of Christ from the Sacrament, but in its right 
administration he joyned together the thing signified with 
the sacred Sign, and taught that the Body of Christ was not 
eaten with the mouth in a carnal way, but with the Mind 
Soul and Spirit.’ § 

Whether a backward or forward view be taken from the 
eleventh century, the position of Berengar will be found to 
be not that of an isolated heretic in the stream of tradition. 
Springing from the source of Augustine’s teaching, gathering 
force and momentum during the two preceding centuries, 
continuing with less impulse, indeed, during the twelfth 

* Cf. Works, i. 193, 458, 546, 563, 577 (J. Ayre, Parker Society, 1845). 


* A History of Popish Transubstantiation (1676), pp. 84, 90 fi., 129.

century, but always creating an impression, coming into notice 
again in the era preceding the Reformation,! the eucharistic 
teaching of Berengar formed a peak in a long line of develop- 
ment. ‘l’o-day there are not wanting signs that his theory of 
dynamic-symbolism, expressed not in the terms of virtue or 
effectiveness, but of value,? will come again into its own. 
The medieval theory of Transubstantiation has long been 
abandoned by philosophic thought, and the doctrine of 
realism, of a presence in or with the consecrated elements is 
definitely losing ground among Catholic thinkers.2 Modern 
thought is moving towards a new interpretation of symbolism. 
In the doctrine of Berengar, derived philosophically from 
Neo-Platonism, theologically from Augustine, a foundation 
can be found upon which to create a new interpretation of 
eucharistic symbolism, centring round the Berengarian con- 
ception of the religious value or effect—the dynamic influence 
of the consecrated symbol upon the believing communicant. 
So the great Reformation doctrine of Faith, which is also being 
re-emphasised,* will be given its true function in sacramental 
doctrine.
